articles.title: DICT welcomes Ombudsman probe into alleged 'ghost internet' scheme
articles.summary: The Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT) on Sunday welcomed the Office of the Ombudsman"s probe into an alleged “ghost internet” scheme involving government IT systems,…

blocks.text: Published September 20, 2026 9:10pm

The Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT) on Sunday welcomed the Office of the Ombudsman’s probe into an alleged “ghost internet” scheme involving government IT systems, saying it is ready to provide the necessary records and data for the investigation.
In a statement, the DICT said it does not tolerate corruption or non-performing contracts and is ensuring that its services are properly delivered.
The agency said it has implemented safeguards, including “stricter service level agreement enforcement, enhanced contract management, regular internal audits, and stronger performance validation.”
“The DICT has likewise introduced procurement reforms that have increased transparency and lowered connectivity costs,” the agency said.

“Service components are now more clearly itemized and evaluated instead of being priced through bundled arrangements, providing greater visibility into costs and better value for public funds,” it added.
Under the program, private contractors oversee the deployment of infrastructure, while the DICT conducts performance monitoring to ensure the services are operating properly.
The DICT said reported non-performing or inactive sites are promptly subjected to technical audits and contractual penalties.
Free Wi-Fi services
The agency also highlighted the upgrade of its Network Monitoring System to Version 2, which it said provides real-time nationwide visibility over all Free Wi-Fi sites, including regional projects.
The DICT said the upgraded system allows it to monitor access points, track service disruptions, validate provider performance, and use actual network data for contract and payment verification.
Ombudsman probe
The DICT said it has not yet received formal notice from the Office of the Ombudsman but welcomed any inquiry.
“Although no formal notice has been received from the Office of the Ombudsman to date, the DICT proactively welcomes the inquiry,” the agency said.
“With full commitment to transparency, it stands ready to provide all necessary assistance, records, and system data to support any investigation,” it added.
Earlier this week, the Ombudsman launched an investigation into an alleged “ghost internet” scheme involving government IT systems that were reportedly rigged with substandard or fake software.

articles.title: UK startup snares $20m to recreate gigs with ‘hyper-realistic’ digital avatars
articles.summary:
Unit1 hopes to offer cheaper version of shows such as Abba Voyage, showcasing living and dead artists in any venue

The former chief executive of Andrew Lloyd Webber’s entertainment group has…

blocks.text: The former chief executive of Andrew Lloyd Webber’s entertainment group has obtained a near-£15m investment for his UK music tech startup that hopes to recreate classic concerts by manifesting musicians as digital avatars.

Unit1 was set up last year by Barney Wragg, an entertainment executive who ran Lord Lloyd-Webber’s Cats-to-Evita empire for five years from late 2011. It has secured the $20m in funding from a group of investors, including tech backer Balderton Capital through its partner Daniel Waterhouse, who made early investments in Spotify.

The company hopes to stage concerts fronted by the “hyper realistic” digital avatars of living artists who are no longer touring and by recreating existing performances from dead musicians. In the latter case, it will develop the avatars through a mixture of archive footage and hiring actors and musicians who either look or play like the departed star, before blending the footage together.

blocks.caption: Barney Wragg, the founder of Unit1, ran Andrew Lloyd Webber’s empire for five years. Photograph: Unit1

blocks.text: Unit1 has tested the technology with Scottish singer-songwriter and musician KT Tunstall, who worked with Wragg during a stint at the music company EMI. In the pilot, Tunstall was filmed in a London studio by motion capture cameras as she recreated a two-decade-old performance on Later… with Jools Holland, using the avatar to update her features to the way she looks now.

The music industry has long flirted with the idea of creating avatars of its biggest stars, such as the 2012 hologram projection of the late rapper Tupac Shakur alongside Snoop Dogg and Dr Dre at Coachella festival.
The concept found mainstream success with the 2022 launch of Abba Voyage, a lucrative virtual concert with avatars of the Swedish pop group, which runs in a purpose-built venue in east London.

Unit1 hopes to offer a cut-price version of the Abba Voyage experience, by providing artists, venues, their rights holders and promoters with a route to digital shows without needing a dedicated space. The setup also means a show could in theory tour in several countries simultaneously.
The business will invest the fresh funds into research and development, as well as securing intellectual property and licensing deals with artists and their estates.

Unit1’s aim is to stage shows with real musicians playing live instruments on stage alongside digital performers. The audience will view a high-definition LED screen, which is combined with extra lights, sound and props to give them the illusion they are watching a fully human performance.

“For the audience member in the room it is seamless between the digital and the physical room, immersing them,” Wragg told the Guardian. “It’s a teleportation of an audience member to a time and place.”

However, some fans have expressed unease about dead musicians being digitally resurrected. Earlier this year, a plan to create a lifesize AI-powered avatar of the late Black Sabbath frontman Ozzy Osbourne was criticised as being disrespectful and in poor taste by some fans.

blocks.caption: Fans of the late Ozzy Osbourne, pictured on a mural near Aston Villa’s football ground, did not approve of plans to resurrect the musician in digital form. Photograph: Nigel French/PA

blocks.text: Wragg said that, in most cases, the startup was “dealing with family members of estates to create something which is well documented and understood – extremely well-known concerts or live recordings. We are mindful that you do not want to be distasteful.”

He was tight-lipped on which classic concerts Unit1 could recreate. He has previously said he wished he could have seen various well-known performances, including Queen at Live Aid, the Beatles’ performances at the Cavern Club and Jimi Hendrix at Woodstock.

Balderton – which has also backed music rights firm Kobalt and fintech Revolut – was joined in the funding round by its existing investors, including the venture capital firm Mercuri and Paul McGuinness, the Irish music executive who managed U2 from the late 1970s until 2013.

articles.title: Viral drone flight in Mindoro linked to alleged plan to help Korean inmate escape Bilibid
articles.summary: A young Filipino man became the center of an unusual story after a video showed him being lifted into the air by a large drone at a port in Sablayan, Mindoro in March.

blocks.text: A young Filipino man became the center of an unusual story after a video showed him being lifted into the air by a large drone at a port in Sablayan, Occidental Mindoro in March.

The video initially appeared to show a man trying out a powerful drone for fun. Months later, however, the footage was linked to an alleged plan to help a Korean inmate escape from the Sablayan Prison and Penal Farm (SPPF) based in Mindoro.

According to “Kapuso Mo, Jessica Soho,” a South Korean television network reported that the flight was supposedly a test run for the planned escape of Korean inmate Park Wang-yeol. The report also identified the Filipino man in the viral video as an alleged accomplice.
The man, identified as NJ, denied having any involvement in the alleged plan.
‘Trip-trip lang’
NJ said that he and his friends were at the port to swim when they saw a Korean tourist flying a large drone.
He said they were impressed by the size of the drone and were told that it could carry a person weighing up to 75 kilograms. NJ then volunteered to ride it.
“Nag-voluntary na po ako sasakay at tatalon po ako sa dagat,” he said.
[I voluntarily decided to get on and jump into the sea.]
He said the Korean tourist taught him how to attach himself to the drone and told him not to let go or move too much. The drone then lifted him above the water before he eventually fell into the sea.
“Trip-trip lang po para pakita sa amin sa tropa namin kung kaya o hindi,” he said.
[It was just for fun to show our group of friends whether we could do it or not.]
Iris, one of the people who witnessed the incident, also recorded the flight. He said they were surprised that the drone was actually able to lift a person and carry him over the sea.

NJ said he did not know the Korean man personally and only encountered him while the latter was staying at a hotel in the area. He said he was surprised when the video later became part of reports in South Korea linking him to an alleged escape plan.
“Ako pa ‘yung napagbintangan na kasabwat doon kahit wala naman akong kaalam-alam,” he said.
[I was accused of being an accomplice, even though I had no idea about it whatsoever.]
NJ said that if the flight was indeed a test for an escape plan, he may have unknowingly been used for it, maintaining that he was not part of any plan to help Park escape.
“Kung kasabwat po ako dun, edi sana hinuli na ako,” he said, adding that his experience also taught him to be more careful about people he encounters.
[If I were an accomplice, then I should have been arrested already.]
“Alamin po muna kung sino ‘yung tao o kung sino ‘yung mga nakasalamuha mo para malaman mo kung masama ba o mabuti ‘yung tao na ‘yun.”
[Find out first who the person is or who they hang out with, so you can know whether that person is bad or good.]
Who is Park Wang-yeol?

Park Wang-yeol was detained at the New Bilibid Prison after his arrest in 2016 in connection with the deaths of three fellow Koreans whose bodies were reportedly found in a sugarcane field in Pampanga.
Park was also previously reported to have escaped from detention.
In 2017, he and another Korean man reportedly opened a hole in the ceiling and roof of their cell at Camp Bagong Diwa.

In 2019, he escaped through a ventilation window in a restroom. The Pampanga provincial government later offered a P300,000 reward for information leading to his capture. He was arrested again in Calamba, Laguna in 2020.
After
In 2022, Park was sentenced to 60 years in prison. During his detention, he tried to escape twice before being transferred to the Sablayan Prison and Penal Farm.
The South Korean report later linked him to an alleged plan to escape using a drone. The report claimed that around US$74,000, or more than P4 million, was spent on the plot.
Authorities looking into the reported escape plot
The Sablayan Municipal Police Station said it had received information about a possible attempt to help Park escape and coordinated with the Bureau of Corrections.
Police said they were still working to establish the identities and whereabouts of the people allegedly involved in the scheme.
Park was temporarily brought to South Korea in March to face a drug-related case.
The Bureau of Corrections, meanwhile, said that even if a drone escape plot existed, carrying it out from prisons would be difficult.

In a statement, Bureau of Corrections (BuCor) Director General Gregorio Pio Catapang Jr. (Ret.) said drones capable of carrying a person would produce significant noise that could be heard by prison personnel. It also noted that the prison is a no-fly zone and has watchtowers operating 24/7.
Hotel confirms Korean guest

The management of the hotel where the Korean individual reportedly stayed declined an interview but confirmed to the “Kapuso Mo, Jessica Soho” team that they had a Korean guest who introduced himself as “Mr. Kim.”
The hotel said the guest stayed for 18 days and did not pay for his accommodations.
“Julia”, not the real name of the sister of the person who uploaded the viral video, also said the Korean man returned several times after the video was posted and went looking for her sibling.
She said she could not confirm whether the person involved was the same Korean man mentioned in the reports because she had not personally met him.
The family also expressed concern about their safety and hoped authorities would identify the drone operator.

articles.title: World leaders return to UN amid wars in Middle East and Ukraine
articles.summary: Compounding the crisis of morale and finance are questions about the next leader of the 80-year-old organization

blocks.text: UN. File photo shows US President Donald Trump addressing the 80th United Nations General Assembly at UN headquarters in New York City, US on September 23, 2025.
Compounding the crisis of morale and finance are questions about the next leader of the 80-year-old organization

items: World leaders gather at the UN General Assembly to discuss conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine, as well as the risks of artificial intelligence.

The UN faces challenges regarding its relevance and leadership, with Secretary-General Antonio Guterres' term ending in 2026 and ongoing financial issues, including the US's significant debt to the organization.
Key topics include the escalation of the US-Israeli conflict with Iran, stalled peace talks, and the impact of the Ukraine war on global food security and energy prices.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

Nearly 130 heads of state meet with the post-World War II order under strain and with the UN itself struggling to remain relevant and weathering attacks from Trump, who has slashed America’s contributions and withdrawn from dozens of UN bodies.

Chinese leader Xi Jinping, who last addressed the diplomatic jamboree via video in 2021, will skip New York in favor of one-on-one talks with Trump in Washington on Thursday, fueling debate about the UN’s relevance in addressing global crises.

Compounding the crisis of morale and finance are questions about the next leader of the 80-year-old organization: Secretary-General Antonio Guterres completes his term at the end of 2026, with no clear frontrunner in the race to replace him.
The 15-member UN Security Council may hold high-level meetings on Ukraine, AI and the Middle East, including talks with Arab leaders, diplomats said.

More than a year into Trump’s second term, “we would no longer say that the UN is in freefall, but we would say that it’s stuck in an open-ended crisis,” said Richard Gowan of the International Crisis Group.
“The UN may not be in emergency care like it was last year, but it seems to be trapped in a trauma center for the foreseeable future,” Gowan said.

The US avoided losing its vote at the assembly by paying $725 million in contributions to the regular budget this week, but it still owes the organization more than a billion dollars and makes ongoing demands for cuts and reforms.

The assembly meets shortly after several artificial intelligence industry leaders called for a coordinated slowdown of the development of the technology, warning that it could soon improve on its own and escape human control.

Guterres has said that AI will be a major topic, adding that countries pushing its frontiers should set up “common guardrails in order to avoid this race to the bottom that could lead one day to a gigantic disaster at the global level.”

The secretary-general has long proposed global governance of AI. In 2023, the UN created an advisory body on the technology, with members including tech executives, government officials and academics.

The warning has put Guterres at odds with Trump, who dismissed AI risks as a “hoax,” saying there is a “sick conspiracy” against it and that China would benefit from the doubt being cast on its development.

The Middle East will again be a focus of discussions, as the US-Israeli war on Iran continues to drive global inflation and destabilize the region. Recent gains by Houthi militants threaten shipping in ​the vital Bab el-Mandeb Strait and could further spike energy prices.

“It’s very difficult to have a military solution for that problem, and the experience of fighting in Yemen demonstrated how complicated it is to have successful interventions,” said Guterres, adding that the UN’s envoy on Yemen was making a “huge effort” to advance talks.
Peace talks remain stalled, however, as Iran and the US continue to exchange strikes and Trump threatens a major escalation of the war.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian is scheduled to address the assembly on Wednesday.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu – wanted by the International Criminal Court over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza that Israel denies – is to speak on Thursday.

Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas will for the second year running not be at the gathering in person. The US, a close Israeli ally, again denied him a visa. On Thursday, the General Assembly voted to allow Abbas to appear via video.
There is likely to be a high-level meeting on the conflict in Sudan on the sidelines, diplomats said, although a diplomatic breakthrough is unlikely.
Also on the agenda is Russia’s more than four-year-old war in Ukraine.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy and Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov will address the General Assembly. Zelenskiy will likely seek to shore up Ukraine’s position ahead of what is expected to be another tough winter, diplomats said.
The Security Council has been unable to take action to end the conflict because permanent member Russia holds a veto.

Trump has at times appeared frustrated that he has been unable to broker an end to the war, a goal he declared a priority when he began his second term in January last year. The US president spoke with his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin earlier this month, but it was unclear whether he plans to meet Zelenskiy in New York.
Guterres highlighted the impact the war was having on civilians but also on food security and energy prices.

“The effective blockade existing in the Black Sea is creating enormous problems that add to the problems generated by the Middle East crisis, and I think it would be very important to find a way to allow Ukrainian exports and Russian exports of food, fertilizers and energy to take place in a safe way through the Black Sea,” he said. – Rappler.com

articles.title: RNLI warns supporters their personal information may have been hacked
articles.summary:
Data raid comes amid targeting of lifeboat charity by far-right agitators who object to migrant boat rescues

Supporters of the Royal National Lifeboat Institution (

blocks.text: Supporters of the Royal National Lifeboat Institution (RNLI) have been warned that their personal information could have been stolen by hackers amid targeting of the charity by far-right agitators.

In a letter accompanying the autumn copy of its Lifeboat magazine, the charity warned members that their “name, contact details and records of interactions with the RNLI” could have been breached in the raid on a company it uses for customer relationship management.

The Telegraph, which first reported the story, said the RNLI told its supporters that Beacon CRM advised the RNLI to “assume that data held within its systems was taken” in a cyber-attack that affected about 1,500 charities in late July.

The letter added that there was no evidence to date that there had been misuse, sharing or publication of members’ personal data. But news of the breach comes as the RNLI has been targeted by people who object to the lifeboat charity going to the aid of people trying to get to the UK on small boats.
On Thursday, it emerged that a lifeboat station in Portsmouth, close to where far-right activists tried to stop asylum seekers landing, had been forced to temporarily shut.

On Sunday 6 September, activists tried to blockade the road leading to a landing spot where two RNLI crews helped bring a dinghy carrying 120 asylum seekers to Eastney in Portsmouth, a few hundred metres from the lifeboat station. Police officers were injured.

In the days after, lifeboat crew members were called traitors and protests took place against the charity, including at the RNLI headquarters in nearby Poole, where a museum telling the story of the RNLI closed temporarily.

Portsmouth lifeboat station took down its Facebook page and RNLI volunteers across the UK were told that they should consider not wearing the charity’s branded clothing if they felt it could put them at risk.
after newsletter promotion

The RNLI vice-president, Sir Robin Knox-Johnston, condemned the intimidation aimed at staff and volunteers, including “online and physical abuse”, as “frankly quite disgraceful”. Far-right protesters had called for people to stop donating to the charity, but it reported that it had subsequently experienced a “significant” boost to its fundraising.
It has stressed that only 1.2% of its rescue work last year – 109 callouts out of 9,058 – was to small boats in the Channel.

A report on the hack published by Beacon CRM earlier this month said there was no evidence that it was a targeted attack on Beacon or any specific customer, and that the cyber-attacker had contacted it “only to indicate they would be deleting any data they have exfiltrated and no copy would be retained, sold, or shared”.

A spokesperson for the RNLI said: “Beacon CRM works with many charities and organisations across the UK and Ireland, and while they cannot confirm exactly which records were accessed or downloaded, it advised all affected organisations, including the RNLI, to assume that data held within its systems was taken.
“At this stage, there is no evidence that information relating to RNLI supporters has been published, shared online or otherwise misused.”

articles.title: Agatha Wong shifts focus to med school after Asian Games swan song
articles.summary: Filipina wushu standout Agatha Wong delivers her Asian Games swan song, finishing 10th in the women's taijiquan and taijijian event

blocks.text: FORM. The Philippines' Agatha Chrystenzen Wong in action in the women's wushu taijiquan and taijijian event in the 2026 Asian Games.
Issei Kato/REUTERS
Filipina wushu standout Agatha Wong delivers her Asian Games swan song, finishing 10th in the women's taijiquan and taijijian event
MANILA, Philippines – Filipina wushu star Agatha Wong turns her attention to her other calling after seeing action at the Asian Games for the last time.
Wong delivered her Asian Games swan song, finishing 10th overall in the women’s taijiquan and taijijian event at the Aichi Prefectural Martial Arts Hall in Nagoya, Japan, on Sunday, September 20.

The 28-year-old stayed within reach of a podium finish after placing seventh in the taijiquan portion with 9.703 points before she bid her medal hopes goodbye as she landed 11th in the taijijian segment with 9.156 points for a total of 18.859.

China’s Tong Xin defended her throne with 19.553 points, Japan’s Shiho Saito (19.473) claimed silver, while Brunei’s Basma Lachkar and Singapore’s Zeanne Law tied for the bronze with identical 19.443 marks.
Although it was Wong’s lowest finish at the Asian Games after she won bronze in 2018 in Jakarta, Indonesia, and placed fifth in 2023 in Hangzhou, China, she remained proud of her effort.

“I think I could have done better but that’s how it is. I’m really happy that I did well in the first event. In the second event, I know that I did my best so that’s enough for me,” Wong told reporters in mix of Filipino and English.

Wong, a champion in the last five Southeast Asian Games as well as a silver and bronze medalist in the World Wushu Championships, earlier told Asian Games broadcaster Cignal that she will not be around for the next edition of the continental showpiece.
That may have something to do with her aspirations of becoming a doctor, as Wong has a lot of catching up to do with her studies at the University of the East Ramon Magsaysay Memorial Medical Center.

blocks.caption: Dual pursuit: Agatha Wong elegantly balances wushu, medical school

blocks.text: Wong, who started medical school in 2023, is now in her third year.

“I have to study already so I’m going to go back,” said Wong. “I’ll still continue training. I have competitions for next year so that’s going to be fun. But I’m already done for this year.” – Rappler.com

articles.title: Former president of Chile abandons UN secretary general candidacy
articles.summary:
Michelle Bachelet drops out after support collapsed in security council straw poll, leaving seven candidates in contest

Michelle Bachelet, a former president of Chile, has withdrawn her…

blocks.text: Michelle Bachelet, a former president of Chile, has withdrawn her candidacy to become the next secretary general of the ⁠UN, ending a ⁠bid ​that had struggled to gain traction among security council members.
Bachelet, 74, announced ⁠her decision in a video posted on Instagram on Saturday, saying: “I will now continue, with the ⁠same determination as always, my international work.”

The two-time Chilean ​president and former ‌UN human ‌rights chief had positioned her campaign around defending multilateralism and ‌international law at a time when she said both were under sustained pressure.

Bachelet’s exit leaves seven candidates in the race to succeed the secretary general, António Guterres, who will conclude his second five-year term on ‌31 December. It is still possible for more candidates to enter the contest.
Her ​withdrawal comes after a third informal straw poll, held on Friday, showed her support had all but collapsed. That same poll put Costa ⁠Rica’s Rebeca Grynspan in the lead.

The UN security ​council ​will formally recommend ​a single candidate to the 193-member general ​assembly for election. ‌The assembly’s ​approval ​has long been seen as a formality once the council reaches consensus.

articles.title: ‘I have nothing in the UK at all’: British man torn from his Swedish wife and home
articles.summary:
Charles lands at Heathrow with just two bags and nowhere to go as a result of Brexit and Stockholm’s hardline immigration position

Doubled over a Heathrow baggage trolley, the former British…

blocks.text: Doubled over a Heathrow baggage trolley, the former British business director is sobbing uncontrollably, exhausted emotionally and physically after being deported from Sweden.
Hours earlier the 65-year-old had been marched on to a plane in Stockholm, separated from his home and his Swedish wife after a five-year battle to stay in the country after Brexit came to an end.
An only child with no children and no property in the UK, Charles has effectively been made homeless. He was last in the UK in 2022 for one week, and before that not since 2017 when he emigrated.
“I have nothing, nothing in the UK at all,” says Charles as he shows a text from the British consulate explaining where in Heathrow the suddenly homeless can get help.
“All I want is to return to my wife, my home and my friends in Sweden and to live a quiet, peaceful life,” adds Charles, who does not want to publicly share his full identity.

His forced flight on Tuesday shows that deportations of British citizens who lived in Sweden before Brexit are continuing. Stockholm has already deported 458 British people after rejected residency applications, a higher proportion in terms of its population than any EU member state.

blocks.caption: Charles is distraught after landing at Heathrow. Photograph: David Levene/The Guardian

blocks.text: The situation persists despite promises from opposition parties now on track to form a government that they will introduce urgent laws to give Britons a second chance to apply for residency.
“I’ve done nothing wrong but feel I’ve been treated like a criminal,” Charles says.

“Since arriving in Sweden nearly nine years ago, I’ve done everything I can to integrate myself into Swedish society. I’ve learned some basic Swedish, contributed to Swedish society and the Swedish economy, and for that, I’m being punished. Why are they doing this to good, honest, hard-working people like me and my wife?”
Shortly after disembarking in London, he is sitting down in an airport cafe processing what has just happened.

Pointing to a small holdall and a large reusable shopping bag, he says: “All I have is what my wife packed in my bag here with clothes and my little bag” in which he has belongings handed back to him by the captain as he got off the plane.
The bag includes a plastic envelope sealed and emblazoned with the words Kriminalvården, the Swedish Prison and Probation Service, containing meagre belongings.
In it is a miniature tube of toothpaste, a toothbrush and earplugs given to him in the detention centre where he was locked up for two weeks.

blocks.caption: A bag containing a toothbrush, toothpaste and earplugs that was given to Charles in the Swedish detention centre where he was locked up for two weeks. Photograph: David Levene/The Guardian

blocks.text: There is also a bright yellow envelope handed to him by the captain before disembarking which he opens for the first time.

One is a police document saying he does not need to be “escorted”. The other says he is being deported over a failed residency application under the Aliens Act – his latest legal attempt to stay in Sweden after a pre-Brexit residency application, made on time, was rejected.
Charles’s plight started just over two weeks ago when he and his wife received a text requesting that they come to their local police station to discuss their migration case.
They thought it was to discuss their five-year battle to persuade authorities they were in the country lawfully before Brexit. But he was immediately detained and told he would be deported.
“It was an incredible shock. I was distraught. This is not about leaving Sweden, this is about me being forced to leave my wife and my house. They are separating me from my wife,” he said.
“They said we think that if we don’t detain you you will abscond from Sweden because you are not co-operating.
“For the last nine years, all we’ve done is cooperate with them.” He said he begged authorities not to detain him, telling them he would go of his own accord but they said no.
He asked if he could drive back to the UK “so at least I could take some belongings with me because I have nothing in the UK, and they said ‘no, the decision has been made’”.

blocks.caption: A document envelope issued by the Swedish police authority. Photograph: David Levene/The Guardian

blocks.text: Before Brexit, British citizens could live, work, study or retire in any other member state. Under EU law deportation was reserved for exceptional cases of criminality such as terrorism.

After Brexit, Britons and EU citizens who had exercised those free movement rights were told their rights to remain in their host country would be guaranteed in the legally binding withdrawal agreement.

Campaign group British in Europe has raised concerns about the hardline treatment in Sweden for years but this summer it became an election issue after a series of controversial cases emerged, including a removal order issued to a 78-year-old British widow, Joyce Thomas, who had been in the country for 21 years.

blocks.caption: Charles looking for help at Heathrow. Photograph: David Levene/The Guardian

blocks.text: A 74-year-old British man with dementia in full-time care was also ordered to leave after 25 years while another British man, 34, in the country since he was 10 years old, was deported in January.
The cases raised questions about whether Sweden’s hardline immigration position had infected decision-making relating to Britons there before Brexit, a cohort with special protection.
Charles says the experience has been humiliating, particularly as he spent a career in public service helping prisoners and unemployed people to start up businesses.

“When I first moved to Sweden, I thought it was a wonderful place to live. Clean air. We were very close to the sea. Forests, nature, the people that I met when I first moved there were all generally very nice people. That did change,” he said.
“Only two friends know what’s happened in the last couple of weeks. And they’re disgusted by it. One of them said, ‘I’m ashamed, I’m ashamed of what we’ve done to you’.”

blocks.caption: Charles leaves Heathrow airport, heading into an uncertain future. Photograph: David Levene/The Guardian

blocks.text: Jane Golding, chair of British in Europe, says “it is another case that raises the question of whether Swedish implementation is in line with the spirit of the withdrawal agreement,” referring to the legally binding treaty that Michel Barnier, then the EU’s chief negotiator on Britain’s exit from the EU, and Boris Johnson, the then prime minister, promised would protect EU citizens in the UK and British citizens in the EU.
“This British man who has sufficient means and a home and a Swedish wife in Sweden now faces homelessness in the UK where he has nothing,” she says.
“This wasn’t the intention of the EU and UK negotiators of the agreement who said that citizens should broadly be able to continue their lives as before,” she adds.
She also points out that, unlike the UK, there is no statutory body in any member state to oversee correct implementation of the withdrawal agreement.

“Monitoring and support resources for UK citizens in the EU trying to enforce their rights are not commensurate with those in the UK, where there is a dedicated independent monitoring authority. Unfunded volunteers trying to help are overwhelmed,” says Golding.

articles.title: Rabies concerns grow in the US – but it’s unclear if there’s an increase of the fatal disease
articles.summary:
Rabid goats at a North Carolina petting zoo and a diseased beaver attacking a Maryland boy have set the public on edge

Recent unusual incidents involving humans and rabid animals and a…

blocks.text: Recent unusual incidents involving humans and rabid animals and a subsequent Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) advisory have prompted concerns about rabies, but it’s not clear if there has actually been an increase in cases of the deadly disease in the United States, experts say.

In recent months, rabid beavers have attacked three people in Maryland, and hundreds of people were exposed to goats with rabies at a petting zoo in North Carolina, according to news reports. The CDC issued a health advisory on 10 September “in response to recent reports of increases in human exposures to rabid or possibly rabid animals”.

Despite the uncertainty over whether people encountered rabid animals or simply were worried that they did, the increased news coverage and greater awareness of the disease is a good thing, experts suggested.

“Any time that the subject gets good coverage and people can learn a little bit about how they can be safe, I think that is a win for public health,” said Zak Mertz, CEO of the New England Wildlife Center.

Hundreds of people used to die annually in the United States from rabies, but measures like vaccines and animal control programs have led to fewer than 10 people typically dying each year from the diseases, according to the CDC.

Still, from July to August, the federal agency received 17% more rabies-related inquiries, including reports of mass exposure events, as compared with the same period last year. The agency also received reports from state health departments of increased administration of post-exposure prophylaxis treatments after a possible rabies exposure.

In July, a wild skunk entered a baby goats’ pen at a farm in Harmony, North Carolina, CNN reported. Months later, hundreds of people interacted with the goats, at least some of which had rabies. Local health departments then monitored those humans, and hundreds received prophylaxis treatment. There have not been reports of any related deaths.
In Maryland, a 13-year-old was swimming at a state park when a beaver attacked him. The boy survived but had to have three surgeries to his chest and hands to repair nerve damage.

When asked if there was a common cause for such incidents, Meghan Davis, an associate professor of environmental health and engineering at Johns Hopkins University said: “I think what we are seeing is a little bit of bad luck.”
The goats had not been old enough to be vaccinated. Beavers rarely get rabies.
Despite all the scientific advancements, people do still occasionally die from rabies.

In 2011, Tonji Durant’s sister, Ivy, called her local animal control office in South Carolina to inform them of bats in her home. The local officials did not provide her with guidance on what she should do to protect herself, such as getting a medical assessment, Durant, a retired CDC epidemiologist, said.
Months later, she developed flu-like symptoms, Durant said. Only then did providers administer a rabies test, which came back positive, but after symptoms develop, there is little doctors can do.
after newsletter promotion

“The older you get, the more you miss your siblings,” said Durant, who thinks her sister’s death was preventable. “Communication is really critical. Clinicians working with state and local health departments; communities working with state and local health departments.”
If a person is worried that they potentially had contact with a rabid animal, they should contact the state or their healthcare provider, Mertz said.
Those who have been bitten by a potentially rabid animal should wash the wound thoroughly and immediately seek medical attention, Davis said.
“Don’t wait; seek help,” she said.
It’s also important for people to ensure that their pets’ vaccinations are up to date.
“Because [rabies] has largely been under control,” Davis said, “it doesn’t always reach the public eye.”

articles.title: US environment agency let Bayer pick regulations for destructive weedkiller, documents show
articles.summary:
Environmental Protection Agency asked firm to choose rules it wanted for dicamba, then put the choices in a proposed federal rule

The EPA allowed

blocks.text: The EPA allowed pesticide giant Bayer to pick from a menu of regulation options for the controversial and destructive weedkiller dicamba, newly released internal agency documents show.

The documents provide an unusually clear look into the process of developing pesticide regulations, which is typically done out of public view. It shows in detail how the EPA asked Bayer which regulations it wanted, received a response from Bayer, then put Bayer’s choices into a proposed federal rule.

Dicamba is drift prone and kills vegetation and crops for miles around fields where it is sprayed, and is linked to liver cancer and Non-Hodgkin lymphoma. Courts have twice ordered it off the market because of its drift problems, but the EPA has re-approved it.

The EPA solicited Bayer’s input on the level of restrictions to limit dicamba volatility and runoff, ranging from more protective to less protective, records released in ongoing litigation over the substance show. The EPA concluded one presentation with a slide entitled “Registrant response needed” which posed the question “Which mitigation option to go forward with?”
Bayer chose the least protective for one regulation, and the middle of three levels of protection for another regulation. It also got one other change it requested into the rule.

Pesticide regulations are typically a negotiation between industry and the EPA, but the exchange that the documents reveal is “crossing a line”, said Nathan Donley, environmental health science director with the Center for Biological Diversity, which is litigating on the issue.

“The EPA is allowing Bayer to choose its preferred measures to limit dicamba’s damage as if it was ordering up a late-night dinner à la carte from Chili’s,” Donley said. “It becomes troublesome when the EPA allows them to regulate themselves by choosing the mitigations.”

The Center for Biological Diversity and the Center for Food Safety brought the lawsuit. The documents come as the EPA has faced criticism for stacking its leadership with industry veterans. The top four toxics office positions at the EPA are held by former chemical industry leaders, including Kyle Kunkler, a former pesticide industry lobbyist who is now a deputy assistant administrator and oversees the pesticides program.

Despite repeated assurances from the EPA that it has put effective protections in place, dicamba drift has damaged millions of acres of farmland and caused damage to orchards, vegetable farms, home gardens, native plants, trees and wildlife refuges across the country since its first approval in 2016. Experts have found dicamba drift damage to be the worst of any herbicide in the history of US agriculture. Still, the current approval provides even fewer protections from dicamba drift and damage than past approvals, the lawsuit alleges.
In a statement to the Guardian, an EPA spokesperson said: “Make no mistake: this is not a compliance failure; it is the regulatory system working exactly as intended.”

“The agency notifies the [pesticide maker] and works with them to identify possible solutions” to risks, the spokesperson wrote. “[Companies] are permitted to submit mitigation ideas that preserve their product’s utility, and EPA also will independently develop its own proposed mitigations. To be explicitly clear: the registrant does not dictate terms.”

During a May 2025 EPA meeting with Bayer, the agency gave Bayer two mitigation choices that would allegedly address dicamba’s high volatility, which is what makes it drift prone. A more restrictive option would have prevented dicamba applications above 85F, and a less restrictive option would allow applications up to 95F, if the acreage treated was reduced.
The EPA also gave Bayer three options for addressing dicamba runoff, documents show. It then concluded the presentation with a solicitation for Bayer to decide.

An EPA manager then wrote in an email that “the next step in the process beyond the [presentation] is getting feedback from the registrants on what mitigation and mitigation implementation option they would like to move forward with”.

Separate documents obtained by the Center for Biological Diversity showed the plan was presented to Nancy Beck, a controversial former lobbyist for the American Chemistry Council who now leads the EPA’s office of chemical safety.

The revelations drew condemnation from “make America healthy again” (Maha) advocate Kelly Ryerson, who said: “It is now undeniable that the EPA remains fully captured by a crooked collection of pesticide company players who so enthusiastically ignore the substantial losses of farmers and the federal courts who mandated a halt to dicamba use.”
Eight days later, a representative from Bayer emailed the EPA: “After discussion with EPA and reviewing these options carefully, Bayer would like to proceed as described below … ”

Bayer chose the less restrictive option for volatility mitigation, which would allow it to be applied at up to 95 degrees as long as the dicamba-treated area would be reduced. Bayer also wanted another option that the EPA had not proposed, emails show. It would allow full-field dicamba treatments at higher temperatures if dicamba was not tank mixed.
The EPA granted both requests, and Bayer’s preferred option for mitigating run off. These were included in the rules proposed a few months later, documents show.
“In return for this egregiousness, I would like the EPA to propose a menu of options to Maha for significantly decreasing our exposure to known carcinogens and endocrine disruptors,” Ryerson added.

articles.title: China’s stranglehold on rare earths must be ended, says hopeful supplier to EU
articles.summary:
Rafael Moreno, whose company has opened demo plant in Brazil, says market is ‘nervous’ as Trump-Xi summit looms

The head of a mining company hoping to supply the EU with rare earths in two…

blocks.text: The head of a mining company hoping to supply the EU with rare earths in two years’ time has said it is “paramount” to end China’s stranglehold on the supply of the raw materials used in everything from cars to wind turbines and military jets.

As Donald Trump and China’s president, Xi Jinping, prepare to meet on Thursday in their second summit of the year, Rafael Moreno said it was also “imperative” that they do a deal for Beijing to ease up, once again, on its threat to ban exports of rare earths.
“The market is nervous,” said Moreno, the managing director of the Australia-listed Viridis Mining and Minerals, which has assets in Brazil, Australia and Canada.
China first brought in controls on rare earth exports in April 2025, hitting the auto industries in the EU, UK, US and Japan hard.
After a summit last October with Trump in South Korea, Xi agreed to suspend the introduction of even stricter global restrictions, but only for 12 months.
Industry leaders had hoped Trump would have sealed a deal to extend the suspension at the two leaders’ last summit in May but the question remains hanging over next week’s summit.

“It cannot not be extended if they are to continue to have these presidents’ meetings regularly,” said Kurt Tong, a managing partner of the Asia Group, a Washington strategic advisory and public policy firm.

But he said a suspension deal could be delayed until November, when Trump is expected to travel to China again to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) governmental forum of 21 countries.
Viridis is already attracting attention in Brussels, where diversification of supply chains away from China is a top priority of Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president.

It has opened a demonstration plant to scrape the surface of its mine in Minas Gerais, Brazil, and produce a crumbly powder, which will then be further separated, potentially in France, to isolate the rare earths.

blocks.caption: Powder containing rare earths scraped from earth’s surface in Brazil Photograph: Viridis

blocks.text: The EU trade commissioner, Maroš Šefčovič, will travel to Beijing for his own summit with China’s commerce minister, Wang Wentao, on 8 October to try to avoid a trade war.

The EU is deeply concerned about what Šefčovič has said is the “unsustainable” deficit with China, now running at €1bn a day, with the scale of exports of electric vehicles, cars and renewable energy machinery as well as components deep in supply chains causing alarm.
While Šefčovič heads up the urgent trade mission, senior EU politicians and officials are scrambling to find alternative supplies of critical raw materials and rare earths.
after newsletter promotion

But their challenge is long-term, as China controls between 80% and 90% of the world’s raw materials and processed end products, giving it powerful leverage over global manufacturing. The Chinese exchange rate is also driving down the cost of imports from China.

Eurometal, a trade group representing buyers of steel products, protests that Brussels does not fully appreciate the pressures industries are under, saying component buyers or original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) are under pressure each day to opt for Chinese goods, which can sometimes be 30% cheaper than domestic alternatives.

The EU’s international partnership commissioner, the Czech politician Jozef Síkela, visited Viridis’s Colossus demonstrating plant this year in Brazil to hear how the company hopes to win 5% of the rare earths market, with production starting at the end of 2028.

Moreno said: “It is natural for a company or OEM to want to buy the cheapest product, but then, you know, the impact of them not supporting a domestic supply chain means that the domestic supply chain just never gets off the ground.”

He is working with the French chemical company Solvay to process the rare earths. “We are looking forward to keep moving forward with our strategic partnership with Solvay to start to supply all the OEMs, car manufacturers, you know, wind turbine manufacturers like Siemens Gamesa, for example, all that sort of stuff here in Europe,” he said.

“What we’ve started to design and build now, is around 5% of the world’s rare earths market share in terms of those precious magnets. So that’s that’s where we’re starting. So this is not a small project, as you can imagine.”

articles.title: ‘It’s transformed the village’: the volunteers greening up Britain’s train stations
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Five gardening teams shortlisted for Royal Horticultural Society’s new Railway Stations in Bloom award

Every year since 1964, towns across the UK have bloomed with hanging baskets…

blocks.text: Every year since 1964, towns across the UK have bloomed with hanging baskets and brightly coloured flowerbeds planted by residents.
They wield their trowels in aid of the Royal Horticultural Society’s Britain in Bloom competition, a coveted accolade for the 1,600 communities that enter each year.
Now, the charity is launching a new award for railway stations to honour the volunteers who keep platforms planted with cheerful flowers and pretty shrubs.

Five of the best have been shortlisted for the RHS Railway Stations in Bloom competition, marked for their beauty but also for how well they welcome wildlife and withstand changing climate conditions.

The winner, announced this week, was the Cardross Community Organic Garden in Scotland. The RHS said: “The judges were especially impressed by how active the group was in including different members of the community in the station’s activities, from school children, Brownies to other volunteering and gardening groups”. But all of the railway gardens are impressive.

blocks.caption: Cardross community organic garden in Scotland. Photograph: RHS

blocks.text: It has been an extremely hot and dry summer in Alresford, Essex, but the gardeners were prepared. Working hard to cut through asphalt to create flowerbeds, they have planted a “dry garden” inspired by the horticultural pioneer Beth Chatto, who died in 2018. Also from Essex, she managed to grow plants in dry ground that had never been cultivated.

“It’s transformed the centre of the village,” said the lead volunteer, Frank Belgrave. Ten years ago the station was described in the local paper as “rundown”. Now, the planting beds rival any at Chelsea flower show.

blocks.caption: The entrance to Alresford railway station. Photograph: Oliver Dixon

blocks.text: Belgrave said residents were very pleased their station had received the spruce-up: “It’s wonderful. People sometimes stop by with plants and compost to help us, and we are very lucky to have some lovely volunteers as the garden requires constant maintenance.
“We used to spend all our time watering. So we decided to seek advice and build a dry garden with drought-resistant plants.”

At a windswept station on the west coast of Scotland, commuters may be surprised to find trees heaving with fruit and a thriving vegetable patch. But Jane Connolly, who heads the Cardross station volunteer group, has found a way to create such bounty.

“Since March 2022, every bit of the station that can be changed, has been changed,” she said. “We do have harsh winters – we don’t take summer bedding plants as we don’t get enough out of them – we choose hardy shrubs. We put up windproofing on the shore side to protect the plants but in general we have had very few failures.”
Connolly and her fellow volunteers filled the station with plants from their own gardens and visit most days to tend to them.

blocks.caption: A boat planter at Cardross station. Photograph: RHS

blocks.text: Having a pretty, flower-filled rail station rather than a neglected one makes a huge difference to the village, she said: “Every time we are down there, somebody will come along and peruse it and say how grateful they are with what we have done. I notice stations now wherever I go, even if it’s a window box. People come to our station just to see our gardens.”

Other shortlisted stations include Maghull in Merseyside, where the ticket office’s window boxes are full of pretty flowers and volunteers have planted a woodland. At Wylde Green in Birmingham, overgrown areas were cleared and replaced with pollinator-friendly plants, creating a “bee corridor”. The volunteers carry out an annual butterfly count and have seen numbers increasing.
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: Pollinator-friendly plants are a focus at Wylde Green in Birmingham. Photograph: RHS

blocks.text: Keynsham station in Somerset on a hot day looks especially exotic because volunteers have filled it with a remarkable array of succulents, of all shapes and sizes. Like the Essex gardeners, they have selected plants that will withstand hot summers.

The volunteers at the stations have spoken of how social the job is and many have made friends. It also gives commuters a chance to chat. Belgrave said: “It’s very rewarding. Lots of people come and chat, they talk about plants, it gives them a social thing.”

He hopes to get funding for a community hub and coffee shop. “On the platform there is a very ancient station house, to the back of that there was an area which was neglected and used as a community rubbish dump. We have turned that into a garden. Now, we hope we can open a coffee shop on the site.”

blocks.caption: The volunteer gardeners at the back of the old Alresford station house. Photograph: Oliver Dixon

blocks.text: In Cardross, the gardeners have become fast friends. Connolly said: “We garden together and there is always laughing and joking and there is often more joking than working! We go out socialising together now as well. It is a very social thing.”

Wildlife has returned to Alresford station, according to Belgrave. “We have noticed incredible amounts of wildlife, bees particularly. Honeybees, solitary bees, butterflies. That has changed a lot, we have seen the return of hedgehogs, we have slowworms.”
The gardeners hope their example will encourage others to get involved.
Belgrave said: “There are lots of stations which aren’t in the scheme, so if people do get involved it would be really good. It would be nice to see more stations planted up.”

articles.title: From Beda to UP: James Payosing brings premium spark to UAAP
articles.summary: James Payosing, an NCAA champion and a Finals MVP with the San Beda Red Lions, brings the same winning mentality to the UP Fighting Maroons

blocks.text: PUMPED. James Payosing in action for the UP Fighting Maroons in the UAAP Season 89 men's basketball tournament.
UAAP
James Payosing, an NCAA champion and a Finals MVP with the San Beda Red Lions, brings the same winning mentality to the UP Fighting Maroons

items: James Payosing made a strong debut for the UP Fighting Maroons, scoring 16 points and contributing to their 94-75 victory over the Ateneo Blue Eagles.
Payosing, a former NCAA champion, emphasizes teamwork and aims to bring a winning mentality to UP, filling the void left by key players from previous seasons.
He believes in the importance of each player excelling in their roles to maintain the team's success, as UP currently leads the standings at 2-0.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
MANILA, Philippines – James Payosing needed just 15 minutes to show he truly belongs on the UAAP stage.
The former NCAA champion poured in 16 points on 4-of-5 shooting and added 3 rebounds and 2 assists as the UP Fighting Maroons dispatched the Ateneo Blue Eagles, 94-75, on Saturday, September 19.
Payosing did it at the Araneta Coliseum, the same venue where he led the San Beda Red Lions to the NCAA Season 99 championship in 2023 and earned Finals MVP honors.
Now, he is looking to bring that same winning mentality to UP.

“As a player, my mindset is that I’m in a team sport, so I’m just doing my role that complements the team. When one wins, everybody does,” Payosing said after just his second game with UP following his initial commitment in 2024.
“Since this is my first season here in the UAAP, I’m just embracing the games and the opportunity. Whenever I play, I aim to stand out in my role.”
That has always been Payosing’s approach, even during his time at San Beda.

The 6-foot-2 guard knows when to pick his spots, rarely forces the issue, and brings an unrelenting intensity on defense. He does not need the ball in his hands to make an impact, and against Ateneo, that versatility proved valuable.

Payosing helped contain Ateneo’s rookie sensation Kieffer Alas, who was held to just 3 points in the second half. Alas finished with 13 points on 5-of-11 shooting as Ateneo struggled to find answers against UP’s defense.
For Payosing, the performance was another glimpse of what he can bring to a team built around a collective identity rather than one dominant star.
The 23-year-old is also enjoying a rare opportunity to bring glory to two of the country’s proudest collegiate programs over the past five years, San Beda and UP.
“I expect a winning culture here at UP. Winning a championship isn’t easy, but I’ve been preparing for it since last year, my residency year,” Payosing said.

At UP, Payosing is expected to help fill the void left by Harold Alarcon, Reyland Torres, and Terrence Fortea, three key pieces of a Fighting Maroons team that reached the UAAP finals in each of the last five seasons.
Payosing appears to be comfortable with the challenge of filling those shoes.

UP now sits atop the standings at 2-0 after the first week of games, and Payosing hopes his role can help keep the Fighting Maroons on the same path that made them a fixture in the UAAP title picture.
“All I’m saying is that let’s be star players in each of our roles so that when the five of us are on the court, we’re all superstars,” Payosing said.
“The level of competition is almost the same [as the NCAA] and it really comes down the mindset that whoever wants to win the most will win,” he added. – Rappler.com
