articles.title: Leftists make waves and Trump flexes muscles: US primary season takeaways
articles.summary:
Candidates have been selected for November’s midterms – have Republicans and Democrats made the right choices?

Primary season has official concluded in the United States, with Democrats

blocks.text: Primary season has official concluded in the United States, with Democrats leading the polls among voters amid widespread economic anxieties, a war with Iran and Donald Trump’s mass deportation agenda continuing into the end of the year.

Democratic and Republican voters have selected contenders for key races in the 3 November midterms that will decide the balance of power in Congress, and the future of both parties. Democrats have been rocked by the primary victories of leftwing candidates. Republicans have doubled down on backing the president’s policies, despite his low approval ratings. And both parties are navigating the fallout from a series of scandals that have forced some candidates from the race, while others decided to press on.
Here’s a look back at what we learned over the past six months of primaries:

items: 1. Lawmakers fled the House in droves, ensuring a reshaped Congress in 2027Viewed as the chamber of Congress most likely to change hands in the midterms, the House saw significant turnover this cycle, with 74 members departing, the most since 1992, according to a tally from the Pew Research Center. Some outgoing lawmakers retired, while others ran for other offices, but generally didn’t fare particularly well – only 13 made it through primaries for governorships, the Senate or other offices, with the remaining 15 were rejected by voters.Among representatives who sought re-election to the House, 11 lost their primaries, the second-highest total since 2022. Seven of these were Democrats, two of whom – Julie Johnson and Al Green – were unseated by other Democratic incumbents after they were redistricted by Texas Republicans to compete against each other.

Of the five House Democrats who lost their primaries to newcomers, four were booted by leftist candidates with ties to the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA). In New York, Congressional Hispanic Caucus chair Adriano Espaillat fell to DSA member Darializa Avila Chevalier and congressman Dan Goldman was ousted by former DSA member Brad Lander, while DSA member Claire Valdez also won the primary to replace retiring congresswoman Nydia Velazquez.In Colorado, DSA member Melat Kiros unseated 30-year incumbent Diana DeGette, and in Michigan, the DSA-endorsed Donovan McKinney beat congressman Shri Thanedar. All are expected to win their seats in the midterms, as their districts are heavily Democratic.“A lot of people were hoping that it was a blip, like oh well, this is a special case,” said the DSA-endorsed Chris Rabb, who is expected to be elected to the House after winning the Democratic primary in deep-blue Philadelphia. “We showed them a different way. So I think all of those things make this election cycle uniquely powerful in ways that most people could not anticipate, myself included.”The fifth sitting Democrat to lose renomination was John Larson. His challenger, Luke Bronin, 47, successfully argued to voters that it was time to replace the 78-year-old incumbent with a younger candidate.

3. ... but centrists are on the frontlinesThe battle for the House will not be decided in safe blue seats, but rather the 21 districts that the Cook Political Report considers to be toss-ups. In those districts, the nominees are almost entirely backed by the Pacs of either the center-left New Democrat Coalition, or the moderate Blue Dogs, which centrists say bolsters their arguments that their policies most closely align with the voters who determine control of Congress. “If Democrats are to win the majority in the House and/or the Senate, it will be because moderates flip seats from red to blue,” said Matt Bennett, an executive vice-president at the thinktank Third Way.There are exceptions to the trend: former DSA member William Lawrence won the Democratic nomination to take on Republican incumbent Tom Barrett in a swing Michigan congressional district, while in that state’s Democratic Senate primary, Abdul El-Sayed beat congresswoman Haley Stevens, who was backed by much of the party establishment.

4. Anti-incumbent sentiment among Democrats had its limitsThe DSA’s wins reintensified debate among Democrats over the political direction of the party, but the left-wing movement’s momentum was not absolute. In Missouri, DSA member Cori Bush failed in her primary challenge against congressman Wesley Bell, who had unseated her two years ago. Hawaii congressman Ed Case fended off state senator Jarrett Keohokalole, who had challenged him from the left and argued it was time for generational change. In Massachusetts, congressman Seth Moulton made a similar argument about the Democratic senator Ed Markey, though in this case Moulton was the moderate candidate and Markey the progressive.It didn’t work, and Markey won renomination, as did other congressional Democrats in the state who faced primary challenges. In Colorado, state senator Julie Gonzales mounted an unsuccessful left-wing challenge to Democratic US senator John Hickenlooper, while in Washington, moderate congresswoman Marie Gluesenkamp Perez again won the Democratic nomination in her right-leaning district against several challengers.

5. Trump flexed his muscles, with much successAs always, Trump sought to play kingmaker in the primaries, endorsing candidates who hewed to his agenda and seeking revenge against those who had broken with him, however small their transgressions. Kentucky congressman Thomas Massie lost his primary after the president campaigned against him, and the president’s decision not to make an endorsement in Texas representative Dan Crenshaw’s primary was likely a factor in him losing the Republican nomination. Trump successfully ousted Louisiana senator Bill Cassidy – who voted to convict him after January 6 – as well as Texas senator John Cornyn, for comparatively murkier reasons.The president may rue the latter decision – recent polls have shown the Democratic nominee James Talarico with a slight lead over Trump’s preferred candidate, Ken Paxton. All told, it was a successful primary for Trump – an analysis of his record by USA Today shows nearly 97% of the candidates he backed in congressional and gubernatorial races won their primaries. There were a handful of misses – five gubernatorial candidates won their primaries without Trump’s endorsement, along with four House aspirants.

6. Aipac spent, for better or worseThe American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac) waded into some primaries at a particularly fraught moment for supporters of the Middle Eastern ally. Surveys show that some Republicans and many Democrats now hold negative views of Israel, amid accusations it carried out a genocide in Gaza, and many of the left-wing candidates who ousted Democratic House incumbents did so after attacking their ties to Aipac. Through its United Democracy Project Super Pac, the group nonetheless scored some wins, including Ed Gallrein’s defeat of Massie in Kentucky, Adrian Boafo’s victory in the Maryland primary to replace veteran House Democrat Steny Hoyer, and Bell’s defense against Bush’s primary challenge in Missouri.But the group failed to keep El-Sayed from defeating Rogers in the Michigan Senate primary, despite spending more than $30m in that race, or prevent progressive Aisha Wahab from winning a special election to replace former congressman Eric Swalwell in California.

7. Some candidates fell to scandals, others pressed onSeveral candidates who ran for office were derailed by scandals. Graham Platner won the Democratic primary to take on veteran Republican senator Susan Collins in Maine, but dropped out amid accusations of sexual assault and misconduct. Swalwell ran for governor of California but exited that race and resigned his US House seat after he, too, was accused of sexual assault. North Carolina Republican congressman Chuck Edwards won his primary but ended his re-election campaign after the House ethics committee said he likely broke rules against sexual harassment, but Republican congressman Max Miller remains in the race amid accusations of domestic violence against his ex-wife.In other instances, the GOP used the primaries to dispose of problematic lawmakers in their ranks. Andy Ogles, a congressman with a history of homophobic and Islamophobic statements, lost in Tennessee after the Republican governor endorsed his challenger and a Super Pac backed by the renewable energy industry spent against him, and scandal-plagued congressman Cory Mills was defeated after other Florida Republicans endorsed his challenger.

articles.title: As White House shields the AI gold rush, Trump family and other allies strike it rich – with few guardrails
articles.summary:
It’s not clear that financial interests are driving White House policy, but they run parallel even as resistance mounts

Donald…

blocks.text: Donald Trump’s sons, through a series of AI-linked defense and technology ventures, have picked up a $620m Pentagon loan, a Marine Corps robotics contract and an undisclosed air force drone deal in the past year. His longtime friend Michael Dell won a Pentagon contract worth nearly $9bn. And this week, as public support for artificial intelligence sinks to some of the lowest levels ever recorded, the president went to bat for the industry. .

“The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades,” he posted on Truth Social Monday. “There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers.” It was the first of many aggressively pro-AI posts he would make this week.

Trump is resisting new restrictions on AI at a moment when his family and some of his closest allies have accumulated financial interests in the infrastructure and defense-technology ecosystem expanding alongside the AI boom, an overlap that has now drawn scrutiny from Democratic lawmakers, government ethics watchdogs and, by some accounts, his own senior aides. It’s not clear that financial interests are driving Trump’s policy, but the two have moved in close parallel.

The administration frames its resistance chiefly as a matter of competitiveness. Trump and officials including David Sacks, who co-chairs his Council of Advisors on Science and Technology, have repeatedly argued that new rules could slow US AI development when the country is racing China for dominance of the technology. Sacks said at a Politico summit on Wednesday that recent warnings from Anthropic and OpenAI about the technology’s risks amounted to political theater, manufactured by advocacy groups and the press, and said existing laws were largely sufficient.

But many concerns are coming from inside the industry itself. In early September, Jacob Coxon – a researcher who spent three years working on the foundational training of AI models at both OpenAI and Anthropic – resigned and published a stark warning.

“Neither company is acting responsibly,” he wrote. “They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” He said colleagues privately believe the technology “could kill us all by the end of the decade”. Anthropic’s head of AI safety, Mrinank Sharma, separately resigned the same week, writing that “the world is in peril.”

Those warnings coincided with a concrete demonstration of AI-enabled risk. A California cybersecurity firm disclosed this month that it had used artificial intelligence to build a self-spreading worm capable of hijacking WeChat accounts through a single unanswered call, and then automatically spreading through the victim’s contact list. The firm estimated the technology could compromise more than a billion devices within hours.

Tencent, the Chinese tech giant that owns WeChat, patched the vulnerability before it was deployed and said no accounts were affected, but the firm noted that building the exploit, work it said would once have taken a larger team months, took roughly 10 days with AI assistance. Around the same time, JD Vance, speaking on a Christian podcast, described certain uses of AI as carrying “really, really weird spiritual dark energy” and said there are “things about the world” that leave him “not shocked if the Antichrist was walking among us”.

Polling shows how far out of step Trump’s posture is with the public, particularly once AI’s costs become tangible. A poll released on Wednesday found just 11% of Americans support an AI datacenter being built in their own community, while 65% oppose one – including 52% of Republicans – and 57% say Trump has handled the issue of AI poorly, up seven points since March. The same day, the House voted 417-3 to require datacenters to bear the costs of the electricity-grid upgrades their operations demand, underscoring how concerns about AI’s infrastructure costs have moved from polling into Congress.

If the federal government did enact regulations that ultimately damaged AI profits, it’s possible some members of the Trump family would feel the pain. Donald Trump Jr and Eric Trump joined the investment firm Dominari Holdings last year and helped launch American Data Centers Inc, an AI infrastructure venture in which Dominari holds a minority stake. The deal came weeks after their father unveiled an expected $20bn datacenter pledge from Emirati billionaire Hussain Sajwani, and $500 bn in planned private sector AI investment, alongside an executive order unwinding Biden-era AI safeguards.

Since then, the brothers have moved from infrastructure into defense contracting, most notably through Vulcan Elements, a rare-earth magnet startup whose products are used in AI datacenters, drones and defense systems. Three months before the Pentagon announced its $620m loan to Vulcan in December – the largest the defense department’s office of strategic capital has ever issued – 1789 Capital, the venture firm where Trump Jr is a partner, quietly took a stake in the company. A ProPublica investigation found the loan request came not from Vulcan or the Pentagon but from Peter Navarro, a senior White House adviser and close friend of Trump Jr’s, and that Pentagon staff were told to move at an “unusually rapid pace”.
“The call came from the White House: We have to get this done,” one person involved in the deal told the outlet.

Trump Jr’s spokesman, the Pentagon and Vulcan have all said he played no role in the deal and that the company received no political favoritism. Eric Trump, separately, serves as chief strategy adviser to Foundation Future Industries, the robotics startup behind the $24m Marine Corps contract; senator Elizabeth Warren called that award “corruption in plain sight”. A third venture, the drone maker Powerus backed by both brothers and having signed a new agreement with Pakistan’s army, also holds a $90m air force contract, and has separately pitched its technology to Gulf states amid Iran’s striking of US bases across the region. Drones are widely expected to increasingly utilize AI technology in the coming years.

A Washington Post analysis in July found 15 companies tied to the brothers’ investment funds have generated at least $3.2bn in direct federal business since they got involved, but SpaceX and Anduril, the latter an AI-powered defense technology firm behind Lattice account for 97% of that figure, and 10 of the 15 companies already had government business before the Trump sons invested.
Excluding SpaceX and Anduril, the remaining 13 companies had received $103m in direct federal funding and nearly $1.8bn in long-term commitments after the brothers’ investments.

The pattern extends beyond Trump’s family to some of his closest technology allies. Sacks’s influence over Trump’s regulatory decisions has been substantial: in May, he reportedly persuaded the president in a last-minute call to scrap a planned executive order that would have subjected AI models to extended government review, overriding the chief of staff, Susie Wiles, and treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, who had spent months negotiating the stronger version.

His own financial position has drawn scrutiny inside the administration as a result. Sacks’s venture firm holds stakes in SpaceX and a range of AI startups, along with earlier investments in Meta, Palantir and Airbnb; federal ethics rules required him to divest only some of those holdings while he served as the White House’s AI and crypto czar, a post he left in March. Some administration officials have privately looked into whether Sacks could personally benefit from blocking new AI rules, the Wall Street Journal reported.

The outlet reported that Musk pushed in the same direction, joining Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg and Nvidia’s Jensen Huang last month in personally lobbying Trump against a proposed industry-funded AI oversight body, helping shelve the plan. Dell, a member of Trump’s science and technology advisory council and a longtime friend and donor to the president, saw his company win the nearly $9bn Pentagon contract in May, prompting ethics watchdogs to question whether his advisory role created an unaddressed conflict.

The technology industry is not uniformly aligned behind Trump. Federal filings on OpenSecrets show the broader communications and electronics sector still sends roughly two-thirds of its political money to Democratic candidates and committees this cycle. Trump’s support among industry figures has come instead from a narrower group: OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Greg Brockman have given tens of millions of dollars to a pro-Trump super Pac and Trump’s inaugural committee, though have also donated to Democrats in the past.

The Pentagon’s own account of its safeguards makes no distinction between a routine contractor and a company whose investors include the president’s son, which is a gap Democratic lawmakers asked the Pentagon’s inspector general to investigate last month.

Next week, Trump is set to host the leaders of the country’s leading AI companies at the White House, a meeting arranged with the House speaker, Mike Johnson, that will coincide with a visit from the Chinese president, Xi Jinping.
In the meantime, the investments continue.

articles.title: [Inside the Newsroom] The tip that led us inside a non-consensual porn forum
articles.summary: Since the investigation on NSFWPH came out, more people have started sending us their own cases

blocks.text: Since the investigation on NSFWPH came out, more people have started sending us their own cases

items: The investigation into NSFWPH began when student journalist Lance Bustos approached the author, leading to months of tracking online behavior and community dynamics within the forum.
The investigation highlighted the challenges of jurisdiction in internet investigations, as harmful sites may operate outside the Philippines, complicating accountability for local authorities.

The most significant aspect of the investigation was connecting with victims of the site, emphasizing the importance of understanding their experiences and shifting the blame from victims to those who violate trust.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
Earlier this year, student journalist Lance Bustos approached me at an event and told me about NSFWPH.
That was how this investigation began.
It sounds simple, but a lot of investigative work starts exactly that way: someone knows something, sees something, or has been watching something for a while, and decides to tell a journalist.

Lance, who would later become a Rappler fellow, had already been looking into NSFWPH for months. He wasn’t just browsing the site. He had been doing OSINT, or open-source intelligence — collecting publicly available information online, making sense of it, and connecting the dots.
You may have heard the term during the Sara Duterte impeachment trial when the National Bureau of Investigation began investigating the Vice President’s threats against President Bongbong Marcos.

In practice, it can be as basic as following usernames, social media posts, links, timestamps, website records, online videos, and other digital crumbs until a pattern begins to emerge. It has become an effective tool for journalists.

In my case, aside from NSFWPH, during the last presidential election campaign, we investigated DDoS attacks against us and other news sites. We followed the digital trail until it led us to one of the people behind the attacks.
With NSFWPH, Lance had already started doing the same thing. When I began working with him, we kept going.

For months, we tracked behavior inside the forum. We documented not just what people posted, but how the community worked, and how members communicated with one another. What earned attention? What behavior was rewarded? What did users brag about? What did they consider normal?
We felt that truly understanding this was important because online communities can shape behavior.

You may remember 8chan, the forum that became notorious after users linked to several mass shootings posted extremist material there before being shut down in 2019. Obviously, NSFWPH is a different case. But the broader point is the same: what gets normalized online can spill into the real world.
And as we’ve written, we found examples of real-world harm, including students who appeared to have been targeted.

After the Tacloban and Zamboanga shootings, whose shooters allegedly had been influenced by malign online forces operating within an amorphous NVE (nihilistic violent extremism) network, it’s only become more important to pierce through these online spaces.
We also looked at how NSFWPH was set up. Using publicly available tools, we found that it was routed through Cloudflare, which made it more difficult to identify the site’s operator.
That led us to another recurring problem in internet investigations: jurisdiction.
A site may target Filipinos and harm Filipinos, but the companies, servers, or operators behind it may be outside the Philippines. Local authorities can quickly hit a wall.

We see versions of this problem with other platforms too, whether the issue involves Roblox, Meta, or other global services. It is one reason authorities have pushed for foreign platforms to have a local legal entity that can be held accountable without having to rely immediately on international cooperation that may take time. New bills in recent months are legislating for exactly this: official local entities for international platforms that can be quickly held accountable.

And yet the most important part of this investigation was not technical. It goes back to the victims themselves, the people most affected. We wanted to find a person who had actually been victimized on the site and was willing to talk.
I eventually came across one who had already shared her experience online and had directly mentioned NSFWPH. I talked to her, and she articulated her experience bravely and well.
She said the shame belonged to the people who spread the material, not to the person who trusted a partner after being promised that those photos or videos would stay private.
Too often, when intimate material leaks, people ask the victim: Why did you send it? Why did you allow yourself to be recorded?
The better question is: Why did someone violate that trust?
Since the investigation came out, more people have started sending us their own cases. We are going through them now and looking at where our reporting can help.

One person came forward with a tip. That tip became months of monitoring and documenting, leading to our final report. The reporting reached victims. And now some of them are coming forward too. It’s a reminder that sometimes that is how an investigation grows, with one person deciding to speak.
Email us at desk@rappler.com. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Manila suspends in-person classes for Martial Law anniversary
articles.summary: In a statement on Sunday, September 20, Domagoso said cited recommendations from the Manila Police District (MPD), which anticipates heavy traffic, road closures, and security risks stemming from…

blocks.text: September 20, 2026 | 5:51pm
This undated photo shows Manila City Hall at night.
CC BY-SA 3.0 / Corteco8 / Wikimedia

MANILA, Philippines — Manila City Mayor Isko Moreno Domagoso has ordered the suspension of face-to-face classes across all levels in both public and private schools in the capital on Monday, September 21.

In a statement on Sunday, September 20, Domagoso cited recommendations from the Manila Police District (MPD), which anticipates heavy traffic, road closures, and security risks stemming from various public gatherings, marches, and freedom rallies marking the 54th anniversary of the declaration of Martial Law.

“This suspension is issued to ensure the safety and welfare of students by minimizing their exposure to potential risks associated with heavy traffic, road closures, and large public gatherings,” Domagoso said.
With the suspension, schools are advised to shift to alternative modes of learning delivery.
Protests are expected as the country commemorates the 54th anniversary of the declaration of Martial Law.
The Philippine National Police (PNP) previously said that law enforcement personnel would be placed on full alert status in anticipation of the protests.
The PNP said more than 15,700 personnel would be deployed on Monday to ensure security during the demonstrations.

articles.title: Akbayan welcomes SC decision on anti-political dynasty law
articles.summary: Akbayan Party-list Rep. Chel Diokno on Sunday welcomed the Supreme Court"s (SC) directive for Congress to enact an anti-political dynasty law.

blocks.text: Published September 20, 2026 5:38pm
Akbayan Party-list Rep. Chel Diokno on Sunday welcomed the Supreme Court’s (SC) directive for Congress to enact an anti-political dynasty law.

"This decision of the Supreme Court is groundbreaking. This is a very welcome decision for us because we have long been advocating for a genuine Anti-Political Dynasty Law," Diokno told Super Radyo dzBB.
The SC directed Congress to enact an anti-political dynasty law at the earliest opportunity, ruling that its failure to do so for 39 years constitutes grave abuse of discretion.
The ruling stemmed from consolidated petitions filed by several groups and individuals seeking to compel Congress to fulfill its constitutional duty to enact a law prohibiting political dynasties.

SC spokesperson Camille Ting said the use of the word "shall" in Article II, Section 26 of the 1987 Constitution makes clear that the State has a mandatory duty to prohibit political dynasties. (Supreme Court of the Philippines)
The provision states that the State shall guarantee equal access to opportunities for public service and prohibit political dynasties "as may be defined by law."
The SC, however, said Congress retains the authority to define what constitutes a political dynasty and determine the scope of the prohibition.

Diokno pointed out that the version of the Anti-Political Dynasty Bill filed by their group in the House of Representatives would ban relatives up to the fourth degree of consanguinity or affinity from running for or occupying a public post in the same constituency or jurisdiction.

"The Anti-Political Dynasty Bill that we are pushing covers up to the fourth degree of consanguinity or affinity and includes everyone. For us, all positions, whether local or national, should be covered by the prohibition against political dynasties," Diokno said.

This version differs from House Bill 8389, which the House of Representatives approved on third and final reading in June. The measure prohibits relatives up to the second degree of consanguinity or affinity from running for or occupying a post in the same constituency or jurisdiction.
"An Anti-Political Dynasty Bill with real teeth should be enacted. If only our version in the House had been passed into law, political dynasties would truly be reduced," Diokno said.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: NIA assures sufficient water supply as strong El Niño draws near
articles.summary: The National Irrigation Authority (NIA) said on Sunday that adequate irrigation water is available as a strong El Niño approaches, adding that it will maintain a double dry cropping calendar to…

blocks.text: The National Irrigation Authority (NIA) said on Sunday that adequate irrigation water is available as a strong El Niño approaches, adding that it will maintain a double dry cropping calendar to maximize the dry season.
In an interview with Super Radyo dzBB, NIA Administrator Eduardo Guillen said the agency actually prefers sunny weather, which is why it is implementing double dry cropping.
“Sa pagsasaka po, sa pagtatanim natin, mas gusto nga po ng NIA ‘yung maaraw, kaya nga po binabago ng NIA ‘yung ating cropping calendar, ginagawa po naming… double dry cropping,” Guillen said.
(When it comes to farming, NIA actually prefers sunny weather. That is why NIA is shifting our cropping calendar and implementing… double dry cropping.)

“... Ang ginagawa po ng NIA ngayon, dinadala natin ‘yung ating cropping sa parteng October, aani tayo ng January, tanim ulit tayo ng March [at] aani ulit tayo ng June. So ‘yan po ‘yung tinatawag [na] double dry cropping,” he added.
(What NIA is doing now is shifting our cropping schedule to around October so we can harvest in January, then plant again in March and harvest in June. So that is what we call double dry cropping.)

Guillen pointed out that this system differs from the previous wet and dry cropping calendar, where planting started in November or December, harvest took place in March, and replanting occurred in July.

He explained that sunny weather yields higher crop output through photosynthesis, which relies on sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide. However, he emphasized that a sufficient water supply remains crucial to sustain crop growth.

Citing PAGASA, Guillen said the effects of the strong El Niño are projected to be felt in the last quarter of the year, between October and December, and will persist until the second quarter of 2027.
NIA stated that storing water is one of the key ways the agency prepares, making high dams like Magat Dam in Isabela vital to operations.
Guillen said the Magat Dam is almost full and is expected to supply irrigation to 90,000 hectares of farmland.
Meanwhile, Pantabangan Dam in Nueva Ecija, which supplies water to five areas in Luzon, is also nearly full and capable of irrigating around 120,000 hectares.
High-value crops
As part of its preparations, NIA highlighted the importance of coordination with the Department of Agriculture (DA) to jointly identify areas likely to face water shortages.
“Doon sa mga irrigated areas natin alam po ng NIA kung ilan ‘yung kaya niyang patubigan, na tataniman po natin ng palay. Kasi yung palay matakaw po sa tubig ‘yan,” Guillen said.
(In our irrigated areas, NIA knows how many hectares can be supplied with water for rice production, which requires a substantial amount of water.)

“Now, kaya po sinusulong… ‘yung masusing koordinasyon namin ng Department of Agriculture, dahil po pag na-identify namin ‘yung mga areas na kukulangin po ng patubig, marami naman po tayong pwedeng itanim na high-value crops diyan,” he added.
(That is why we are pushing for close coordination with the Department of Agriculture. Once we identify areas that will lack irrigation, we can plant various high-value crops there instead.)
Among the high-value crops he mentioned were corn and mung beans (munggo).
Guillen clarified that a lack of full irrigation does not mean fields must remain unplanted, emphasizing the critical role of interagency coordination.

NIA also urged collaboration with other government agencies, including the Department of Labor and Employment and the Department of Social Welfare and Development, to provide additional intervention measures once El Niño hits.
Farming along irrigation canals
NIA assured the public that irrigation shortages will not cause food prices to increase.
The agency highlighted its program promoting vegetable planting along irrigation canals.

“Pagkahaba-haba po ng ilang, daang libong kilometro po ang ating irrigation sa buong Pilipinas, eh kung magsipag lang yung ating mga farmers, yung ating mga irrigators association at magtanim po sa mga gilid ng irrigation natin ay malaking bagay po yan,” Guillen said.

(We have hundreds of thousands of kilometers of irrigation canals across the Philippines. If our farmers and irrigators' associations actively plant along the banks of these canals, it will be a huge help.)
Guillen said that from 2023 to 2025, vegetable farming along irrigation canals generated P1.6 billion in extra income for farmers nationwide. —RF, GMA News

articles.title: Chel Diokno: Prosecution to respect court's voting threshold decision
articles.summary: The prosecution team will respect whatever decision the Senate impeachment court makes on the voting threshold needed to either convict or acquit Vice President Sara Duterte in her impeachment trial,…

blocks.text: SARA DUTERTE IMPEACHMENT TRIAL
Published September 20, 2026 5:16pm

The prosecution team will respect whatever decision the Senate impeachment court makes on the voting threshold needed to either convict or acquit Vice President Sara Duterte in her impeachment trial, Akbayan Party-list Representative Chel Diokno said on Sunday.
“We believe that this matter is truly in the hands of the Senate as the impeachment court. Whatever decision they make on this issue, we will respect it,” Diokno told Super Radyo dzBB.
Diokno said the prosecution team is not focused on the number of votes needed for conviction but on presenting solid evidence before the impeachment court to secure Duterte’s conviction.

“We are not focused on the issue of the voting threshold. Our focus is on presenting the strongest possible case. Whatever decision the Senate impeachment court makes, we will abide by it,” Diokno said.
Oral arguments between the prosecution and defense teams are scheduled for Tuesday, September 23, 2026, in relation to the 16-vote threshold currently set for Duterte’s conviction.
In a separate dzBB interview, Senator JV Ejercito said he hoped senator-judges would be given time to study the arguments and inputs presented on the voting threshold.
“I'm asking for a few days, if possible, to absorb and study it,” he said.

Earlier this week, senator-judges sought the insights of former Supreme Court justices on whether senators who are detained, in hiding or abroad should be included in the voting on whether to convict or acquit Duterte.
Three of the four legal experts said the Senate impeachment court could change the 16-vote threshold for conviction, arguing that the Senate has the authority to try and decide impeachment cases.

Currently, Senators Jinggoy Estrada and Rodante Marcoleta are detained over separate plunder charges, while Senator Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa is in hiding amid an arrest warrant issued by the International Criminal Court. Senator Loren Legarda, meanwhile, has been absent for weeks due to health concerns and is currently abroad.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: UK minister warns of impact of Trump’s Iran war on next month’s budget
articles.summary:
Bridget Phillipson says Burnham’s past criticisms of US president not an issue as PM prepares to meet Trump at UN

Next month’s budget will be made more difficult by Donald Trump’s war with…

blocks.text: Next month’s budget will be made more difficult by Donald Trump’s war with Iran, one of Andy Burnham’s cabinet ministers has said, while adding she did not expect the prime minister’s previous disparaging comments about the US president to be an issue.
Burnham is expected to meet Trump early next week at the UN general assembly summit in New York, the pair having previously spoken twice by phone since Burnham entered No 10.
As Greater Manchester mayor, Burnham said Trump would not be welcome in the city, saying also that UK politicians who indulged him “should be ashamed”.

Asked about the comments, Bridget Phillipson, the Labour chair and minister for women and equalities, told Sky News: “Look, I think what you’ve just described there is politics. The president knows that. This is far from unique.
“People will express views at different points on different topics. And that’s no bar to having a strong relationship.”

She nonetheless repeated UK condemnation of Trump’s on-and-off military campaign against Iran, which has disrupted global oil supplies, causing significant inflationary pressures, saying this would make life more difficult for John Healey, the chancellor, as he plans the budget.
The economy was, Phillipson said, “in a strong position”, especially with growth figures.

She said: “But that’s not to take away from the very real challenges that you identify, particularly where it’s come to the conflict we’ve seen in the Middle East and the impact that that’s been having on businesses and on families close to home.

“We took the decision not to involve ourselves in that conflict. That was the right call. The US will take their own foreign policy decisions, but I believe, and still believe now, it was the right decision for us as a country not to get involved in that conflict. Of course, something that, had Kemi Badenoch and Nigel Farage been running the country, we would have jumped headlong into a conflict with it without end.

“And yet, and we do see the consequences here at home and as we go into the budget, making sure that we are doing everything we can to give people that breathing space to tackle those challenges around the cost of living has been at the forefront of everything that Andy Burnham has done since becoming prime minister.
“I know it’s at the forefront of the chancellor’s mind as he’s planning for that budget later on next month.”
after newsletter promotion

In a later interview with the BBC, Phillipson was dismissive of comments by Jim Ratcliffe, the petrochemicals billionaire, who said this week he had lost confidence in the UK due to levels of immigration and taxation.
She said: “You’ll forgive me if I do take with a pinch of salt what someone who is a tax exile has to say about our country.” Ratcliffe is resident for tax in Monaco.

Burnham has previously defended his comments about Trump in a similar way, saying of the US president: “Well, he’s said things as well, and everyone says things as politicians. In the moment, you meet people where they’re at, and you find a connection with people, and that’s always been my style.”
With the wider UK-US relationship, there were “differences of opinion”, Phillipson said, while arguing that Burnham could see beyond those differences with Trump in maintaining invaluable ties.
She said: “We don’t have the same political outlook, but the relationship between the UK and the US goes beyond any one president, any one prime minister.

“It’s something that has stood the test of time over many centuries, despite political differences. They come and go. What matters most is the British national interest. And that’s what Andy Burnham will deliver for our country.”

articles.title: Ukraine fires more than 1,000 drones at Russia, including hundreds launched at Moscow
articles.summary: Across the wider Moscow region, the attack killed two people and wounded 20, local Gov. Andrei Vorobyov said. The dead were a 74-year-old man and a 44-year-old woman, he said.

image.caption: An apartment building damaged in what authorities described as a Ukrainian drone strike, amid the Russia-Ukraine conflict in Sofyino settlement in the Ramensky district of the Moscow region on Sunday. (Reuters)

blocks.text: World
Across the wider Moscow region, the attack killed two people and wounded 20, local Gov. Andrei Vorobyov said. The dead were a 74-year-old man and a 44-year-old woman, he said.
Moscow's mayor described wave of drones as 'largest ever' attack on Russian capital

Ukrainian forces fired more than 1,000 drones at Russia overnight, including hundreds launched toward Moscow, officials said Sunday as the Kremlin was wrapping up the third and last day of its parliamentary elections.
Moscow's mayor described the wave of drones as the "largest ever" attack on the Russian capital and said there had been damage to a Moscow oil refinery and a residential building.
There was no immediate comment from Ukraine on the attack.

The voting in Russia was the country's first wartime parliamentary election — a balloting that was virtually devoid of opposition to President Vladimir Putin's policies and is all but certain to cement the Kremlin's dominance.
One of Russia's deadly jet-powered drones crashed in this backyard

Russia also held voting in four Ukrainian regions that Moscow illegally annexed after the war began but still doesn't fully control, and in Crimea, the Black Sea peninsula that was illegally annexed by Russia in 2014. Kyiv has denounced the action as illegal.
Russia's Ministry of Defence said that its forces shot down 1,100 Ukrainian drones across the country, as well as over the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea and the waters of the Black Sea.

items: Russian drones are stalking Ukrainian trains and trying to hobble the country's rail system

blocks.text: Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said that 450 drones had been destroyed en route to the Russian capital, and that the attack had damaged the Moscow Refinery and a residential building.
He said the "unprecedented attack" on the capital was an attempt to disrupt the elections.
"The enemy failed in this regard," he said.

articles.title: Chel Diokno: Higher penalties should be imposed on irresponsible gun owners
articles.summary: Higher penalties should be imposed to irresponsible gun owners who are found negligent in storing their firearms, Akbayan Party-list Representative Chel Diokno said Sunday.

blocks.text: Published September 20, 2026 4:59pm
Higher penalties should be imposed to irresponsible gun owners who are found negligent in storing their firearms, Akbayan Party-list Representative Chel Diokno said Sunday.
"Dapat rin bigyan rin ng mas malaking parusa ang mga gun owner kung sila ay pabaya," Diokno told Super Radyo dzBB.
(Gun owners should have heavier penalties if they are found to be negligent in storing their firearms.)
Diokno made the statement following a deadly school shooting in Banga, South Cotabato on Friday, where three students were killed and eight others were wounded.
The lawmaker said firing ranges should also be meted stricter penalties if these are found to allow children to handle firearms and teach them to shoot.

"Dapat mas mahigpit ang parusa dun sa mga firing range na pumapayag humawak ang bata ng baril at tinturuan kung paano bumaril, and that is also a factor na pwede ma-inflict na may hawak ng baril," Dikono said.

(There should be stricter penalties for firing ranges that allow children to handle firearms and teach them how to shoot, as these can also be factors that may lead to situations where a child has access to and being armed with a gun.)
Banga Mayor Albert Palencia reported that the weapon used in the incident belonged to the student's father, who is an employee of the Department of Education (DepEd).
Diokno said even without a law, the executive department can audit the firearms owned by all public officials and employees and require them to be inspected.

"Puede gawin ng Executive Department, mag utos sila ng isang audit ng lahat ng mga public official na may baril at alamin din nila yung safety steps na sinasagawa ng opisyal that is within their authority," Diokno said.

(The Executive Department can order an audit of all public officials who own or carry firearms and also review the safety measures being practiced by these officials, as this is within their authority.)
For private individuals, Diokno suggested that once a firearm is registered, owners should be required to agree to inspections on storing their firearms.
"Owning a gun is a big responsibility and there must be very stiff penalties for those who are negligent in terms of gun safety," Diokno said.
The lawmaker called on to strengthen the country's Anti-Bullying Law, as shooting incidents in schools have been rampant.
"Mayroon pang mas malalim na mga isyu na dapat tugunan at tingnan ang pamahalaan. Mukhang may koneksyon itong mga pangyayari sa bullying," Diokno said.
(We have more concerning issues we need to address. It seems that this has a connection with bullying.)

DepEd earlier said it would seek the help of the Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT) and the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) to investigate the “true crime community” aspect following reports that the Banga National High School shooter was involved in it.
The student shooter was reportedly part of a “true crimes community" which may have led him to copy other shooting incidents, according to Banga Mayor Albert Palencia on Friday.
DILG Secretary Jonvic Remulla on Saturday said the shooter was into the deep dark web which influenced him. —RF, GMA News

articles.summary: An oil refinery was hit in one of the largest attacks so far on the Russian capital, as the country holds a parliamentary election. Meanwhile, at least four people were killed in Russian strikes in…

image.caption: Smoke was seen rising from a refinery near MoscowImage: REUTERS

blocks.text: Two people were killed in a Ukrainian drone attack on the Moscow region, local authorities said Sunday, with an oil refinery in the region also being hit.
Energy infrastructure has been repeatedly targeted by both Ukraine and Russia, despite US President Donald Trump saying both sides had agreed to stop.
Ukraine's repeated targeting of oil refineries has led to oil product shortages and fuel price increases in Russia.
Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the strike had "a very significant impact," saying the oil in the hit refinery funds "billions of dollars to sustain the war machine."
"Moscow must end its brutal war and choose peace instead of building layered rings of air defense at the expense of other regions," Zelenskyy posted on X.

According to Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin, more than 1,600 drones have been intercepted by Russia since Saturday, including 450 aimed at the Russian capital, making it one the largest Ukrainian drone attacks on the city since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022.
Moscow mayor accuses Ukraine of trying to disrupt parliamentary election
Sobyanin said that numerous drones had made it to the oil refinery, and another one hit an apartment. The scale of the damage done to the refinery has not been confirmed.
This comes as Russia is entering the last day of its three-day parliamentary election.
Sobyanin said the "unprecedented attack was clearly planned with the aim of disrupting the elections."
Meanwhile, in the eastern Ukrainian, Russian-occupied region of Kherson, a drone attack on a bus had killed two people, including an election official, Russian state news agency RIA reported.
War anxiety casts shadow over Russia's election
Three children killed in Kyiv region
In Ukraine, four people were killed in a Russian drone attack in the Kyiv region, local authorities said.
Among the casualties are a mother and her two 3-year-old children, as well as a girl who was taken to hospital in another district and later died.
The southwestern Fastiv district suffered damage to homes and industrial buildings.
Russia has been repeatedly carrying out drone attacks on the Ukrainian capital in recent weeks.

articles.title: ‘Terribly sorry’: Wrong Korean anthem played in Asian Games hockey
articles.summary: Lined up before their match in Asian Games men's hockey, South Korean players look around in confusion as the North Korean national anthem rings out at the stadium

blocks.text: REPRESENT. Athletes of South Korea in the athletes' parade during the opening ceremony of the 2026 Asian Games at the Paloma Mizuho Stadium in Nagoya, Japan.
Eloisa Lopez/REUTERS
Lined up before their match in Asian Games men's hockey, South Korean players look around in confusion as the North Korean national anthem rings out at the stadium

NAGOYA, Japan – The South Korean men’s hockey team was left bemused before its Asian Games match against Bangladesh on Friday, September 18, when North Korea’s national anthem was played instead of its own.
Lined up before the match, the South Korean players looked around in confusion as the anthem rang out at Green Stadium in Gifu, Japan.
The stadium announcer was quick to apologize for the mistake.
“We are really sorry, terribly sorry. National anthem for the Republic of Korea, we played a different song,” he said.
“I’m really sorry.”
South Korea won the match, 5-0.
The North Korean national anthem is banned in South Korea along with other symbols of its wartime foes.
The 1950-1953 Korean War ended in an armistice rather than a peace treaty, meaning the North and South are still technically at war.
The Asian Games organizing committee did not provide immediate comment on the anthem mix-up.

South Korea has complained of a number of organizational problems at the Games, with basketball players unhappy with the size of their rooms and transport issues disrupting preparations for the men’s football team, the defending champions. – Rappler.com

articles.title: The gunzels’ grand final: Melbourne Tramaroos’ campaign derails at European TramDriver Championship
articles.summary:
The Warsaw event saw 26 teams compete across a series of demanding tasks, inspired - to varying degrees - by tram drivers’ day-to-day tasks

  • Get our

blocks.text: It’s the grand final for gunzels. But despite having one of the largest tram networks in the world, Melbourne’s Tramaroos finished second last at this year’s European TramDriver Championship, just ahead of London.
The event, held in Warsaw on Saturday, saw 26 teams compete across a series of demanding tasks, inspired – to varying degrees – by tram drivers’ day-to-day work.

In smooth stop and go, drivers travelled with a bowl of water attached to the front of the tram – with points deducted for every drop spilled. Other precision tasks involved speed control at 25 km/h, target braking, tram bowling, lateral distance, basketball, a perfect stop with the second door, and a reverse ride guided by whistle commands.
Daniel Bowen, a spokesperson for the Public Transport Users Association, said it was “an unusual event in the pantheon of world sports”.
“It’s pretty entertaining,” he said, and an opportunity to look for inspiration from great other tram systems around the world. “Everyone looked like they were having a great time.”

blocks.caption: The basketball component. Photograph: Dawid Wolski/East News/Shutterstock

blocks.text: This year’s title went to Vendula Tmejová and Zdeněk Rychtář, from Prague, in the Czech Republic.

In 2022, Australia was the first ever non-European country chosen to participate. This year, Yarra Trams sent Ivan Cavanagh of Southbank depot and Claudia Barrientos from Kew depot to compete as the “Tramaroos”. Had they won, the trophy would have gone “straight to the pool room”, Cavanagh said.
“You would hope our team would do well but I’m sure there’s pretty stiff competition against you know the Europeans,” Bowen said. “Perhaps it’s a bit like Eurovision – it’s great to participate.”

blocks.caption: A member of the Danish team from Odense celebrates after their final run. Photograph: Wojtek Radwański/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Thousands of fans followed the spectacle live in Warsaw, with about 80,000 viewers worldwide watching the competition via livestream.
Melbourne is set to host the next event in 2027.
Bowen said it would be interesting to see if other Australian cities joined the competition, given recent extensions to light rail systems in Adelaide, Sydney, Canberra and the Gold Coast.

“Back in Melbourne, it’s a reminder that trams do form a vital part of the transport system. We do have the biggest tram network in the world, but there’s more to do in terms of accessibility and on-road priority and service frequency.”

articles.title: Victims say Home Office attempt to curtail spycops inquiry will result in a ‘cover-up’
articles.summary:
Shabana Mahmood is concerned about length and £144m cost of inquiry into intrusive police surveillance

Victims of intrusive police surveillance have accused the government of seeking to cut…

blocks.text: Victims of intrusive police surveillance have accused the government of seeking to cut short the spycops public inquiry that has been examining widespread misconduct committed by undercover officers.

The independent judge-led inquiry is scrutinising how officers, who spied on tens of thousands of political activists over more than four decades, carried out abuses such as deceiving women into sexual relationships and fathering children.
The inquiry has been running for more than a decade, and is expected to last another two years.

The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, has said she is concerned about the length and cost of the process. It was set up in 2015 and was supposed to have been completed within three years. Latest figures show the inquiry, which has been led by retired judge Sir John Mitting, has so far cost £144m.
Mahmood initiated a public consultation, which closes on Sunday, that she said would help determine whether the inquiry should continue in a different format.

However, those who were spied on say that the Home Office is looking to severely limit or scrap the later stages, leaving the full extent of wrongdoing by the police hidden. They say more than 2,000 people have objected to what they believe would be a cover-up.

The spycops inquiry is one of the longest-running public inquiries. According to the House of Commons, the longest in modern times was an inquiry into a sectarian murder in Northern Ireland which reported last week, 22 years after being commissioned.
It has so far been investigating the Special Demonstration Squad (SDS), a Metropolitan police unit that infiltrated political groups between 1968 and 2008.

The inquiry has heard how the SDS officers formed long-term relationships with women without disclosing to them their true identity, spied on grieving families such as the parents of murdered teenager Stephen Lawrence, stole the identities of dead children and lied in court hearings.
It is due to examine a second undercover squad, the National Public Order Intelligence Unit, which infiltrated political groups between 1999 and 2011.

One of the unit’s key undercover officers was Mark Kennedy who infiltrated environmental and left-wing groups for six years. He deceived a large, but unknown, number of women into intimate relationships.
Environmental campaigners had their criminal convictions overturned because crucial evidence gathered by Kennedy was withheld from their trials.

The inquiry is also scheduled to look at the case of an undercover police officer who used his fake identity while infiltrating serious crime to deceive a woman into a 19-year relationship during which they had a child together.

Victims of the surveillance say that the consultation is phoney and rigged as it only offers three alternatives: an inquiry with a narrower remit, one that would not have legal powers to force reluctant witnesses to testify or asking the police to disclose documents to victims without any type of inquiry.

Kate Wilson, who was deceived into a two-year relationship by Kennedy, said: “Whatever the intentions of the Home Office in doing this, the practical effect of them curtailing the inquiry or reducing its powers to compel evidence will be a cover-up, and we may never understand the full extent of the misconduct that has occurred in undercover policing.”
A Home Office spokesperson said: “The historic failings in undercover policing continue to shock the public. We are determined to get justice and hold those responsible to account.

“However, the undercover policing inquiry was established more than a decade ago, and is yet to deliver justice for those affected, at significant cost to the taxpayer. It’s only right that we ask those affected themselves about the future of the inquiry.”

articles.title: Canada's 'Railway City' wants passenger trains back. Like much of the country, it's not so simple
articles.summary: Canada is spending billions to expand passenger rail after decades of decline, but torn-up tracks, lost corridors and a surviving network built around freight means communities trying to bring trains…

image.caption: The former Michigan Central Railway Locomotive Shops sit on 3.2 hectares of former railway lands in St. Thomas, Ont. Built in 1913, the building is now home to the Elgin County Railway Museum, but is closed to the public because of structural concerns. (Patrick Morrell/CBC News)

blocks.text: Canada·New

Canada is spending billions to expand passenger rail after decades of decline, but torn-up tracks, lost corridors and a surviving network built around freight means communities trying to bring trains back face a very different railway than the one they lost.
St. Thomas, Ont., is a vivid example of the obstacles facing communities across Canada
What happened to Canada's 'Railway City?'
To an outsider, the 3.2-hectare sea of grass surrounding the Elgin County Railway Museum in the heart of St. Thomas, Ont., might look like an urban park. That's not what Wil Zufelt sees.
To him, it's an enormous open wound.
"You say green space," he said. "We're actually sitting in the middle of a brownfield site that was left behind from the railroads."

Built in 1913, the hulking red-brick building was once the Michigan Central Railway Locomotive Shops, where locomotives were maintained and overhauled by a staff of 400 workers. It's one of three survivors of a sprawling railway complex that once had 112 buildings.
The old building is now a museum, but it can't welcome visitors. It's literally crumbling. The city engineer ordered it closed after finding its walls were bowing and its ceiling was unsafe.
'Pay attention to what we're losing'
"People need to wake up," Zufelt said. "Pay attention to what we're losing."
Zufelt heads Railworks, the organization behind three of St. Thomas's surviving railway landmarks. He's launching a campaign to raise $8 million to save and restore the former locomotive shops.
The goal is to turn the old locomotive shops into not just a museum, but an active gathering place at the centre of a redeveloped downtown.

"I want it to be more than alive. I want it to be the centre of St. Thomas," he said. "That's what success is, is putting a heartbeat back in the core and then you have your arteries and everything pumps out from the middle."

By 1914, eight railways converged on St. Thomas, bringing more than 100 trains through the southwestern Ontario city every day. Its location made it a major hub for American rail traffic between Detroit and Buffalo and between New York and Chicago. The cross-border connection was so important, at one point, St. Thomas even had a U.S. consulate.
Today, the community that calls itself the "Railway City" has no rail connection at all.
Tracks that snake everywhere and nowhere

The railways are long gone, but their remains are scattered across the city — empty lots filled with rubble from where railway buildings once stood, abandoned shunting yards, railway spikes that turn up like seashells on a beach and tracks that snake everywhere and nowhere.
The old London to Port Stanley Railway runs past a restored station in St. Thomas before it abruptly ends — disappearing into the grass of a residential neighbourhood.

The missing connection was the subject of a 1990 federal transport order requiring CN to replace the missing diamond at its own expense once the line reached CN tracks. But the physical connection was never completed.
Today, part of the former route is blocked by a parking lot enclosed by a fence.
The Canadian Transport Agency told CBC News the order remains in effect and CN's obligation would still apply if the physical connection were made.
CN did not respond to a request for comment by publication time.
What St. Thomas tells us about Canada's railways

St. Thomas is an unusually stark example of what happened in communities across Canada as the railway era receded, according to Thomas Blampied, a historian who studied Canada's railway history at the University of Toronto.
"Cars started to eat away at passenger revenue from railways and trucks started to take some of the freight traffic," he said.
As passengers moved to cars and freight moved to trucks, railways abandoned increasingly unprofitable routes. They didn't simply stop running trains. Much of the infrastructure was removed with them.
"Do we keep the infrastructure — so the track, all the signals, all the crossing warnings — do we keep it all intact?" Blampied said. "Increasingly, the answer was no."
In some cases, the rails were sold for scrap, in many cases, he said, "it made economic sense to completely withdraw."
But even where the railway lines survived, the network changed.
Canada looks to bring passenger rail back

Anthony Perl, a transportation policy expert at Simon Fraser University, said railways removed passing tracks and other infrastructure once passenger trains disappeared, reshaping the network around the needs of freight.

"We had a great streamlining, or right-sizing, or value engineering, pick your term — of the national rail infrastructure in Canada as passenger trains went away," Perl said. "To optimize it for long, slow freight trains."
He said that matters now because Canada is trying to put passenger trains back on a network that, in many places, was either removed or rebuilt for another purpose.

In Ontario, the province is preparing to restore Northlander passenger service between Toronto and northeastern Ontario, more than a decade after it was cancelled. The federal government meanwhile, is developing Alto, a new high-speed passenger railway between Toronto and Quebec City that would run largely on its own tracks.
Other communities are pushing for passenger rail to return, including on Vancouver Island, in Alberta between Calgary and Banff and in Cape Breton.
The power of owning the tracks
But Canada's railways have something airlines and trucking companies don't: control over the infrastructure they use.

"No one is going to build an alternative set of rails across this country under any circumstances," Perl said. "That's why they make the call on whether to put in or take out tracks in particular places."
In St. Thomas, CN has yet to restore the missing connection between London and Port Stanley.

"Even when the Canadian Transportation Agency orders them to do something they don't want to do," he said, "it can take quite a while, if ever, that they will go along with it because they have the ownership of that infrastructure."
Perl argues that kind of power has deep roots in the railway business and points to language the industry has given us.
"To 'railroad someone' is to take advantage and treat someone unfairly or unjustly," he said. "You don't see that with too many other industries."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Colin Butler is based in London, Ont., where he reports for Ontario and national audiences. He covers investigative, science, public policy and government accountability with a particular interest in using public records to uncover hidden stories.
