articles.title: Why Prince Harry and Meghan face more challenges after their return to the U.K.
articles.summary: Issues that arose when Prince Harry and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, stepped back from official duties in 2020, along with new challenges around concerns such as security, are front and centre after…

image.caption: Prince Harry speaks to members of the Irish Guards' Band as he arrives at the Invictus Games Foundation's inaugural Invictus Spirit Awards at Old Royal Naval College in London, England, on Thursday. (Aaron Chown/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Public or private? Personal or officially royal?
In ways, it can get confusing — there was Prince Harry, smiling for the cameras that often capture his comings and goings as he arrived at a charitable event Thursday night in London.

His attendance at an awards ceremony connected to the Invictus Games, which he founded for wounded and ill service members, garnered headlines. Media reports noted that it was his first appearance in public since he and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, returned to the U.K. from California with their two children late last month.
Still, in the past few days, it has also been made clear — via a letter from Buckingham Palace — that he and Meghan remain non-working members of the Royal Family.
"In short, their position is akin to ​private citizens with commercial and charitable interests," the letter stated.

The missive from the palace and all the media attention it garnered in recent days are a stark reminder that issues that arose when Harry and Meghan stepped back from official duties in 2020 remain front and centre with their return to Britain.
Harry and Meghan moving back to the U.K.

The letter affirms that King Charles agrees with his late mother, Queen Elizabeth, that there can't be members of the Royal Family “who are half in and half out, especially in the 21st century,” Toronto-based royal historian Carolyn Harris said in an interview.
At the beginning of Elizabeth’s reign, she was “quite inclusive” in terms of bringing in members of her extended family to carry out royal duties, Harris said.
But times — and public expectations — have changed.

“In the current climate, when there's a lot of scrutiny of how taxpayers’ money is being spent … the emphasis now is on a small, streamlined Royal Family and for there to be a clear divide between those who are working members of the Royal Family and those who are not,” Harris said.
The letter — particularly the timing of its release — seemed to catch Harry and Meghan off guard, and was seen by some royal observers as a “brutal put-down” for the couple.
The line “has been drawn in the sand quite clearly,” Chandrika Kaul, a professor of modern history at the University of St. Andrews in Scotland, said in an interview.

“The palace … has issued statements very clearly saying that if Harry and Meghan wish to do whatever they wish to do in terms of charity work or other engagements, they're doing so in their own capacity as private individuals,” she said.
“They are not representing the Royal Family or the monarchy.”
Harris sees parallels between Harry and Meghan’s return to the U.K. and their departure six years ago.
“As in 2020, Harry and Meghan might have thought making a major life change is going to lead to certain decisions unfolding in their favour, and instead there are challenges.”

Six years ago, one initial challenge was whether Harry and Meghan might, as they seemed to hope, essentially be part-time working royals while also pursuing private, commercial interests. The answer from the Queen ultimately was a clear “No.”

This time, one challenge has been around security, an issue that has been of particular concern and spawned a previous, unsuccessful legal challenge from Harry. Now, however, the U.K. government committee that oversees tax-funded security for public figures and royalty will reconsider the level of police protection for the couple.

Earlier this week, word also emerged that Harry and Meghan’s children, Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5, were changing schools, reportedly because of security concerns raised over traffic and the length of the commute from their home.
“Prince Harry may be hoping that a decision will be made in his favour regarding security now that they are back in the United Kingdom,” said Harris.
“But there is a long history of Harry and Meghan making a major life change, but the details are still to be arranged, and that can lead to tensions on all sides.”

items: Charles confirms Harry and Meghan to remain non-working royals after their return to U.K.
The 'shockwaves' of Prince Harry and Meghan's return to the U.K.

blocks.text: Overall, says Kaul, attention and reaction to Harry and Meghan’s return has been “relatively muted.”
“It has been noticed and covered and discussed on national mainstream media, but … the popular media haven't gone berserk over the impact.”
She also sees the potential for Harry to carve out a new identity now that he’s back in the U.K.
“There has always been and there continues to be a great deal of public affection and regard for Harry. I don't think that's ever gone away.”
The King and AI

Inside the restored 18th-century Palladian country house that serves as the home of his charitable foundation, King Charles signalled both the hopes and risks that surround a very 21st-century concern.

“AI is already showing its immense capacity to improve and save life — for example, in the field of life sciences and medicine,” Charles told leaders of some of the world’s leading AI firms who accepted his invitation to come to Dumfries House in southwestern Scotland on Thursday.

“Yet, those who have created these technologies are now increasingly warning that AI risks developing darker capacities — perhaps even to take life. In this regard, if I may say so, there seems urgency in adequately considering the existential dangers of such technologies falling into the wrong hands, and being used in potentially catastrophic ways.
“Surely, we need sufficient means of control before it is all too late?”
Charles’s convening of AI leaders is in keeping with both longstanding interests the monarchy has had in technology and his own efforts to bring people together on issues of the day.

“There's always these intersections between royalty and new technology, whether it's Queen Victoria embracing photography and then right at the end of her reign, film, or Queen Elizabeth II embracing video conferencing during the COVID-19 pandemic,” Harris said.
King Charles warns AI leaders of 'existential dangers'
But there was more than that at play on Thursday, Harris suggested.
“For King Charles III, it's clear that he sees his role as King is to bring people together in the hope that solutions to complicated issues may be found.”
Charles does that from a unique position, Harris suggested.
“It's part of that unifying role of the monarch, the ability to bring people together. Anyone who receives an invitation to Buckingham Palace is likely to accept.”
Kaul also saw the focus on AI as a reflection of some of Charles’s longstanding interests and perspectives.

“It testifies to the King's lifelong commitment not just to technology, but to this kind of harmonious balance between nature and human beings and his deep interest in civilization and the continuation of culture.”
Charles’s actions also reflected an effort to bring people together in a way that differed from how his mother might have approached issues of the day.
“I think there is a greater sense that it is Charles who's driving the agenda,” Kaul said.

“The Queen's way of handling it was always to clearly weigh up the issues, but … particularly in her later years, [she] seemed to … put the royal mark of approval on an agenda rather than necessarily take a leading role in pushing an item onto the agenda.”

items: The pandemic puts the royals online — and 'at their best'

blocks.text: In his speech on Thursday, Charles posed two questions:

“First, how can we harness the benefits of AI, with safety at its heart? And, second, how can we build international co-operation and consensus to achieve this, so no nation is left behind, but the human race is left in place?”
Humanity, he said, “must remain sacred.”

“The decisions taken at this formative time will shape the world inherited by future generations. And so, the task before you is not merely to advance technology, but to ensure that it remains firmly in the service of humanity, community and the natural world. As we embrace what is new, we must not lose what is timeless.”
Coming together to prevent suicide
Prince William was doing some convening of his own the other day on one of his key charitable priorities when he met with star athletes and leaders of sports organizations.
Along with Catherine, Princess of Wales, William was on hand at the Everton Football Club to launch a suicide prevention initiative.
“Sport creates belonging. It creates identity. It creates connection. And those connections matter,” William said.

“When somebody is struggling, often it is not a professional who first notices. It is a friend. A coach. A colleague. A teammate. Someone who sees a change. Someone who asks if everything is all right. Someone who starts a conversation. And that conversation could make all the difference.”

items: Prince William embraces 'change for good' — but how radical will he be?
Huge wildlife corridor project is 1st Canadian finalist for Earthshot Prize

blocks.text: The suicide prevention toolkit launched by William aims to help people across sport have “the confidence to recognize warning signs, start supportive conversations and connect individuals with help before they reach crisis point,” Kensington Palace said.
In the initiative, Harris saw a reflection of the interests of several members of the Royal Family.

“We see a bit of Prince Philip's influence in terms of the interest in sport, but also William and Catherine, and at one time Prince Harry as well, were all very concerned with mental health and mental health initiatives.”

There is also the concern William’s mother, Diana, Princess of Wales, had in marginalized people and making “them feel loved and accepted,” Harris said, along with the concern his father, King Charles, has had in youth and opportunities for them.
A brother's claim and a palace response
The response came quickly, by royal standards.

Not long after the first headlines emerged online Wednesday about claims the brother of the late Diana, Princess of Wales, is making in a book to be released this coming week, Buckingham Palace had a statement of its own.
In a published excerpt of Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, Charles Spencer claims that King Charles said his former wife would soon be forgotten after her death.

Spencer says he told Charles that Diana would not have wanted their sons, William and Harry, then 15 and 12, to walk behind her coffin in the funeral procession. He claims Charles told him: "Rest assured, we'll forget her soon enough." He also accuses Charles of having "contempt" for his ex-wife.
The palace responded later Wednesday with a statement of its own.

"While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognize, even many years after such a loss," it said.
Harris sees parallels in that statement to another high-profile reaction from the palace.

“In common with Queen Elizabeth II's statement that ‘recollections may vary’ after Harry and Meghan were interviewed by Oprah Winfrey, King Charles III is refusing to allow Earl Spencer to have the last word on circumstances concerning the Royal Family,” she said.
“The King has his own memories of the days following Diana's death and they are not the same as those of Earl Spencer.”
Diana died after a car crash in Paris in 1997.

items: Buckingham Palace hits back at claims in a book by Princess Diana’s brother
Diana's legacy: Why it still resonates 25 years after her death

blocks.text: Nearly 30 years after her death, she continues to captivate and draw headlines, and says Harris, her legacy continues to be debated and contested.

“Diana combined glamour with vulnerability and people from a variety of social and cultural backgrounds saw themselves in aspects of her experiences even though she was born into the aristocracy and married a prince,” said Harris.
“Recent films, television series, plays and novels have revived interest in Diana for a new generation who remember the princess through popular culture portrayals rather than historical events.”
Royally quotable
"The shock of witnessing these fires around the world in recent months reminds us forcibly of the mounting pressures that prolonged heat and drought are placing upon our precious Earth.”
— King Charles, in a message where he expressed his admiration for those who helped tackle wildfires across the U.K. this summer.
Royal reads

Enslaved African people were seared with hot metal brands bearing the royal crown, according to research by historians who have documented the monarchy’s centuries-long involvement in Britain’s slave trade. [The Guardian]
Prince William has launched a community fund to revive a village in southwestern England. [The Independent]
The Princess of Wales visited the cancer hospital where she was treated for the illness and praised the "incredible" care she received. [Sky News]
The Duchess of Edinburgh tried her hand at polishing gemstones at a local family jewellery business in Zambia on the second day of her tour of the African country. [Daily Mail]
Prince George posed for a portrait in his new school uniform after arriving for his first day at Eton College accompanied by his proud parents, the Prince and Princess of Wales. [Daily Mail]

Prince Harry and Meghan's highly publicized return to England got the full Saturday Night Live UK treatment — and in true British fashion, the welcome was served with a distinctly chilly reception. [CBC]
Lost or long-discarded items revealing glimpses of the behind-the-scenes life of Buckingham Palace staff over decades have been uncovered during the restoration of the monarchy’s HQ. [The Guardian]

articles.title: Protection for women who defy the Mafia is changing in Italy. Does it go far enough?
articles.summary: For women speaking out against the Mafia, the protection offered can be both practically and emotionally challenging. A new Italian law extending protection from organized crime to children and the…

image.caption: Piera Aiello spent nearly three decades living under another identity to keep her safe, after testifying about the Sicilian Mafia family she had married into. (CBC)

blocks.text: The women who defied the Italian Mafia — and the price they paid
"Take a map of Italy, tear Sicily from it and throw it away."

That was the advice the late anti-Mafia prosecutor Paolo Borsellino gave a young Piera Aiello in 1991, when she came to him to say she was ready to tell all about the Sicilian Mafia family she had married into.

Aiello's husband had been gunned down in front of her in the pizzeria they ran together. He was the abusive son of the local Mafia boss, and Aiello had been coerced into marrying him as a teen. Still, she wanted his killers caught.
"I have already decided," she recalls telling Borsellino about her decision to testify. "I just need to pack my bags."
Three days later, Aiello left Sicily with two suitcases — one filled with clothes, the other with toys for her three-year-old daughter.
The following year, Borsellino was killed, along with five members of his police escort, in a Mafia car bombing in the Sicilian capital of Palermo.
Aiello would spend most of the next three decades living under another identity, which kept her safe from the Mafia.
But cut off from her Sicily and her old life, building a new one was lonely and arduous.
"I couldn't find work, and I had to support my daughter," she said, explaining how she found work in the countryside harvesting olives, eventually saving enough to open a small business.

Aiello's early years in protection reveal a less visible aspect to Italy's long fight against organized crime: what happens after someone speaks out. For women, the rupture can be both practically and emotionally tougher.

A new Italian law extending protection from organized crime — and providing social, economic, educational and psychological help — to children and the adults caring for them, often their mothers, is designed to address some of those gaps.
Limits of protection
Liberi di scegliere — the "Free to Choose" bill — became law in July and entered into force on Aug. 9.

Sen. Vincenza Rando spent years pushing for the law and working with women who wanted to break away from Mafia families. Many of them, she says, fall outside the categories around which Italy's traditional protection system had been built.
"Women who are neither justice witnesses nor co-operating witnesses, I call them 'cultural collaborators.' They leave that environment and build a culture of legality," Rando said.

They may not be informants or have any useful intel about a murder, a drug shipment or an extortion racket. Their act of rebellion, she says, may simply be deciding that their children will not grow up inside a Mafia family and culture.

Rando says some leave homes flush with cash, only to end up with nothing. Others need a new identity just to sign an employment contract without being traced. Their children are forced to change schools and friends, thrust into a life with entirely different moral codes.
"If you move somewhere where nobody knows you and you cannot even say who you are, who can you talk to?" Rando asked. "Who can you safely tell your story to?"

Under the new legislation, people under the age of 25 and relatives who care for them may be relocated outside their home region, provided with education and psychological support and, where necessary, given new identities.
Critics say the law gives the state too much power over family life, allowing for the separation of children from parents, which could be seen as punishing children for their parents' crime.

items: Lea Garofalo was killed by her Mafia family. Now she's the face of anti-mob protests

blocks.text: But Rando and supporters say the law prioritizes keeping mothers and children together when the mother breaks with the criminal group.
Aiello supports its aims, but worries short-term intervention will not be enough to permanently break the cycle. She says longer-term support through education and job training is essential.
"What does it mean for the State to take responsibility for them for two years?" Aiello asked. "It means nothing."
For Aiello, the lesson from her own experience is that protection has to mean more than physical safety: it also has to provide the tools to build an independent life.
The 'privilege' of never walking alone
Anti-Mafia prosecutor Nino Di Matteo has spent most of his career seeing the cost of protection from the inside.

He has lived under police escort since 1993, at times under Italy's highest level of security. His two children were born while he was already under protection; within days of leaving hospital, he recalls, they too were travelling in an escort car.
Now based in Rome, he says people outside Sicily sometimes perceive police protection as a mark of status, which he says irritates him.

"People can tend to see the protected person as privileged," Di Matteo said. "From that point of view, I would rather not be 'privileged.' People should perhaps think about the sacrifice involved in never being able to take a walk alone."

Di Matteo is equally wary of a lot of the mythology surrounding the Mafia itself. He points to the media's focus on its most cinematic elements of violence and overt criminality — "the so-called military Mafia" — rather than the white-collar Mafiosi who appear to be part of legitimate businesses and cultivate relationships with political and institutional power.
And he says women's roles in that world have also frequently been misunderstood.
"Women have always played a fundamental role, for both good and bad," Di Matteo said.

Some wives and mothers are the family enforcers of the Mafia identity of husbands and sons. Others have rebelled against it — often painfully breaking away — to become justice witnesses and campaigners.
"For a woman I imagine it may be even harder," Di Matteo said of criminal organizations built heavily around kinship. "Especially when speaking out means accusing your own son, your own blood."
When Mafia threats reach your family
Federica Angeli came to protection by a very different route.
An investigative journalist in Ostia, Rome's gritty seaside district, Angeli spent years reporting on local criminal clans and their grip on parts of Ostia's lucrative beachfront economy.

In 2013, during one investigation, Mafia boss Armando Spada discovered the hidden camera she was carrying. Angeli says he detained her upstairs in a room, placed a gun between them and made clear that he knew where she was most vulnerable.
"You have three children. What shall we do?" Angeli remembers him saying to another man. "Shall we start with the youngest one, the one with the pretty eyes?"
A month later she witnessed an attempted double murder near her home. She testified and was placed under police protection.

For 13 years, armed escorts have followed Angeli through ordinary life: work, dinner out with friends, a day at the beach, family outings. She says friends stopped inviting her over because security officers first had to inspect their homes. Restaurants meant being seated according to security requirements. Spontaneity vanished.

Angeli chronicled her ordeal in the memoir A mano disarmata (Unarmed), later adapted into a feature film. In 2016, Italian President Sergio Mattarella made her a Knight of the Order of Merit of the Italian Republic.

But despite the public recognition, the beachfront clean-up in Ostia has sometimes generated resentment: Angeli says she hears residents complain that some establishments worked better under Mafia-linked operators. Other criticism aimed at her is more gendered.

"As a woman, and as a mother, I was heavily criticized for my choice," she said. "Everyone said, 'You put your children in danger,'" who for five years were placed under protection, too, due to threats.
But she rejects the idea that there is one correct maternal response.
"There is no handbook for being the right mother," she said of the decision to denounce organized crime. "But I wanted to free my children from having to bow to the Mafia."

items: The Mafia from the mountains

blocks.text: Piera Aiello wanted the same thing for her daughter when she left Sicily.

She built a new life near Rome, and in 2018, she was elected to parliament — Italy's first sitting justice witness — after a long battle to regain her real name. She sat on the Antimafia and Justice committees, where she pushed for stronger witness protections.
And, this summer, more than three decades after Borsellino told her to tear Sicily from the map, she moved back to her beloved island.
"I kept that crumpled piece of Sicily in a drawer," she said, "And I picked it up and glued it back on."

articles.title: MPs are heading back to Parliament Hill. Here's what to watch this sitting
articles.summary: MPs are heading back to Parliament Hill on Monday to pick up where they left off in June. Here are some key things to watch this fall sitting.

image.caption: MPs are back on Parliament Hill for the fall legislative sitting. (Brian Morris/CBC)

blocks.text: MPs are heading back to Parliament Hill on Monday to pick up where they left off in June.
While the break is usually a quiet time in the political world, this past summer seemed anything but.

U.S. President Donald Trump threatened new tariffs in July (including over wildfire smoke) and trade talks subsequently ramped up only to collapse in August. Prime Minister Mark Carney made moves to deepen Canada's ties with the European Union.
All of this happened after the final whistle blew at the FIFA World Cup — which, to some, may feel like more than two months ago.
Carney's government will now be turning from diplomacy to its legislative agenda with an opposition that will be pushing for answers. Here are some key things to watch this fall sitting.
Economic legislation will be 'centrepiece' of fall sitting, says MacKinnon
The prime minister just returned from Strasbourg, France, where he addressed the European Parliament about forming some kind of new alliance with the 27 countries that make up the European Union.
The precise details of that arrangement still need to be worked out, but Carney suggested it could touch on things like critical minerals, AI, defence, energy and finance.

items: Canada won't pay directly into EU budget under Carney's plan: ambassador-designate

blocks.text: Regardless of what is agreed to between the federal government and the powers that be in Europe, Carney said the agreement would be debated and voted on in the House. A final vote might not happen this fall but debate about the relationship is likely to be ongoing with more details expected to be unveiled at the Canada‑EU summit in October.
Conservatives seeking 'a lot of accountability' from Carney on EU proposal

There are no signs that trade talks with the U.S. will happen anytime soon and the Trump administration will likely be fixated on the upcoming midterm elections rather than Canada. But things may change once those ballots are tallied in November.

On both fronts, the Conservatives will be pushing the government for more details. Leader Pierre Poilievre has called on Carney to release the text of the rejected trade deal — which negotiators say is protected by confidentiality agreements — and present a cost analysis of Canada's counter-tariffs.
Poilievre has also come out against getting too close to the EU, arguing Canada can't "afford European taxes, laws and open borders chaos."
Legislative agenda
The government will have to balance new bills they want to bring to the House floor this fall with legislative work they have left over from the spring.
Government House leader Steven MacKinnon told CBC's Rosemary Barton Live that the economy, jobs and trade will be major focuses for the Liberals this fall.
"Affordability is, of course, a major preoccupation for the government alongside our continued prosperity," he told host Rosemary Barton.

The biggest highlight will most likely be the budget. Last year, Carney bucked the trend of the federal government unveiling its overall spending plans in the spring and instead opted to introduce budgets in the fall.
Carney: 'High standards do not mean decisions have to be slow'

The prime minister gave some hints of what to expect in the upcoming budget during last week's investment summit. During an address at the event, Carney said the government will be able to balance the operating budget — which it loosely defines as day-to-day spending on government programs — by next year, one year ahead of schedule.

Carney also announced that he plans to build on a tax deduction announced in last year's budget by introducing a productivity "mega-deduction" that will allow companies to expense the total cost of new investments across a number of sectors.

items: 'Mega' tax writeoffs, private money for airports: How Carney's investment summit unfolded

blocks.text: But speaking of last year's budget, there is still a touch of work to be done. Bill C-31, which officially implements portions of the 2025 budget, will be before committee this fall and needs to have a few more votes in Parliament before it passes. That bill includes tax changes and defence procurement provisions.

There are a number of other bills left over from the spring, including legislation to restrict access to social media platforms for kids under the age of 16, create a framework to protect drinking water in First Nations communities (which is receiving heavy scrutiny) and tighten privacy rules and regulations for companies handling Canadians' data.
A number of new bills are expected to be brought forward this fall, starting with legislation to extend the excise tax holiday on gasoline which will be introduced this week.

The Liberals are also expected to table legislation to further streamline the review process for major projects and make changes to the Labour Code. Two sources told CBC News that the bill is expected to be tabled this week.

The Labour Code changes will focus on industries that impact Canada's global exports, such as ports and railways, the sources said. Under the new rules, the labour minister would be explicitly allowed to direct the Canada Industrial Relations Board to end work stoppages in high-risk bargaining situations, the sources said.
A special mediator would have to issue a report prior to the minister intervening. That mediator would be appointed by the minister.
Key voting days, provincially and federally
Opposition parties are coming back to the House with less leverage than they had a year ago after the Liberals were able to secure a majority government in April.

The Liberals bolstered numbers over the summer, sweeping three byelections in August. Two wins were in ridings previously by the governing party, but the Liberals picked up a seat in Quebec that was previously held by Conservative Richard Martel.

As things stand, the Liberals have 173 seats (including the Speaker who only votes when there is a tie) to the oppositions' combined 164 seats. There are half a dozen vacancies that still need to be filled which will give parties opportunities to boost their numbers.

Three of the six vacant seats are in Quebec: Laurier-Sainte-Marie, Rosemont-La Petite-Patrie and Saint-Hyacinthe-Bagot-Acton. Scarborough North and Brantford-Brant South-Six Nations in Ontario as well as Saskatchewan's Yorkton-Melville round out the list of currently empty sets.
Two of the seats were last held by Liberals MPs, including former cabinet minister Steven Guilbeault. Two others were previously Conservative while the Bloc Québécois and NDP held one each.

A byelection needs to be called between 11 and 180 days after an MP officially resigns. Given most of the currently empty seats were vacated in the last month, Carney could wait until February to call those votes.

But Saint-Hyacinthe-Bagot-Acton needs to be called by Dec. 19 because former Bloc MP Simon-Pierre Savard-Tremblay stepped down in June and there has been a tendency to lump byelections together. The Liberals also currently have a strong lead in polls and Carney may be tempted to strike while the iron is hot.
Federal byelections aren't the only races that politicians in Ottawa will be having an eye on as voters prepare to cast their ballots at the provincial level this fall.
Alberta referendum campaigns prepare for final push ahead of the October vote

Out west, Albertans are set to vote on 10 referendum questions, including whether they want to remain in Canada or start the legal process required to hold a second, binding referendum on leaving the country.
Polls indicated that the remain side has vastly more support, but the outcome may come down to voter turnout. Regardless of the results, there are bound to be some ripple effects in Ottawa.

On the eastern side of the country, Quebec is having a provincial election with the separatist Parti Québécois aiming to form its first government in over a decade. Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon had promised a separation referendum in the first year of a new mandate, but has since backtracked a tad to suggest he would wait until Trump is no longer in office.
The House of Commons is expected to sit until Dec. 11 when it will break for the holidays.

articles.title: New Brunswick is weaving AI into its K-12 curriculum, drawing praise — and pushback
articles.summary: New Brunswick is incorporating learning about AI into its anglophone K-12 curriculum, amid wider calls to emphasize teaching young Canadians how to responsibly use the technology for school. However,…

image.caption: A Moncton teacher discusses activities with her Grade 7 tech class. New Brunswick has unveiled a school curriculum update that blends in learning about AI, from kindergarten through Grade 12, for anglophone schools. Yet amid wider calls for teaching youngsters if, when and how AI should be used for

blocks.text: In a Moncton middle school this week, students entered a virtual dungeon, tasked with escaping from the dragon within while learning about cybersecurity.
After, some moved on to designing a visual presentation, while others tapped through colourful screens to read and answer questions for a unit about food. A few more programmed tiny robots.
Artificial intelligence tools were part of the activities, as the Grade 7 students worked under the watchful eyes of their teacher.

For the last few years, the Anglophone East School District has been exploring bringing AI into its classrooms, but now more New Brunswick schools are joining them, after the Department of Education added learning about AI into its updated anglophone K-12 curriculum.

The move comes as some international school systems recently set strict prohibitions around AI, with Norway banning most student use of generative AI through Grade 7, and the two largest U.S. school boards (New York and Los Angeles) restricting student use.

Amid wide, ongoing calls for more consistency and clarity teaching students when, how and if AI should be used, some are calling for more deliberation and pushing back against the technology in classrooms right now, especially for younger learners.
New Brunswick's approach

The curriculum update in New Brunswick basically fleshes out its digital literacy curriculum to incorporate AI in a structured way, according to André Côté, executive director of public policy think tank The Dais at Toronto Metropolitan University.

It's an important first step he hopes other provincial and territorial peers will soon follow, given that our education systems generally haven't moved urgently enough to address the "tsunami of AI use that has washed into schools," he said.

New Brunswick has "mindfully integrated" AI so educators can teach students in an age-appropriate way and to consider the technology with a critical eye, says Jordan Smith, Anglophone East's tech, innovation and AI subject coordinator.

That means students in kindergarten through Grade 2 start to learn basic digital literacy concepts via classroom discussions, says Smith, a former elementary teacher. They will talk about how they feel during and after using technology, for instance, or noticing that information from digital sources or tools isn't always correct.
As students get older, they start practising on digital devices like tablet computers, but AI in the curriculum doesn't mean primary students using chatbots, she said.

Smith noted that any school use of AI tools must adhere to platform age restrictions and, of Anglophone East's nine approved platforms, about half are listed as for students 13+ (younger students require parental consent) and a third are for teachers alone.

Along with the Microsoft chatbot Copilot (accessible to Grade 9 and up), that approved list includes visual design platform Canva, music-maker Suno and chatbot Gemini Notebook that works from user uploads (for educator use).

In high school, a student might input their interests into Copilot to generate potential book choices for an independent study, she shared as an example, or use it to analyze the intro to an essay they're writing. Students learn to consider any use or interaction with AI critically, Smith emphasized, and use it as support but not a shortcut for their own work.

Smith also said teachers are getting professional development on multiple fronts, with educators in her district trained at periodic professional development sessions and supported in class by a roving team of tech coaches. The province has also released learning modules about AI for teachers.

New Brunswick's anglophone curriculum update incorporates safe and ethical AI use in schools and development of AI literacy, Education Minister Claire Johnson told CBC News in a statement Friday, noting similar work is ongoing on the francophone side.
Integration, however, doesn't displace "fundamentals of literacy and numeracy," she said, nor the importance of teacher judgement for learning.

This is a learning journey schools and families are on together, according to Anglophone East Superintendent Randolph MacLean. "It's very much a Rubik's Cube that we're all working on at the same time — and we don't have all the sides figured out yet," he said.
However, "introduction of any new piece of technology, any new curriculum ... these are not done rapidly or without thought."

items: Parents are pushing back on classroom screen time in a 'techlash' over too much technology in schools

blocks.text: Digital consent forms for using AI tools have already gone home this year, MacLean added, so if parents don't want their kids engaging with AI, they don't.
"We've had very few parents who have pushed back on us, but the ones who have, [we] engage in the conversation. It's not an us-versus-them," he said.
Calling for a pause
There's been a renewed wave of parental concern over tech use in classrooms today, with some highlighting AI amid broader alarm bells over the breakneck pace of AI development.

Generative AI made its public debut less than four years ago and research remains early about its impacts on learning, but many parents are concerned "things were going too fast," said Ben Humphreys, father of a seven-year-old and co-founder of Vancouver group Parents for AI Caution in Schools.

items: B.C. schools are bringing AI into classrooms, but some parents worry it will harm critical thinking
In the age of AI, how do we teach young people to think critically?

blocks.text: Many also don't want kids serving as test subjects for new technology without oversight, he added. "Is the tool there just because it's a tool that is popular right now or does it help students learn?"
Along with worrying about the social development of kids befriending AI chatbots, Humphreys is wary of student overreliance on AI stunting cognition and wants schools to take a pause right now.
Emotional support chatbot? Research looks at how teens are using AI

"Having that time in school where they can learn to think for themselves and figure out what they feel about the world, to learn ... determination to really push through tasks even when it's difficult — that's something that I'm worried will go away."
Many educators have similar concerns, according to Canadian Teachers' Federation president Clint Johnston, whose national alliance represents more than 370,000 elementary and secondary teachers.
President of the Canadian Teachers' Federation Clint Johnston on the latest PISA scores for students
"Slow down, give proper support and training to educators," many of whom feel unprepared, Johnston said from Ottawa.
"Right now it's this presumption that [AI] will be pervasive and therefore everyone needs to be using it all the time."

items: A U.S. prof suspects most of his students used AI to cheat. It's a growing concern here, too

blocks.text: More policy, guidance needed

A recent KPMG Canada survey of 1,009 Canadians over 17 attending or teaching at secondary or post-secondary schools on their use of AI found that students' use is dramatically overshadowing that of educators.

"Students are absolutely using it, educators are starting to ... but we're not on the same page in terms of what it shouldn't be used for and how it should," said Rob Clayton, KPMG Canada's national education leader.

Both student and teacher respondents indicated we're not teaching responsible AI use adequately or enough, he said. Clayton thinks part of the disconnect "comes down to a lack of clear policy and guidance" from above.

Change "really does need to start at the top," Dais executive director Côté said, noting that ministries of education should be moving in unison: sharing successes "at a pan-Canadian level" and leveraging AI in education best practices and research from global organizations like the OECD and UNESCO.

He also wants to see movement to tackle thornier issues, including evaluating teaching, learning and assessment against the backdrop of AI and the multitude of risks facing students, from cognitive offloading to data privacy and online safety.
"This is a really generational and systemic change that we're experiencing and it can't just be dealt with at the classroom level."

articles.title: Ed Sheeran speaks on Gaza in concert after Macklemore controversy
articles.summary: Sheeran called the Hamas-led attack in Israel "horrific" and described the war in Gaza as "catastrophic and unjustifiable" during his first concert since the Macklemore controversy erupted.

image.caption: Ed Sheeran, who had previously maintained an apolitical stance, broke his silence on the Israeli-Palestinian conflict in his first show since the Macklemore controversyImage: Ed Sheeran via Instagram/Handout/REUTERS

blocks.text: British pop star Ed Sheeran has addressed the Israel-Palestine conflict, following a row over Macklemore's removal as a supporting act on the tour after the US rapper made pro-Palestinian comments on stage.

Performing in Philadelphia on Saturday night, the first concert since the controversy erupted, Sheeran said the October 7, 2023 Hamas-led attack, which killed around 1,200 people and saw dozens taken hostage, was "horrific."
He also described Israel's subsequent war in Gaza, which killed more than 70,000 people, as "catastrophic and unjustifiable and disproportionate."

Sheeran also condemned the "systemic injustice" in the occupied West Bank, where the Israeli government is pushing to expand Jewish settlements, which the United Nations has called a "flagrant violation of international law."

"I don't want to disappoint fans, and I've never wanted to be an activist musician, but this has put me in the middle of an important and passionate argument about freedom of speech and the most complex political issue on the planet," Sheeran said.
"I've had to take and make difficult decisions, and I am making mistakes, and I'm so, so sorry," he said.
Sheeran's latest statement was a reversal from his earlier stance on Instagram, when he said that his concert audiences "do not expect a political forum."
Ed Sheeran tour drops Macklemore after Gaza speech
How did the controversy occur?

The pop singer's tour faced controversy after rapper Macklemore was dropped as a supporting act after he said "Free Palestine" at the opening of Sheeran's US Loop Tour in New Jersey in early September.
Sheeran has denied being responsible, saying venues had threatened to cancel shows if Macklemore remained on the tour.
Macklemore posted on Instagram that billionaire Robert Kraft had told Sheeran that the rapper would not be allowed to perform at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts, which he owns.

Several supporting acts subsequently withdrew in solidarity with Macklemore, including musician Finneas, Danish band Lukas Graham and Irish singer Aaron Rowe, as well as Sheeran's backing band — leaving one of the best-selling musical artists of all time without an opening act.

blocks.caption: Dozens of pro-Palestinian protesters demonstrated outside the Philadelphia stadium before the concertImage: Eduardo Munoz/REUTERS

blocks.text: Pro-Palestinian demonstrators protest outside concert venue
Dozens of pro-Palestinian protesters rallied peacefully outside Philadelphia's Lincoln Financial Field before Sheeran's concert, waving Palestinian flags and chanting "Free, free Palestine."
Among the demonstrators was 18-year-old Brandon Ateke, who accused Sheeran of "complicity" with Kraft and others in silencing Macklemore.
"I decided to not attend the concert and instead attend the protest to bring light to the genocide going on in Gaza today," Ateke told AFP news agency.
The Palestinian Campaign for the Academic and Cultural Boycott of Israel (PACBI), a pro-Palestinian group, has called for a boycott of Sheeran's world tour.

articles.title: German elections under way which could decide fate of Chancellor Merz
articles.summary: The chancellor is facing intense political pressure which will increase if his party struggles in Sunday's polls.

blocks.text: Local elections are taking place in two German states on Sunday which could increase the political pressure on Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
Opinion polls in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Vorpommerm suggest Merz's Christian Democratic Union (CDU) is at risk of damaging defeats, which would raise further questions about the chancellor's future.
These latest elections come after the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party won a major victory in the state of Saxony-Anhalt two weeks ago, while the CDU saw its vote halved.
There has been speculation in Germany that Merz could be replaced as chancellor mid-term unless the CDU's political fortunes improve.

He has said he will carry on but is facing poor approval ratings amid rumours of a so-called chancellor swap, though his challengers are "still hesitating", writes German news site Tagesschau, external.
According to the polls, Merz's conservatives could lose power in Berlin as it tussles with Die Linke (The Left) over first place.

Meanwhile in the north-eastern state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, the CDU has only just been hovering above the 5% threshold needed for a party to enter the state parliament. It could spell their worst ever result in a state election.

How did it come to this after just 16 months in power? Friedrich Merz is having to answer for the tumbling popularity of his own party, while the political force that he aimed to counter - the AfD - continues its rise.
Some branches of the AfD are classed as right-wing extremist by domestic intelligence, a designation it strongly rejects.
But its anti-immigration, Russian-friendly, Germany-first agenda has found fertile ground in the country's former communist east.
The AfD is hoping to build on its recent landslide win in Saxony-Anhalt by topping the polls in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern.
However, the centre-left SPD has staged a late comeback to be in contention for the top spot through its lead candidate, Manuela Schwesig.
Currently the state premier, Schwesig is trying to sweep up the anti-AfD vote as she bills herself as the "Die Frau gegen Blau" - "Woman against Blue", the AfD's party colours.
But her local popularity belies the far poorer fortunes of her national party which is locked in a loveless coalition with Merz's CDU.
In a queue for a campaign event in the city of Neubrandenburg, AfD supporter Reinhart tells us that the traditional parties are being washed away.
"Not only in Germany. In Italy, in France, in Great Britain. Everywhere the traditional parties go down."
He smiles when asked what he thinks of Merz, saying: "Oh well everyone thinks the same about him.
"He is arrogant, out of touch, not on the same level as the general public."
Merz's backers argue that the chancellor has had a tough time with global events and that a lot of the problems the nation faces are ones he has inherited.
But whatever faith people had in his ability to fix those problems, it is apparently ebbing away - and, the brutal truth is, it can be hard to find voters who like him.
The former corporate lawyer's tack to the right on issues like immigration has failed to erode AfD support while also alienating people further to the left.
His blunt communication style has also caused irritation, such as his dismissal of "work-life balance", telling Germans they need to work more and take less sick leave.
Supporters would argue he is a man who is ready to administer the medicine the nation needs, even if people do not like the taste of it.
But the country's long-stuttering economy, high energy costs and fraught debates about immigration are feeding a sense of national gloom.
Earlier this week, the leaders of eight German states backed Merz and said restorting trust in the CDU lay in "listening ​and taking political action, not in debates ​over personnel".
But while no one within his party has openly challenged Merz for the top job, murmurings of discontent have grown louder.
Martin Rohloff, the CDU candidate for Neubrandenburg, thinks Merz does not have the "Fingerspitzengefühl, the feeling for the small persons".

articles.title: Sherwin Gatchalian pushes school safety bill after South Cotabato shooting
articles.summary: Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian on Sunday called for the passage of legislation to strengthen school safety plans and policies following the latest school shooting incident in South Cotabato.

blocks.text: Published September 20, 2026 3:16pm
Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian on Sunday called for the passage of legislation to strengthen school safety plans and policies following the latest school shooting incident in South Cotabato.
Gatchalian co-authored and co-sponsored Senate Bill No. 2426, or the Comprehensive School Safety Act, which seeks to establish a National Comprehensive School Safety Framework.

“The Department of Education, in coordination with various government agencies, including local government units, shall lead in establishing, maintaining, and periodically updating this framework,” Gatchalian said.
The framework “shall prescribe standards for the prevention of, response to, and recovery from threats and incidents relating to school safety,” he added.
According to Gatchalian, the proposed measure would require schools to:

items: develop and annually update a School Safety Plan to localize and operationalize the school safety framework;
prepare and regularly update a School Safety Handbook outlining policies, procedures, emergency information and learner support services; and
include the School Code of Conduct in the School Safety Handbook to clearly define unacceptable acts, as well as corresponding disciplinary and restorative interventions.

blocks.text: Gatchalian said recent threats underscored the need for authorities to adopt a proactive approach aimed at preventing incidents before they turn fatal.
“A reactive response is not enough. We need to be proactive—identify threats, stop incidents before they happen, and ensure that every school is safe,” Gatchalian said.
The latest shooting incident occurred at Banga National High School in South Cotabato on Friday, leaving three students dead, including the Grade 9 student identified as the shooter. — MCG, GMA News

articles.title: In cosmopolitan Berlin, elections still closed to foreigners
articles.summary: A quarter of Berlin residents will have no say in the German capital's city-state election because they lack citizenship. That's the highest proportion of residents excluded from the election yet,…

image.caption: Berliners head to the polls September 20 to elect a new state parliament. The anti-immigrant AfD party has been making significant gainsImage: Sonam Mishra/DW

blocks.text: Abdu, an Egyptian software developer, ended up in Germany's capital more or less by chance seven years ago. "I wouldn't say I chose Berlin," he told DW. "It was just that the company that offered me a job was here."

But now he loves it. The culture is "better than any other city I have experienced," he said. That's partly because of its diversity, but he also likes the way Berliners approach life. "They're more interested in living than just working," he said. "Here I feel life is more relaxed, and this also offers the opportunity for people to get more creative."

But there's plenty about the city that he's not particularly happy with, including Berlin's rapidly rising rental prices, and the notoriously opaque bureaucracy is a constant source of annoyance. "I myself would like to start my own business, but it is difficult because of all the bureaucracy," he said.

In general, Abdu is dissatisfied with Berlin's current government, a conservative-led coalition of the Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) — but the trouble is, as a non-German national, he has no say in deciding whether it should stay in office or not. That is particularly frustrating at the moment, when the streets are bristling with campaign posters ahead of the election on September 20.
"We are people who pay taxes, but we don't have any representation at all, even on local level," he said. "The cuts to health care and German courses, for example, affect me directly."
Berlin initiative helps immigrant moms find their feet
Berlin: Bigger and more international

The German capital is growing and becoming more international. While the voting population in the upcoming election will be bigger than ever — mainly because the voting age has been lowered to 16 — so is the number of the disenfranchised.
Of Berlin's population of 3.9 million, a full quarter — around 976,000 adults — cannot vote because they don't have German citizenship. That number has doubled since 2011.

This is partly because of Germany's political structure. In Germany and across Europe, citizens of other EU countries can vote in municipal elections. In London, people from Commonwealth countries can do the same as long as they have UK residency. Spain, meanwhile, also has reciprocal voting agreements with several non-EU countries — in South America and elsewhere — that allow their citizens to vote in municipal elections, including for the mayors of Madrid and Barcelona.

Berlin's Sunday election is not a municipal one. Since Berlin is one of Germany's 16 federal states, it is holding a state election, which means that voting rights are more restricted. Berlin's municipal elections, where EU citizens are allowed to vote, only decide who governs the city's individual districts, and their political influence is limited.

The disenfranchisement is particularly acute in central Berlin. For that reason, Stefanie Remlinger, Green Party mayor in the district of Mitte, has organized a "symbolic election" for the non-Germans in her area — some 135,000 adults out of a population of 365,000. The initiative invites foreigners to vote at 15 ballot stations over a two-week period in early September to "raise awareness for the issue of voting rights for all."

"Mitte is an extremely heterogeneous district with a very international population," Remlinger told DW via video call from her office. "We have people from 170 different countries living here, and a lot of them don't have the right to vote. It's important to us to signal to those people that we value their opinions, that we see them."

blocks.caption: Around a third of adults in Stefanie Remlinger's district don't have German nationality Image: Annette Hauschild

blocks.text: Germany's 'rightward shift'

Getting people to vote in a meaningless election is a tough sell. Remlinger said she expected only a few hundred people to take part, and, anyway, she thinks the political climate in Germany is not exactly immigrant-friendly at the moment. Even in cosmopolitan Berlin, the anti-immigrant Alternative for Germany (AfD) is currently polling in second place, with nearly 20%.

"We as the Greens would liberalize voting rights even more, but I don't see the general debate in Germany going that way," she said. "We're fighting a rightward shift and a lot of hostility to immigration, and I think the chances of changing something on that issue right now are very bad."

To illustrate the state of the current debate, Remlinger mentioned a recent panel discussion she was part of, where a politician from the neoliberal Free Democratic Party (FDP) — a party that calls itself socially liberal — said voting rights shouldn't be opened to foreigners because they might start their own parties and take over the government. "And that from someone from the FDP!" said Remlinger, exasperated.

Abdu is also aware of this anti-immigrant shift in German politics. In fact, he said, that was one of the reasons he was considering leaving Germany altogether. "All the parties are trending right-wing, so it's getting more hostile," he said.
How Berliners are reshaping their city for the future
Is expanding voting good for the economy?

From an economic perspective, it might be considered a shame if qualified people like Abdu decided to leave Germany. The country lacks workers. The government estimates that the country will be short of about 440,000 workers by 2029, and even the AfD leadership claims it has nothing against immigrants who contribute to the economy.
Though some German cities and local authorities do have an elected advisory board for non-German residents, offering immigrants a real vote is frequently seen as a step too far.
Remlinger herself thinks that the best path to enfranchisement is not to offer foreign nationals voting rights, but to make it easier for immigrants to become German citizens.
That happens to be another one of Abdu's complaints about Berlin: "I applied for citizenship two years ago, and I didn't get any response," he said.

Germany has recently tightened citizenship rules again. Last year, Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government reversed the three-year "fast-track" citizenship option introduced under his predecessor, Olaf Scholz. Still, the government did keep another of Scholz's reforms, which allows people to apply for citizenship after only five years of residency.
More and more Berliners are in fact becoming German: 2025 saw about 39,000 people naturalized in the capital, 17,000 more than in 2024.

That avenue is still closed for Abdu, but in the meantime, a little more political participation would go a long way. "If I could vote, I would reconsider leaving, to be honest, because then I could affect things, but now I'm just like a bank machine — they come to me and take half of my salary."

articles.title: Eumir Marcial sits out 2026 Asian Games after latest pro win
articles.summary: Eumir Marcial is skipping this Asian Games edition owing to the 'tight timeline' that requires him to promptly fly to Nagoya, Japan, from San Diego, United States, where he scored a third-round…

blocks.text: POWER. Eumir Marcial in action for the Philippines in the 2025 Southeast Asian Games.
POC Media Pool

Eumir Marcial is skipping this Asian Games edition owing to the 'tight timeline' that requires him to promptly fly to Nagoya, Japan, from San Diego, United States, where he scored a third-round knockout win over Omar Ulises Huerta
MANILA, Philippines – The power Eumir Marcial showcased in his latest professional fight will not be on display at the Asian Games.

The Olympic bronze medalist is sitting out this edition of the continental showpiece owing to the “tight timeline” that requires him to promptly fly to Nagoya, Japan, from San Diego, United States, where he scored a third-round knockout win over Omar Ulises Huerta on Saturday, September 19 (Sunday, September 20, Manila time), to keep his professional record unblemished at 8-0.

Association of Boxing Alliances in the Philippines president Marcus Jarwin Manalo said he spoke to Marcial after the bout, and they agreed that it would be best for the pride of Zamboanga to skip the Asian Games and allow himself to rest and recover.

“It would be very hard for him to immediately transition from a professional fight in the US, into long-distance travel to Nagoya with 16-hour time difference, and then into another high-level boxing competition with such a short recovery period,” Manalo said in a statement released on Sunday.

“Boxing is a physically demanding and inherently risky sport, and adequate time to rest and recover is extremely important, and we do not want to compromise Eumir’s health and safety because of the tight timeline.”
Losing Marcial is a major blow to the Philippines’ hopes of ending a 16-year gold-medal drought in Asian Games boxing, considering his performances in the last two editions.
Marcial fell short of gold in the 2023 staging in Hangzhou, China, where he suffered a contentious unanimous decision loss to home bet Tuohetaerbieke Tanglatihan in the men’s 80kg final.
He also bagged bronze in the men’s 75kg class at the 2018 edition in Jakarta, Indonesia.
But for Manalo, it was a necessary move, with Marcial’s long-term career in mind.
“Eumir himself was very much looking forward to the opportunity to represent the flag once again. This is therefore a difficult decision for everyone involved,” said Manalo.
“However, representing the Philippines is not only about stepping into the ring. It is also about making responsible decisions that protect our athletes and allow them to have long, healthy careers.”
Marcial is still slated to represent the country at the Asian Indoor and Martial Arts Games in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, in December.

“We sincerely hope for understanding that this decision was made with Eumir’s best interests in mind. His commitment to Philippine boxing and to representing the country has never been in question,” said Manalo. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Groups march for accountability ahead of Martial Law anniversary
articles.summary: Several groups marched through the streets of Metro Manila on Sunday, September 20, on the eve of the 54th anniversary of the declaration of Martial Law.

blocks.text: September 20, 2026 | 3:09pm
Several progressive groups march to protest at EDSA Shrine in Quezon City on Sept. 20, 2026, during the eve of the 54th anniversary of the declaration of Martial Law in the Philippines.
The STAR / Mark Villeza
MANILA, Philippines — Several groups marched through the streets of Metro Manila on Sunday, September 20, on the eve of the 54th anniversary of the declaration of Martial Law.

Youth and student groups marched from La Salle Green Hills in Mandaluyong to the EDSA Shrine in Quezon City, while the August Twenty One Movement (ATOM) held a separate march in front of the Supreme Court in Manila.
The protesters called for government transparency, accountability over corruption, and the passage of legislation against political dynasties.
The march also called for the conviction of Vice President Sara Duterte in the Senate impeachment trial.
The protest was spearheaded by Akbayan Youth, the Student Council Alliance of the Philippines, Youth Against Kurakot and various university student leaders.

Meanwhile, ATOM marched to the Supreme Court to protest the high court’s ruling that reverse the conviction former First Lady Imelda Marcos. The group called for accountability for what it alleged the Marcos family had stolen.
RELATED: What Supreme Court's Imelda Marcos acquittal means, and what it doesn't
The group, along with Tindig Pilipinas and Partido Manggagawa, also marched toward the EDSA Shrine.
Monday, September 21, marks the 54th anniversary of the declaration of Martial Law in the Philippines.
The proclamation placing the country under martial law was signed by then-President Ferdinand Marcos Sr. on Sept. 21, 1972, but it was only announced on national television on September 23.
Martial Law was lifted on Jan. 17, 1981. Human rights groups estimate that the regime resulted in 70,000 arrests, 34,000 cases of torture and 3,240 deaths.

articles.title: Day jobs and dreams: Dubai OFWs chase indie film spotlight
articles.summary: Despite the demands of their regular jobs, these passionate Dubai OFWs pursue unpaid acting projects, with some even earning recognition at international film festivals

blocks.text: DUBAI, United Arab Emirates – Some 70 overseas Filipino workers (OFWs), whose day jobs range from hairdressers and grocery store merchandisers to office clerks, teachers, DJs, and finance professionals, have pursued their dream of acting on camera with the help of an award-winning Filipino indie director who brought them together and produced films for competition.
No one gets paid, including the director, and the films explore alternative themes seldom found in the mainstream.
“Cinema has never been simply about entertainment,” said Francis L.J. Gacer, director and founder of Kikoman Films (KMF), an independent production outfit. “It is about bearing witness.”
Francis, fondly called “Direk Kiko,” said he has been engaged in filmmaking for the past 10 years because “every Filipino has a story worth telling, and every voice deserves to be heard.”

And so the KMF, a UAE-licensed “creative sanctuary” for migrant artists where every talent can “flourish,” hopes to discover more experiences that “could become stories…voices [that could be heard on] the screen.”
The production house has been the go-to place of OFWs wishing to hone their acting talents.

blocks.caption: Actresses Pamela Villadiego and Trixie Mae Tautuan

blocks.text: “I wanted to continue growing as an actor and be part of a community of people who genuinely love filmmaking,” said Pamela Villadiego, who works in the marketing department of a company while freelancing as a DJ.
“Acting has been part of my life since I was young, and being in Dubai didn’t make me want to stop. Instead, I wanted to find a way to continue telling stories and challenging myself as an artist.”

Pamela has won Best Actor in the American Golden Picture International Film Festival (AGPIFF), Southeast Asia International Film Festival (SEAIFF), and the Sweden International Film Festival (SIFF) for her role as a human trafficking victim in the 45-minute, true-to-life short film Alimbukay (Nausea). The film also won Best Psychological Film in the recent Emirates Film Festival (EFF).

“I have upcoming films this year, Sa Manlulupig and When Life Gives You Lemons, which we will shoot this month. Aside from acting, I’ve also been involved behind the scenes, particularly in production as camera woman,” said Pamela.
Gudelia “Lia” Rodriguez said she was just a curious bystander when she found herself playing a role.
“Acting has always been one of the things on my bucket list and I really thought it was a long shot, but here I am. Never did I imagine that a dream, at my age, may come true,” she said.

“I joined because it gives ordinary people a chance to shine, explore their creativity and discover talents they may not even know they have,” added Lia, who has been working in finance for the past 24 years.

blocks.caption: Lia Rodriguez

blocks.text: Lia played a role in the award-winning horror film Batingaw, where she played the lead character’s sidekick. She also appeared as an extra in Alimbukay and in 100 Uploads.
“There are two lined-up films where I am part of this 2026 for scheduled shooting as well,” Pamela shared

Another artist, Trixie Mae Tautuan, works as an administrative assistant at a trading company. She has starred in three short films — Alimbukay, Sa Paghupa ng Unos, and Salamism — and remains busy shooting other projects this year.

“At first, it was not in the plan. A friend just had me tag along to an acting workshop. I tried it out of curiosity, and, at the same time, for experience since I’m fond of movies. I thought there was nothing to lose anyway,” Trixie said.
Also looking for something new to do on her weekends, hairdresser and makeup artist Jessica Leano Miranda replied to a KMF social media casting call.
“As I am an artist doing hair and makeup, I worked in an Arabic TV Channel here in Dubai years ago and I love watching movies, I got so interested to try it,” she said.

Jessica so far has two films under her belt: Tahan Tahanan, her first supporting role where she played a grandmother left to take care of a physically-challenged grandchild; and Batingaw, where she won an EFF acting award.

blocks.caption: Jessica Leano Miranda
KMF director and founder Francis L. J. Gacer

blocks.text: Amor Nano Matildo, a finance and logistics assistant at a manufacturing company for 16 years, said acting is one of her “passions in life” and a dream she hopes to conquer.
“I joined Kikoman Films because the films I’ve seen have meaning and sense, and also lessons,” she said.
Amor has played roles in four films last year: Bidyo-Oke, Remember Mercy, Paghupa ng Unos, and Tilamsik sa Dakilang Apoy. She’s busy shooting two films this year: Ang Dalisay and Reasong Razon.

blocks.caption: Amor Nano Matildo

blocks.text: Ron Jordan de Ocampo, a supermarket shelf stocker by day, has likewise become a regular actor for KMF, playing roles in 12 films.
“Each project has given me valuable experience and helped me grow as an actor,” he said.
Becoming an actor was “already a dream” for De Ocampo, who has always loved watching movies, especially indie films, even when he was still in the Philippines.

One of the most intense films De Ocampo has appeared in is Tilamsik sa Dakilang Apoy, where he starred as a former New People’s Army (NPA) combatant who, having been afflicted with a medical condition in the hills, returned home to his wife and daughter.
In playing the role, De Ocampo won Best Actor at the Global India International Film Festival (GIIFF) and Most Promising Actor at EFF.
He also won Best Actor in two other films, Apo and Malakaya, at the World Film Carnival Singapore (WFCS) and the Gully International Film Festival (GIFF).

blocks.caption: Ron Jordan de Ocampo

blocks.text: What started as a dream became a passion for De Ocampo, who met his wife at KMF.
“And now we have our baby girl, Baby Melon, who has also become part of some of our film experiences,” De Ocampo shared.
The actors said time management plays an important part in their task, as they memorize and practice the scripts after work on weekdays and shoot the film on weekends.

Since KMF’s inception in 2016, more than 25 film productions have reaped awards and recognition in various festivals in France, USA, Russia, Singapore, India, Turkey, Czech Republic, Spain, Philippines, Sweden, Italy, Hungary, and UAE, among others.
Direk Kiko, who usually comes up with ideas for the scripts, said 12 films are being lined up for 2027. He also supervises the acting workshops.
The director noted that plans are also underway to open KMF to non-Filipino talent, building on the six foreign members already among its 76-strong roster.

“Whenever I drive, I record my voice and speak of an idea for a story. Also, most of the time, I keep a small notebook and a pen in my bag,” said Direk Kiko, who also works as a producer and designer at a big retail firm. His superiors at the company support him, he shared, even attending last month’s KMF Gala Night.

“I still remember writing a script on the plane on my way back to Dubai from Saudi Arabia and the film eventually won awards in Kalayaan Independence Day celebration.” He also listens to nationalistic and progressive songs, the director said, “and from there, ideas flood me.” – Rappler.com
Some quotes have been translated to English for brevity.

articles.title: DFA: One China policy does not prevent PH from cooperating with Taiwan
articles.summary: The Philippines' One China policy does not prevent the country from pursuing economic, cultural, and functional cooperation with Taiwan, the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) said Sunday.

blocks.text: Published September 20, 2026 2:50pm
The Philippines' One China policy does not prevent the country from pursuing economic, cultural, and functional cooperation with Taiwan, the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) said Sunday.
The DFA reaffirmed the Philippines' adherence to the policy, which recognizes the government of the People's Republic of China as the sole legal government of China.
"The Philippines recognizes the Government of the People's Republic of China as the sole legal government of China. This policy remains consistent, clear and unchanged," the DFA said in a statement.
Citing President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., the DFA said the Philippines and Taiwan are "close neighbors with a long history of doing business together."
"The One China Policy does not preclude the Philippines from pursuing economic, cultural and functional cooperation with Taiwan," the agency said.
The DFA also reaffirmed its mandate to conduct diplomacy, maintain communication and pursue the peaceful resolution of disputes in accordance with international law.

"Consistent with this mandate, the Department will continue to rely on effective diplomacy, open communication, and the peaceful resolution of disputes in accordance with international law to advance the national interest and promote peace, stability, and prosperity in the region and beyond," the DFA said.
In May, Marcos said the Philippines had always upheld the One China policy, which recognizes the People's Republic of China as the only Chinese sovereign state.
Marcos, however, said any confrontation should be avoided and conflicts should be settled through peaceful means.

"We have many other considerations, but we end up in the same position that we want to avoid any confrontation. We want to avoid any hostilities around...Taiwan simply because we do not want to be involved in any war, we do not want to be involved in any conflict," Marcos said.

"Conflicts be resolved peacefully. And again, it all revolves in peace. And that is, I think, what everyone's ultimate goal is in Japan, the Philippines, and all the countries around the region," he added.— MCG, GMA News

Vice President Sara Duterte has yet to confirm her attendance at the Senate budget hearing of the Office of the Vice President (OVP), Senator JV Ejercito said Sunday.
"Wala pa hong pasabi. Hindi pa natin alam (she has not said anything so we don't know yet)," Ejercito told Super Radyo dzBB.
According to Ejercito, the budget hearing of the OVP and Office of the President will be tackled last due to the tight schedule of the Senate, as they also convene as an impeachment court.
The OVP has proposed a P785.204-million budget for 2027, 11.7% lower than its P889.236-million appropriated budget for 2026.
In a statement, the OVP said the 2027 budget aims to support the agency’s continued delivery of assistance and services to beneficiaries nationwide.
Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian earlier said issues being tackled by the impeachment court cannot be raised during the OVP budget deliberations.

“She will appear as the head of the agency. Her budget will be discussed in her capacity as head of the agency, but the issues currently being tackled by the impeachment court can no longer be discussed because they are already part of the case,” Gatchalian said.
Meanwhile, the Senate will not provide confidential funds to the OVP, DepEd and other civilian agencies, Gatchalian said.

“Not just the OVP and DepEd, but other civilian agencies as well. As a rule, we will not allow confidential funds. If there are any requests, they will have to be properly justified, and we will scrutinize them closely,” he said.

Article 1 of the impeachment complaint accused Duterte of the systematic misappropriation and irregular liquidation of confidential funds amounting to ₱500 million released to the Office of the Vice President (OVP) and ₱112.5 million to the Department of Education (DepEd) during her tenure as education secretary. —RF, GMA News

articles.title: Germany news: Doctors offer Oktoberfest flu jabs
articles.summary: Oktoberfest 2026 is underway but it's not just beer on offer in Munich this year; revelers can also get themselves a flu jab before heading to the tents. DW has more.
articles.byline: Matt Ford, Rana Taha, Timothy Jones

image.caption: Munich mayor Dominik Krause had the honor of tapping the first beer keg to officially open OktoberfestImage: Sven Hoppe/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: September 20, 2026
O'piekst is!: German doctors offer Oktoberfest flu jabs

blocks.caption: Tightly packed groups of revelers raise trhe risk of the spread of illnessImage: Felix Hörhager/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Munich's annual Oktoberfest officially got underway on Saturday when the first beer keg was opened with the traditional cry of O'zapft is! ("It has been tapped!").
But another slogan is also being promoted in Bavaria this year: O'piekst is! ("It has been pricked!") — as doctors offer vaccine jabs against flu and Covid-19.

"With so many people coming together in such tight spaces in the beer tents, the risk of infection at Oktoberfest is higher," explained Christoph Spinner, head of infectiology at Munich's Rechts der Isar hospital.
Oktoberfest coincides with the start of the annual flu season, and Spinner warned that less than a third of people who are recommended a flu jab have actually had one.
Beatrix Zurek, a health expert from the city-led initiative München impft! ("Munich vaccinates!") said: "It's our job to go where people are. And that means: Oktoberfest."
