articles.title: Thick smoke seen near Riyadh airport after air-raid alerts in Saudi capital
articles.summary:
Authorities also issued warnings for Jeddah and Yanbu, a major industrial port and home to vital oil facilities

Flames and a large plume of black smoke were seen rising above Riyadh airport…

blocks.text: Flames and a large plume of black smoke were seen rising above Riyadh airport in Saudi Arabia on Saturday after the government sent air-raid alerts to citizens by phone overnight warning of aerial attacks.

Explosions were heard in the capital and firefighters battled to extinguish the flames of a burning fuel tank emblazoned with the logo of the Saudi oil company Aramco near the city’s King Khalid international airport.
It is the first time the government has issued such alerts for Riyadh since fighting with the Iran-backed Houthis in neighbouring Yemen escalated in July.
Residents told Agence France-Presse that hours after the alert, they had heard what sounded like another round of explosions echoing through parts of the Saudi capital.
According to tracking website FlightRadar24, there are “major problems” at the airport and it has been listed under its maximum disruption index.
“In the direction of the airport, we saw black smoke and fire,” one resident told AFP, speaking on condition of anonymity.

The Saudi civil defence force sent air-raid alerts overnight on Friday to residents of Riyadh, Jeddah and other cities including Yanbu, a major industrial port which is home to critical oil facilities.
The all-clear was given shortly afterwards, but residents were encouraged not to gather in crowds.

The UN security council condemned the continued ​Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia in a statement on Friday. It said they had included attacks that affected civilian and energy infrastructure and had injured civilians, including women and children.
It also condemned the Houthis’ military offensive in Yemen, where nearly 105,000 people have fled their homes, the International Organization for Migration said on Wednesday.

The security council’s 15 members called for “practical cooperation” to prevent the Houthis from acquiring arms, military training, financing and other military-related assistance needed to carry out their attacks. They stressed that all countries must enforce the UN arms embargo against the group.

The Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the group had foiled unspecified “criminal attempts” ⁠in the Yemeni capital of Sana’a, blaming Saudi Arabia and vowing a response. The group also says the Saudi air force has conducted hundreds of airstrikes against it in recent days.

The Houthis recently seized control of strategic the Red Sea islands of Greater and Lesser Hanish. Earlier this month, the group captured the port of Mokha and Perim island in the Bab al-Mandab strait, fueling fears the world could face a second oil supply crisis.

articles.title: Jewish heirs of Holocaust victims sue California museum over Nazi-looted art
articles.summary:
Pasadena’s Norton Simon Museum holds 16th-century paintings stolen by the Nazis during the second world war

Jewish heirs of

blocks.text: Jewish heirs of Holocaust victims and their representatives have filed two lawsuits in California staking their claims to Nazi-looted paintings that still hang on the walls of prominent museums in Los Angeles and Auschwitz.

This pair of lawsuits are the first to be filed after the recent passage of laws by California and the US Congress, which strengthen US-based claims to artwork that were forcibly taken from Jewish families during the second world war.

One lawsuit was filed in Los Angeles superior court on Monday by the Jewish Federation of Greater Los Angeles and its board chair, Daniel Gryczman, against the Norton Simon Museum in Pasadena for the return of painting Adam and Eve. These are two lifesize oil-on-panel masterpieces created by Lucas Cranach the Elder in 1530.

The other lawsuit was filed in federal court in Los Angeles the same day by the daughters of the late Dina Gottliebova Babbitt, a Holocaust survivor and California-based animator who was held in Auschwitz. It demanded the return of watercolors of fellow prisoners that the artist was forced to paint for Josef Mengele, a Nazi physician who had earned the nickname the “Angel of Death”, from the Auschwitz-Birkenau museum in Poland.
Spokespersons for both museums say the museums legally hold titles to the works, and intend to continue displaying them to the public. The lawsuits don’t specify the monetary value of the paintings.

The issue of Nazi-looted art is an emotionally, legally and ethically charged topic that pits Jewish families that have suffered intergenerational trauma against museums that say they are trying to preserve a painful, yet important, chapter of history.

Between 1933 and 1945, the Nazi regime orchestrated the largest art theft in world history, seizing more than 600,000 works of art across Europe from Jewish families, collectors and museums. Decades later, many of these masterpieces reside in prominent museums around the world, making the push for their recovery more complex than a simple property dispute.

Rabbi Noah Farkas is president and CEO of the Jewish Federation of Los Angeles, the organization to which Marei von Saher, sole heir of Dutch Jewish art dealer Jacques Goudstikker, has signed over her rights. The paintings were seized from Goudstikker’s collection by Hermann Göring, Adolf Hitler’s second-in-command, and changed a number of hands before being sold in the 1960s to the Pasadena Museum of Modern Art, which was renamed the Norton Simon Museum in honor of its benefactor.
Farkas said the federation plans to use most of the net proceeds from the recovered art to provide much-needed help to the approximately 2,500 Holocaust survivors living in the Los Angeles area.
Von Saher, in a statement, said she is grateful to the Jewish organization for taking up her family’s cause.
“This effort represents a meaningful step toward justice for Holocaust survivors and victims of Nazi-era atrocities,” she said.

The Norton Simon Museum released a statement pointing out that a federal court in 2018 unanimously determined that the museum had proper title to the Cranach paintings. In May 2019, the US supreme court declined to get involved in the case, leaving in place lower court rulings.

They said the Cranach paintings, which originally belonged to the Stroganoff family, were put up for sale in 1931 by the Soviet Union in an illicit auction in Berlin, where they were purchased by Goudstikker. After a complicated journey, the paintings were sold to the museum by a Stroganoff family descendant. The museum later restored and preserved the pieces.
“For nearly 50 years, they have been on view at the Norton Simon Museum and will continue to be accessible to the public for years to come,” the statement said.

Pawel Sawicki, a spokesperson for the Auschwitz-Birkenau museum, said the watercolors of Roma victims that Gottliebova Babbitt was forced to paint by Mengele to document his horrendous experiments and racial research “must remain in the memorial” to document the man’s crimes. He said these paintings must not be mischaracterized as “Nazi-looted art” because Gottliebova Babbitt painted them against her will as a prisoner and therefore didn’t have ownership of the watercolors.

While he understands the family’s sentiments, Sawicki said the portraits of Roma and Sinti victims are among the few remaining documents of Mengele’s criminal experiments and should be treated as unique documents related to the history of the Auschwitz concentration camp.

“While fully respecting the rights of people who created some of the documents here, we are of the opinion that any loss in the collections of the memorial will constitute irreparable harm,” he said. “The loss of even the smallest part of the documentation is an irreparable loss and blemish on the memory of the victims of Auschwitz.”

articles.title: CNN, MS NOW say journalists denied access to White House grounds after Trump's ban
articles.summary: Two major news networks' journalists said they were denied access to the White House on Saturday morning, with reporters from CNN and MS NOW both going live to report about the circumstances of the…

image.caption: The CNN booth at the White House is shown after U.S. President Donald Trump announced he would ban CNN, MS NOW and Politico, in Washington, D.C., on Friday. (Evan Vucci/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New

Two major news networks' journalists said they were denied access to the White House on Saturday morning, with reporters from CNN and MS NOW both going live to report about the circumstances of the ban imposed by U.S. President Donald Trump.
Politico also included in White House restrictions announced by U.S. president Friday

The actions escalated Trump's long-running efforts to restrict news coverage by journalists he finds objectionable and is the latest test of First Amendment protections in the United States. Trump said on Friday he would ban both organizations and Politico because of their coverage.

CNN issued a statement saying it stood behind its reporters. "We will not be deflected from our duty to hold the government and other public bodies to account," it said. The statement was shown on the air before senior White House reporter Betsy Klein began to report on her ban.

items: Trump announces White House ban on CNN, other media outlets

blocks.text: MS NOW, which until last November was called MSNBC, also said it stands behind its journalists.

"The White House belongs to the American people and the decisions made inside are funded by our tax dollars," the network said in a statement on Saturday. "MS NOW intends to take any and all steps necessary to defend our First Amendment rights and the essential role of independent journalism in our democracy."
Trump bans CNN and other media outlets from White House
Trump said on Friday that he was barring the news channel, along with CNN and Politico, from the White House due to what he called unfavourable coverage and "fake news."
Politico journalists are typically not at the White House on Saturdays.
MS NOW White House correspondent Akayla Gardner was turned away and her entry badge was confiscated, she said on air Saturday morning.

Gardner said she had walked through two gates successfully, but once she got to where her badge needed to be scanned, an officer told her it was disabled and asked her to hand it over. He said the decision "was above him," she reported.
An MS NOW producer was able to get in, but a photographer's badge was also disabled, Gardner said.
Trump calls news outlets 'fake news'

The president wrote on his social media site on Friday that effective immediately, "I am banning" CNN, MS NOW and Politico "from the White House as a result of their constant ‘reporting' FAKE NEWS!" Minutes later, speaking at an event in the Oval Office, Trump was asked to explain his statement.

"Because they're fake news," he said. "You get so tired of reading and seeing fake news. When you look at CNN, it's just fake. That's why their ratings are no good. When you look at MS NOW ... it's fake news.

"And when you look at Politico ... the stories they wrote are fake. So there's a lot of news and there may be others to join them, and maybe they can get better," he said. "But our country has to have honest news."

items: 'Quiet, piggy': As Trump berates female reporters, what's the breaking point?
Judge throws out Trump's $15B US lawsuit against the New York Times

blocks.text: In his second term, Trump and his administration have upped the ante and punished certain media outlets, both in the courtroom and through regulatory action. Trump has also lashed out at individual reporters in person or over social media, sometimes in strikingly personal terms.

The move follows the president's decision last year to bar Associated Press reporters from the Oval Office, Air Force One and other events in retaliation for the news outlet's decision not to follow his lead in changing the name of the Gulf of Mexico, which lies partially in Mexican and other waters.
The AP said that it would note when appropriate that Trump had ordered it renamed the "Gulf of America."

articles.title: Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania: Will economy shape the vote?
articles.summary: Voters in the eastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania head to the polls on Sunday, with the Social Democrats and far-right AfD neck and neck. Here's a look at key economic issues that could…

image.caption: Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania is Germany's second-most popular vacation destinationImage: Jens Büttner/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The recent election victory of the far-right AfD party in Saxony-Anhalt has shaken up Germany's political landscape. Although Saxony-Anhalt is only a small state, the AfD's landslide win with nearly 44% of the vote has drawn considerable international attention, as it means this would the first time that a far-right party will likely enter a German government since World War II.

That is not expected to happen in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, where voters head to the ballot box on Sunday. State Premier Manuela Schwesig of the center-left Social Democrats remains popular, as polls show, though she isn't without her critics.

The latest polls suggest a neck-and-neck race between the Social Democrats and AfD, rather than a landslide victory for any one party. In fact, the Social Democrats' approval ratings have been on the rise and could indicate a successful final push, potentially returning Schwesig to power.
Lower wages, but solid economic growth

Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, like Saxony-Anhalt, is in eastern Germany, but its economy is relatively stable, even though unemployment stands at 7.8%, slightly above the national average, and the median gross annual salary is €47,750 ($54,800) — about €6,000 less than the German average. But Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania has seen solid economic growth in recent years.

Jochen Schulte, state secretary in the state's Economy Ministry, said Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania's economy has expanded by 5% in inflation-adjusted terms since 2020, compared with 4.6% for Germany overall.

Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania has a large agricultural sector, although it employs relatively few people. Back when the state was part of East Germany, farms were consolidated into large, state-run enterprises known as agricultural production cooperatives, rather than privately organized as in West Germany.

blocks.caption: Farms in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, once consolidated into large, state-run cooperatives, are still bigger than the German averageImage: Jens Büttner/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: In many instances, these farm sizes have remained the same since reunification. A typical agricultural company in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania will control about 280 to 283 hectares (up to 700 acres) of land, whereas the national average is only about 65 hectares.

The state's now private agricultural companies continue to benefit from their large size, ensuring efficient labor use, strong market positioning, greater market power through centralized purchasing, and a strong negotiating position when selling produce.
Many jobs in shipbuilding, tourism

The state's second major industry is shipbuilding and maritime services, which accounts for a significant share of economic output. Being on Germany's Baltic Sea coast, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania has also benefited from the recent investment boom in its defense sector. This has brought business — and jobs — to major shipyards in Wismar and Stralsund, at companies like Thyssenkrupp Marine Systems and other shipbuilders.
Hundreds of fake posts target German elections

Tourism is another key sector in the state. Until 1990, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania was one of the most important travel destinations for East Germans. Since the fall of the Berlin Wall, Germans from east and west have continued to flock to the Baltic coast, and the region is Germany's second-most popular vacation destination.

That said, relatively few people are directly employed in the tourism sector. That is in part merely a statistical quirk, as many tourism jobs overlapping with service jobs, and also because many tourism jobs are seasonal.

According to figures from the Economy Ministry and industry reports, some 150,000 to 160,000 jobs depend on tourism, either directly or indirectly. Water-based tourism, whether on lakes or the Baltic Sea coast, accounts for an estimated 19,000 jobs.
Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania has few large enterprises, such as automakers and chemical companies, which makes its state and civil service branch the region's largest employer.

Rostock-based AIDA Cruises is another major employer. So is Nordex SE, a manufacturer of wind turbines with production facilities in various regions. German rail operator Deutsche Bahn provides many jobs through its service and maintenance hubs, as do the major ports of Rostock and Sassnitz.
5 things you need to know about Nord Stream
Fossil fuels, renewables power regional economy
Another key industry is the energy sector, with large quantities of Germany's fossil fuels brought in via the Baltic Sea.

When imports of Russian gas came to a standstill in 2022 following the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the Nord Stream gas pipeline connection points near Lubmin lost their significance. However, a large portion of Germany's liquefied natural gas imports are still unloaded, processed and distributed in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.

blocks.caption: The coastal state has increasingly invested in renewable energy, including wind powerImage: Jens Büttner/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Energy availability, not only from fossil fuels such as oil and gas, but also from green sources such as wind and solar power, is becoming increasingly important for the state as well.
In August, the Schwarz Group — which operates the Lidl and Kaufland supermarket chains — announced it would invest €5.6 billion ($6.4 billion) in the construction of a data center south of Rostock.
During the project's presentation in the state capital, Schwerin, the company said its investments in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania could reach tens of billions of euros.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia: Houthis claim strikes on Riyadh, Yanbu port
articles.summary: The Yemen-based Houthis said they targeted "sensitive sites" in Riyadh, hours after a blaze at a fuel depot near the Saudi capital's main airport.

image.caption: Saudi Arabia has not commented on the threat mentioned in the warnings sent overnightImage: REUTERS

blocks.text: Yemen-based Houthi rebels said they targeted "sensitive sites" in Saudi Arabia's capital, Riyadh, and oil facilities in the port city of Yanbu on Saturday.
A statement posted to Telegram from the Iran-backed group came hours after firefighters extinguished a blaze at a fuel depot near King Khalid International Airport in the Saudi capital.
Earlier, residents reported hearing explosions in the vicinity, following overnight warnings by Saudi authorities of a "hostile aerial threat."
The Saudi government has yet to confirm the blasts.
What did the Houthis say?
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the rebels had "carried out two successful military operations using a large number of ballistic and cruise missiles.
Saree continued: "The first targeted sensitive sites in the Saudi capital, Riyadh, and the second targeted Aramco facilities in Yanbu."
He said the attacks were in retaliation for recent Saudi attacks on the Yemeni capital Sana'a.
The fresh violence comes just days after Riyadh accused the Houthis of targeting the Holy city of Mecca, which the Iran-backed militants denied as a "worn-out lie."

blocks.caption: An overnight air raid alert was issued by Saudi authorities, the first since fighting in neighbouring Yemen intensified this monthImage: REUTERS

blocks.text: What do we know about the airport strike?
"The area is under a hostile aerial threat," a message sent to Riyadh residents warned overnight, urging them to stay indoors, AFP news agency reported.
AFP journalists then reported hearing two explosions before the Saudi civil defence agency lifted the alert half an hour later.
News agency Reuters later published video and photos of a large plume of black smoke rising from an area near a highway to the airport.
Saudi authorities also reported intercepting incoming Houthi missiles and drones.
Saudi Arabia short of options against Iran-aligned Houthis
Tracking website FlightRadar24 reported "major problems" at the King Khalid International Airport, listing it under its maximum disruption index.
Unravelling security situation
The latest developments come amid an escalation between the Houthisand the internationally recognized government in Yemen that is supported by Saudi Arabia.
A 2022 truce between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia fell apart in July after the rebels allowed an Iranian plane to land in Yemen's capital Sanaa, which defied the Saudis' control over Yemeni airspace.
As a result of the escalation, the Houthis announced a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia.

The group has reported dozens of Saudi strikes since its recent offensive to secure control over the coastal areas near the Red Sea's Bab al-Mandeb Strait — a vital global shipping route — from government hands.

articles.title: 6 people injured after vehicle strikes pedestrians in Saint-Tite, Que.
articles.summary: The incident happened on Saint-Joseph Boulevard as the town is hosting the Festival Western de Saint-Tite, a major attraction for the region.

image.caption: Several people are injured in St-Tite, Que. (Martin Labbé/Radio-Canada)

blocks.text: Montreal·Breaking
The incident happened on Saint-Joseph Boulevard as the town is hosting the Festival Western de Saint-Tite, a major attraction for the region.
A criminal investigation is underway
Quebec provincial police are investigating after six people were injured after they were struck by a vehicle in Saint-Tite, Que., early Saturday morning.
Police say a collision between a vehicle and pedestrians took place on Saint-Joseph Boulevard. Witnesses say police arrived on scene around 4:30 a.m.
The vehicle fled the scene, according to the Sûreté du Québec. It was later found in the Quebec City region around 5:30 a.m.
A man in his 20s was arrested by police and is being questioned by investigators.
The victims were transported to hospital with various injuries, the extent of which are unknown at this time.

items: After 20 years with no police force, safety tops voter concerns in this Quebec community

blocks.text: The town is hosting the popular Festival Western de St-Tite and three Quebec political leaders are expected on site today as part of their respective campaigns.
Festival officials say Saturday's activities will go ahead as planned.

"An isolated incident beyond our control occurred early this morning on Saint-Joseph Boulevard. Our thoughts are with those involved and their families. We wish them a speedy recovery," the organizers said in a statement.

"The safety of our festival-goers, volunteers, and staff remains our top priority. The Festival is a festive event where everyone should feel safe. That's why every effort is being made to ensure this."
Police say Saint-Joseph Boulevard will remain closed to vehicle traffic between Du Couvent and Moulin Streets for most of Saturday as investigators and technicians work on the scene.
Quebec leaders react

The early morning incident took place as three Quebec party leaders were expected to attend the festival. The Quebec Liberals (PLQ), Coalition Avenir Québec (CAQ) and the Parti Québécois (PQ) all had stops planned for Saturday.
CAQ Leader Christine Fréchette posted her condolences to the victims on X.

“My thoughts are with the victims, their loved ones, and all those affected by the events that took place at the Western Festival in St-Tite. The ongoing investigation will determine the causes of this act,” Fréchette said.
PQ Leader Pierre St-Pierre Plamondon also offered his condolences.

“My thoughts are with the injured individuals, their loved ones, and all those who witnessed the distressing scene in Saint-Tite.,” St-Pierre Plamondon wrote on X. "Thank you to the first responders who acted quickly. Quebecers should be able to enjoy places where they can gather and celebrate safely."

articles.title: P12/L fuel subsidy on hold amid BSKE ban on social services spending
articles.summary: The Land Transportation Franchising and Regulatory Board (LTFRB) has suspended the distribution of the P12-per-liter fuel subsidy for public utility vehicle (PUV) drivers due to the election ban on…

blocks.text: Published September 19, 2026 10:03pm

The Land Transportation Franchising and Regulatory Board (LTFRB) has suspended the distribution of the P12-per-liter fuel subsidy for public utility vehicle (PUV) drivers due to the election ban on public spending for social services ahead of the upcoming Barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan Elections (BSKE).

In a "24 Oras Weekend" report by Bernadette Reyes on Saturday, several jeepney drivers expressed frustration over the suspension, appealing to the government to either increase the fuel subsidy or approve their pending request for a fare hike.

“’Yung ibinigay nilang subsidy, dagdagan nila kasi ayaw nilang taasan ‘yung pamasahe eh tapos taas nang taas ’yung [presyo ng] diesel. Paano naman kaming mga drayber?” said Arturo Vinluan, a jeepney driver.
(They should increase the subsidy if they refuse to raise fares, especially with diesel prices continuously rising. What will happen to us drivers?)
Another driver said he might temporarily stop plying his route because of low passenger volume and soaring fuel costs.
“Gagarahe na muna kasi walang pasahero, walang sakay, hangga’t wala pa 'yung subsidy namin. Sobrang taas eh. Wala naman gaanong sakay,” the driver said.
(I’m just going to park the vehicle for now while waiting for our subsidy. Fuel prices are just too high, and there aren’t many passengers.)
Under the election code, public welfare and social service programs are prohibited during the election period unless granted an exemption by the Commission on Elections (Comelec).
The Comelec said it is open to allowing the fuel subsidy to proceed once an exemption is requested. However, it has yet to receive a formal request from the LTFRB.
Trip adjustments
At a bus terminal in Sampaloc, Manila, a bus company was forced to cut trips and adjust departure schedules to cope with rising fuel prices.
In Reyes' report, a bus bound for Tuguegarao that was originally scheduled to depart at 8 a.m. remained at the terminal past 9 a.m. because only four passengers had boarded.
The bus operator explained that it needs a higher passenger turnout to avoid operating at a loss amid the high cost of fuel.
“Nagbawas po kami ng kaunting biyahe. Nag-iipon muna po kami ng mga pasahero,” Victory Liner terminal master Ariel Santos said.
(We have reduced some trips to allow more passengers to gather.)
“Kapag nakaipon na po kami ng mga 30 pasahero, doon pa lang po namin bubuksan ‘yung makina at ang aircon ng bus, tsaka doon pa lang po kami magpapasakay ng mga pasahero,” he added.
(Once we have around 30 passengers, that’s when we start the engine and turn on the air-conditioning, and only then do we allow passengers to board.)
The Department of Transportation (DOTr) has already met with interagency officials to formulate measures to address the looming fuel crisis.
Among the key measures discussed was a proposed public transport fare hike.

Meanwhile, stakeholders are still awaiting Malacañang's decision on the possible removal of excise taxes on petroleum products, especially with Dubai crude prices reaching US$123 per barrel, well above the US$80 threshold for tax relief intervention.

The DOTr has also approved an additional round of targeted relief assistance under the Department of Social Welfare and Development's (DSWD) Assistance to Individuals in Crisis Situations (AICS) program.

“We are examining possible implementation arrangements. We will continue to advance social protection mechanisms to help affected transport workers,” DSWD spokesperson Assistant Secretary Irene Dumlao said. — Lyjah Tiffany Bonzo/MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Drone sightings briefly shut Luxembourg airport
articles.summary: Flights were diverted and hundreds of passengers affected after unauthorized drones appeared near Luxembourg's only international airport.

image.caption: Drone sightings forced Luxembourg's only international airport to briefly suspend flights overnight [FILE: August 11, 2026]Image: Steven Mohr/SNS/picture alliance

blocks.text: Luxembourg authorities are investigating drone sightings that forced the country's main airport to temporarily suspend flights overnight, Prime Minister Luc Frieden said on Saturday.
Frieden said Luxembourg was working with its NATO allies following the incident, which comes amid heightened European concern over suspected hybrid attacks linked to Russia.
What happened at Luxembourg airport?
National carrier Luxair said more than 1,800 passengers were affected, with 17 incoming flights diverted to airports including Brussels, Paris and Frankfurt.
Flights resumed on Saturday, although Luxair warned that delays and knock-on disruption could continue.
The airport said the closure was a precautionary measure to protect passengers, airline crews, airport employees and aircraft.
Frieden stressed that it was too early to determine who was responsible.
"We are analyzing the situation," Frieden told a televised press conference after an emergency meeting with the country's defense and interior ministers.
Have other drones been spotted?
Frieden said "potentially larger drones" had also been observed in Luxembourg's airspace in recent days.
"This is new for Luxembourg, but it is not completely new for our neighboring countries," he said.
Germany blames Russia for attempted terror attack in Leipzig
Unauthorized drones have previously been detected near sensitive sites elsewhere in Europe, including Belgium, Germany and Denmark.
"We will ensure, together with our partners, that we can guarantee the security of our populations," Frieden said.

European governments have repeatedly warned of Russian-linked hybrid activities since Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Such incidents have included suspected sabotage, cyberattacks and unauthorized drone flights.
There is currently no evidence establishing who was responsible for the Luxembourg sightings.

articles.title: The province is proposing a ‘working forest’ model — but what does that mean?
articles.summary: B.C. is testing out a new forestry model in Campbell River that it says will reduce industry red tape for the struggling sector. But advocates and experts have concerns over its "no-net-loss"…

image.caption: The province has said the model is part of its response to ongoing pressures facing B.C.'s forestry sector. (Hyunjung Kim/CBC)

blocks.text: British Columbia

B.C. is testing out a new forestry model in Campbell River that it says will reduce industry red tape for the struggling sector. But advocates and experts have concerns over its "no-net-loss" approach.
Advocates and experts raising concerns over 'no-net-loss' approach
B.C.'s Ministry of Forests announced last Tuesday it would begin piloting its new Working Forest Landscape Model.
The model aims to support the province’s goal of an annual timber harvest of 45 million cubic metres, while reducing industry red tape, such as cutting permits.

It will be tested out in an area near Campbell River, by splitting forests into three zones: a working forest zone, a multiple-use zone and a conservation and protection zone. The system is designed to work in tandem with forest landscape plans (FLP), according to the province.
The pilot marks the beginning of the province's exploration phase, the ministry said, noting it will be a multi-year process before the model is fully implemented.
What is different about this forestry model?
Instead of relying on individual cutblock permits for Crown land, this model would divide areas in the province into three zones.

A working forest zone would prioritize commercial timber harvest. Forestry companies operating within it would be able to plan for the broader area from the start rather than incrementally adding more cutblocks.
This would help alleviate inefficiencies in the permitting process, so forestry workers "finally have a stable land base," said Forest Minister Ravi Parmar.
A multiple-use zone would have various functions aimed at "the restoration and enhancement of biodiversity and ecosystem functions," such as wildfire mitigation, according to the province.
And a conservation and protection zone would ensure "long-term ecosystem function and biodiversity through protected habitat and conservation networks."

items: B.C.'s forestry sector on verge of collapse, industry leaders warn as they urge province to act

blocks.text: Parmar said the model addresses a problem he described as "cutblock by cutblock permitting" by providing certainty over where forests can be logged through an area-based management approach.
Why are there concerns about it?
Under the new system, the province would explore a "no-net-loss" principle, which would see new land added to a zone if land is removed from it.
"If you take from the working forest, you [give] back to the working forest. If you take from your conservation zone, you add back into the conservation zone," explained Parmar.
It’s that aspect of the model that has some advocates and experts concerned about sustainable forestry.
It’s not yet clear how the province would decide what land is added to the working forest zone if an area within it is later marked for protection.

items: B.C. to pilot forestry model to assist industry, improve wildfire mitigation
UNBC launches engineering PhD to advance research in environmental and resource management in the north

blocks.text: Ken Wu, executive director of the Endangered Ecosystems Alliance, said he's concerned that could put ecologically valuable forests at risk.

It's a worry shared by Annie Booth, University of Northern B.C. professor in environmental and sustainability studies. She described the zoning issue as allocating the most "diverse, rich ecosystems" the same way as it allocates "big timber."
"The new plan will simply allow forestry companies to liquidate the last remaining stands of harvestable wood," she said in an email.
Harry Nelson, a University of B.C. professor in forestry and environmental stewardship, said those concerns are grounded, but the outcome depends on how the province rolls the model out.

It could provide more certainty around harvesting, he said, but how that’s achieved is the remaining challenge. He added that he questions whether the province has the "tools or capacity" to address that challenge, particularly as environmental, economic and social pressures differ between communities.
“I think the road to peace in the woods lies through communities, not through Victoria,” he said.
Why is the province doing this now?
Parmar said he's focused on balancing those concerns with the need to deliver a "sustainable working zone" for the industry.
According to the province, the model is a response to the "ongoing pressures" faced by B.C.’s forestry sector.
Those pressures include limited access to wood fibre, climate-driven wildfires, timber market volatility, rising operating costs and U.S. lumber tariffs.

items: How Trump’s lumber tariffs made a bad situation worse in B.C.
Forestry giant behind idled B.C. mill received millions in government funding

blocks.text: Parmar said the model would give the industry more consistent access to timber, while bringing First Nations to the table earlier in decisions about how forests are managed.

Huu-ay-aht First Nations Chief Councillor John Jack said area-based planning gives First Nations a greater role in coordinating forestry efforts and weighing areas for protection, habitat, wildfire mitigation and harvest.
The forestry sector, he said, also has a direct effect on the economic resources available to First Nations that depend on the industry, like his own nation located just south of Ucluelet.

"Getting involved in business means that we help create value and share in the value that’s created to help pay for things like community infrastructure, housing, early childhood educators, daycares, trauma-informed counsellors and beyond," said Jack.
Is there more history here?
The model has been floated in varying forms since the 1990s, according to several experts.
Advocates have pointed out that the B.C. NDP opposed a similar model when the B.C. Liberal party brought forward its own working forest initiative more than 20 years ago.
"The B.C. NDP supported our efforts to stop the working forest initiative under the B.C. Liberal government and we succeeded by 2004 with the NDP’s help," recalled Wu.
But Parmar pushed back against that characterization.
"[The B.C. Liberals’] approach to forestry was to gut the principle that matters most to people and forest communities, and that is local logs for local jobs," he said.

Parmar said his party’s opposition at the time was to the B.C. Liberals’ broader approach to forestry, including allowing more raw logs to be processed outside of B.C., rather than the principle of a working forest itself.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Arden McLeod, from Vancouver, is an associate producer with CBC News. He has a passion for community storytelling, local news, and reflecting the values of B.C. He graduated from the British Columbia Institute of Technology's broadcast and online journalism program. You can reach him at Arden.McLeod@cbc.ca.

"This is for her - we just want to live and go running and come back home without having to think that it may be one of us", said Nonhle Mpohlo.

articles.summary: Protesters took part in a "Hands Around the Kennedy Center" human chain. The demonstration comes amid fears the Trump administration could tear the arts hub down.

image.caption: Protesters joined hands to form a human chain around the venueImage: J. Scott Applewhite/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Thousands of people have demonstrated at the Kennedy Center in Washington D.C. amid fears President Donald Trump's administration could demolish the arts hub.
Crowds of people gathered in the Foggy Bottom area of the US capital city, many carrying signs as they joined in "Hands Around the Kennedy Center."
Some of those gathered held hands and formed a human chain around the center.
Protesters waved placards reading "hands off Kennedy Center" and sang songs close to where workers removed Trump's name from the building in June following a court order.

blocks.caption: Actor Lynda Carter, a vocal Trump critics, addressed the rally on FridayImage: Jose Luis Magana/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Protesters, residents condemn move to demolish Kennedy Center
"It makes me sick to my stomach," the AFP news agency quoted Neal Racioppo, a Washington resident who runs marketing and communications for a theatre, as saying.
Trump "can't get his name on this cherished building, so he is depriving the world of what it could be."
"He does not have a right to decide that an institution, a living memorial to a past president, can be demolished," another protester told AFP.
"The Kennedy Center is vital to the arts in Washington. We need it. We need this,” said local arts community member Bud Wilkinson.
"This is not just about putting the president's name on the Kennedy Center. It's about censoring the performances and the programming," Wilkinson said.
Trump and the Kennedy Center
The Kennedy Center — inaugurated in 1971 following the assassination of US President John F. Kennedy — has been a focal point of Trump's plans for Washington since 2025.
Trump has been pushing for major renovations and claims the building was left in a severe state of disrepair by those previously in control.
Trump's handpicked Kennedy Center board voted last year to rename the institution the Trump-Kennedy Center.
In May, a judge ruled that his name was illegally added and ordered it removed.

blocks.caption: The Kennedy Center board voted last year to rename the institution the Trump-Kennedy CenterImage: Cliff Owen/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: What has Trump said about the Kennedy Center?
On Wednesday, Trump appeared to imply that the Kennedy Center could be torn down if his administration did not receive "recognition."

"For the Trump administration, for me to get involved and to take that on long term and to carry it or to raise money to carry it, I think that the Trump administration should certainly have recognition, because frankly, if we don't do that, it's going to close," Trump said.
"It'll end up being ripped down. It's in very, very bad shape, very dangerous shape," Trump told reporters.

articles.title: Millions without power as Cuba hit by latest major blackout
articles.summary: Widespread power outages have become increasingly common due to fuel shortages made worse by a US blockade.

blocks.text: Millions in Cuba were left without power on Friday as the country was plunged into yet another major blackout.
The country's entire electricity grid suffered "total disconnection" that triggered a nationwide outage, Cuba's energy ministry said.
Power was restored to some priority areas by late evening, including those near hospitals and water pumping stations in the capital Havana, grid operator UNE said.

It is at least the sixth partial or total blackout to hit Cuba this year, where ageing electricity infrastructure and chronic fuel shortages have been placed under further strain by a US blockade on oil shipments to the communist-run nation.
UNE said the outage started just before 14:00 local time on Friday (18:00 GMT) due to a transmission fault coupled with poor weather conditions in central Cuba.
Protocols to begin the "gradual restoration" of power were activated, the operator's national load dispatch director Felix Estrada said, with the process ongoing on Saturday.
Cuba relies heavily on fuel imports, meaning tight US sanctions and an oil blockade since the start of the year have exacerbated existing shortages.
Food and medicine have also become more scarce, with hospitals struggling to function normally and schools and government offices having to close.
"Lately, it's becoming a habit," Havana resident Frank Lorenzo told news agency Reuters on Friday.
"Before it happened less frequently - once a month… just yesterday we were 24 hours without electricity, they turned it on for just an hour and it went down again."
"It's one thing after another: no water, no gas for cooking, no electricity," 36-year-old schoolteacher Lidia Fernandez told news agency AFP. "Honestly, I don't know how we haven't gone crazy."
Francisco Rodriguez, 78, said his home had already gone without power for 28 hours on Friday and feared he would not have light "for several days".
The repeated blackouts have prompted rare protests in Cuba, where unauthorised demonstrations are illegal and those who defy the ban risk being jailed.

Havana has blamed its fuel crisis on the Trump administration and denounced all of its sanctions - including a new round announced in August - which are part of a wider pressure campaign against the Caribbean island's leadership.

Cuba's regional ally Venezuela was believed to have sent it around 35,000 barrels of oil a day - about half of its oil needs - until Venezuela's own supplies were cut off following the US seizure of its President Nicolás Maduro in January.
US President Donald Trump has threatened tariffs on countries shipping oil to Havana, and a number of such shipments have been seized by the US.

Washington meanwhile attributes Cuba's energy crisis to poor internal management and has accused it of posing a "national security threat". Trump has openly discussed toppling its leadership, including threatening a "friendly takeover" in March this year.

articles.title: Oktoberfest 2026: Everything you need to know
articles.summary: This year, AI will be used to manage overcrowded situations. Find all the numbers surrounding the fest — including the price of water!

image.caption: Oktoberfest attracts millions of visitors every yearImage: Wolfgang Maria Weber/IMAGO

blocks.text: On Saturday, September 19, at noon, Oktoberfest will once again open with the ceremonial tapping of the keg, during which the mayor of Munich drives a tap into the first wooden barrel of beer and calls out "O'zapft is," a Bavarian phrase that translates to "It's tapped."
His call will be followed by 12 gunshots, a signal that lets all festival tents know that they can start serving beer.
More than 6 million people are expected at the world's largest Volksfest, which runs this year through October 4.
Oktoberfest: What to know about 'the best party in Germany'
Expanded security measures to prevent overcrowding
The festival grounds are enormous: Oktoberfest takes place on Munich's Theresienwiese, a 34.5-hectare site roughly the size of 48 soccer fields.
But crowds can swell, especially on weekends — sometimes to dangerous levels.
Last year, officials had to temporarily close the entrances.

One reason is that nearly all 38 beer tents operate in two or three reservation shifts. When one group of guests leaves and the next arrives at the 14 large tents — which each accommodate several thousand people — huge numbers of visitors end up trying to enter and exit at the same time.
That's how, on one Saturday afternoon at last year's Oktoberfest, the crowds became so dense that movement temporarily came to a standstill. The crush caused some visitors to panic.
To prevent that from happening again, the city of Munich has overhauled its security plan for this year's festival.
Twenty-six new cameras, in addition to 56 police cameras, will monitor the grounds, while an AI system will analyze visitor flows and issue alerts if areas become overcrowded.

blocks.caption: Around 300,000 people were at Oktoberfest simultaneously on the second Saturday of the festival in 2025Image: Frank Hoermann/SVEN SIMON/picture alliance

blocks.text: A newly established coordination center is also intended to improve communication between security agencies and event organizers.
Organizers and police have drawn up a plan to defend against drones over the grounds, though no details have been disclosed.
In addition, 600 police officers will be deployed on site.
Oktoberfest is famous worldwide, but most visitors are local
Oktoberfest may be known around the world as an international tourist attraction, but most of its visitors don't travel very far to get there.
A study commissioned by the city of Munich last year found that the festival remains overwhelmingly regional.

blocks.caption: Statistically speaking, two international guests sit at every 10-person table in the festival tentsImage: Maryam Majd/REUTERS

blocks.text: In 2025, 41% of visitors came from Munich, another 25% from the surrounding area and 9% from elsewhere in the region. In all, three-quarters of Oktoberfest's roughly 6.5 million visitors came from Bavaria. Another 4% came from elsewhere in Germany.

About 21% of visitors — roughly 1.35 million people — traveled from abroad. Americans made up the largest group of international visitors, accounting for just under 20% of the total, or more than 270,000 people. Italians were next, at just over 13%.
Beer prices rise again
Cannabis is banned throughout the festival grounds.

Alcohol, on the other hand, is available in whatever quantities visitors are willing — and able — to pay for. A Mass, the traditional 1-liter mug of beer served at Oktoberfest, costs between €14.80 and €15.90 ($17-$18.25) this year, only slightly more than last year.
A liter of table water comes in at a hefty €11, although the grounds also have several free drinking water fountains.
Visitors planning to enjoy one of Oktoberfest's many rides would be wise to stay relatively sober. Tickets cost anywhere from just under €5 to €14.

Germany's traditional fairground culture was officially added to the UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage list in 2026, and that tradition remains very much alive at the 191st Oktoberfest. According to organizers, about 90% of the festival's more than 130 fairground operators can trace their roots back to the 19th century.
The festival remains decidedly traditional when it comes to payment, too: Many vendors still accept cash only. Visitors caught without any can withdraw money from ATMs on the grounds.
Dirndl or lederhosen for Oktoberfest?
Then there's the question of what to wear.
Bavarians who take pride in doing things properly generally show up in local traditional dress.

blocks.caption: Traditional garb can be seen at the annual breweries' paradeImage: Felix Hörhager/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The dirndl is the traditional dress worn by women and girls, which consists of close-fitting bodice with a low neckline, a blouse worn under the bodice, a wide high-waisted skirt and an apron.
Men wear lederhosen, the traditional leather shorts or knee-length breeches with suspenders.

For those who are not Bavarian, lederhosen and dirndls are certainly an option, but they're by no means required. Munich's event marketing department, Simply Munich, advises first-time visitors to consider renting traditional garb rather than buying it.

Be aware that locals find cheap imitations of traditional dress off-putting, as Simply Munich points out: "If you want to avoid wry looks, steer clear of Seppl hats, 'leather pants' made of cloth and garish mini plastic dirndls. With jeans and a checkered shirt, you'll definitely be more suitably dressed."
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Deadly shark attack prompts rare kill order in Western Australia
articles.summary: Police boats and helicopters are patrolling Perth's beaches as authorities continue their search for the swimmer's body, and the shark that attacked him.

blocks.text: A rare catch-and-kill order has been issued for a great white shark off the coast of Western Australia, after a man was killed while on a morning swim at a popular beach on Friday. His body has still not been found.
Authorities have said that beaches along the state's coast, including in the capital Perth, will remain closed until at least Sunday as the search for the shark continues.
It is the second shark attack in Western Australia (WA) this week, and the third fatal attack in the state this year.
The incident, at Sorrento Beach in Perth's north, has reignited debate about how to keep beachgoers safe in Australia.
The swimmer has been identified as 63-year-old Greg O'Neill, the Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC) has reported.
"Greg loved the ocean and was known as a passionate swimmer, sports lover, dedicated worker and an all-round generous, witty guy," his family said in a statement to the broadcaster.
Witness Jacqui Rapaic told the ABC that two men were swimming, but only one made it back to shore, and that she could see "a pool of blood" in the water.
Another witness told WAtoday that she saw the man being "mauled" as the shark "tossed him around like a fish".
Members of the public reported seeing a 2.5m-long (8ft 2in) shark at around the same time.
Authorities in Perth's Joondalup area, where Sorrento is located, said all beaches were closed "as a precautionary measure" and would remain so until at least midday on Sunday.
Pictures on Saturday showed the coastline being patrolled by a police boat and helicopter.
Catch-and-kill orders are rare and controversial in Australia, where great white sharks are a protected species.

WA Fisheries Minister Jackie Jarvis said that she took the "extraordinary step" of issuing the order after the shark was spotted by water police on Saturday morning, and "positively identified as the shark involved in the incident".
The minister said she authorised fisheries officers to "destroy the shark" if it could be captured because of the "exceptional circumstances" of the attack and the "hazard posed by the shark".
It is believed to be the first time in 10 years that such an order had been issued in WA, Jarvis added, emphasising that the order was not a widespread cull as the state has seen in the past.
The minister also said that the use of drones and tagging would be increased to help protect beachgoers.

Catching and killing sharks has a long and controversial history in Western Australia - there were months of huge protests in 2014 when the state government authorised a cull after a spate of attacks.

The incident in Sorrento is the second in WA this week - on Monday a 56-year-old man was bitten while surfing off the coast of Geraldton, 430km (270 miles) north of Perth. He survived but lost part of his leg, another surfer who rescued him told the ABC.
There have been five fatal shark attacks in Australia this year.

A 12-year-old boy died after he was bitten in Sydney Harbour in January, and three divers were fatally mauled in separate incidents between May and June - two in Western Australia and the third in Queensland.

articles.title: Rebels, workers, radicals: The making of 'Red Berlin'
articles.summary: Bloody May, student sit-ins and the squatter movement: Berlin has a long history as a hotbed for working-class organizing and radical left-wing politics.

image.caption: A Molotov cocktail explodes during the forced eviction of a squat in the Berlin district of Friedrichshain in 1990Image: Stefan Trappe/IMAGO

blocks.text: Berlin has a reputation for being unruly. When Jospeh Goebbels was appointed the Nazi Party's district leader in 1926, he described Berlin as "the reddest city in Europe besides Moscow." From the Tailors' Revolution of 1830 and the barricades of 1848, to the rise of a vast industrial working class later in the 19th century, revolution, protest and rebellion run deep throughout the city's history.

While the future German philosopher and revolutionary socialist Karl Marx was still in high school in the small town of Trier in Prussia's Rhine Province, Berlin was fast becoming a center of the country's labor movement. It was during the March Revolution of 1848 — a failed attempt to create a democratic German nation-state — that the General Workers' Brotherhood was founded, one of the first worker's organizations to become active in Germany.

blocks.caption: In March 1848, Berliners fought for basic freedoms and German unityImage: United Archives International/IMAGO

blocks.text: By the 1870s and 1880s, major industries from mechanical and railway engineering to ready-made clothing were located in the city. As the working-class population grew, this in turn impacted the city's political culture. "It became more populist in a positive sense: moving away from the traditional, elitist politics of the bourgeois liberals who had long dominated Berlin, and toward the inclusion of ordinary people, since at least men were now also important voters," Axel Weipert, a historian and author of the book "Red Berlin" (2019), tells DW.
Emergence of a radical labor movement

Berlin's labor movement became increasingly radical, partly in response to heavy-handed repression under the Chancellor Otto von Bismarck. Although Bismarck created the first modern welfare state to try and undercut the rising popularity of the socialist movement, he also introduced laws banning socialist and communist organizations, newspapers and public gatherings, as well as independent trade unions.

blocks.caption: A memorial to Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels, who co-authored 'The Communist Manifesto' in 1848, still stands close to Berlin's city hallImage: Jürgen Ritter/IMAGO

blocks.text: After Bismarck resigned in 1890, the anti-socialist laws were repealed and the ideas of Karl Marx and his fellow revolutionary socialist Friedrich Engels became the ideology of what Weipert describes as a "genuine mass movement" in Berlin. The Social Democratic Party (SPD), Germany's oldest political party, was formed out of a merger between the General German Workers' Association and the social Democratic Workers' Party in 1875. Before World War I, the SPD was able to win far higher vote shares in Berlin than elsewhere in the country.

In 1914, the labor movement was seriously discredited when the SPD leadership and the trade unions decided not to oppose the war pushed by Kaiser Wilhelm II. But from 1916 onwards, Berlin became the center of mass labor strikes against the war. One of the earliest strikes was against the trial of anti-war socialist campaigner Karl Liebknecht. Together with Rosa Luxemburg and other left-wing radicals, Liebknecht founded the Spartacus League in Berlin, an underground group that later became the Communist Party of Germany (KPD).

blocks.caption: Karl Liebknecht (left) and Rosa Luxenburg were murdered by right-wing paramilitary soldiers of the Freikorps in BerlinImage: akg-images/picture-alliance

blocks.text: Triggered by war-weariness, severe food shortages and economic ruin, around half a million Berlin workers joined the January Strike of 1918. Supported by the Spartacus League, the anti-war strike was led by the Revolutionary Stewards, a clandestine network of factory workers and trade unions from large munitions and metal-working factories. The same group became a core organizing force behind the overthrow of the Kaiser in Berlin on November 9, 1918.
From left-wing unity to division

In the chaotic, war-torn city gripped by violent revolution, the Spartacist Uprising of 1919 was launched to overthrow Germany's provisional government and establish a republic of workers councils. Its violent suppression, which resulted in scores of deaths — Liebknecht and Luxemburg were both murdered by soldiers of right-wing paramilitary militias — permanently fractured the political left.

blocks.caption: Spartacist revolutionaries armed with machine guns aimed to establish a communist stateImage: Cola Images/IMAGO

blocks.text: As the capital of the newly founded Weimar Republic, Berlin remained a hotbed of radical politics in the interwar period. This was especially true in neighborhoods with large numbers of tenement buildings, such as Wedding, Kreuzberg and Neukölln, where thousands of factory workers lived in squalid conditions. The many large factories in Berlin also created shared interests and laid the groundwork for collective action.

"Bloody May" in 1929 saw brutal attacks on illegal May Day demonstrations which left at over 30 people dead. The SPD police president of Berlin had issued a ban on all public demonstrations for May Day, a ban defied by the KPD. In response, the police opened fire on protestors in the streets and also shot through windows in residential buildings, primarily in the working-class districts of Wedding and Neukölln.

blocks.caption: 'Bloody May' inspired the labor movement song 'Red Wedding' by Hanns Eisler and Erich WeinertImage: Atlantic Photo-Co/SVT/TT/IMAGO

blocks.text: During the Great Depression era, the SPD lost much of its support between 1929 and 1933, as joblessness ravaged the city. "Unemployment is critical — it meant that men were no longer attached to the SPD-led factory floor and trade union and the social bonds of these spaces and organizations," explains Pamela Swett, a historian at the University of Rhode Island. "Unmoored from the rhythm of daily life, men sought new bonds — new ways to feel self-respect and camaraderie with others." Some joined the KPD, which became known as the "Party of the Unemployed." Others joined far-right paramilitary groups such as the Nazi stormtroopers.
From student sit-ins to the housing crisis

After the Nazis took power in 1933, many of the labor movement leaders were killed or exiled. Then, in the aftermath of World War II, Berlin was divided into two separate political systems. East Berlin became the capital of the communist German Democratic Republic. Isolated from the Federal Republic of Germany, West Berlin deindustrialized, the labor movement weakened, and the SPD moved to the right.

During the Cold War, many left-leaning young men moved to West Berlin to evade military service. This intensified the student movement, the center of which was Berlin's Free University (Freie Universität). It was there, in leafy southwest Berlin, that historic sit-ins were held to protest the perceived authoritarianism of the government and the presence of former Nazi officials in positions of power. The fatal shooting of student Benno Ohnesorg by a police officer during a demonstration against the visiting Shah of Iran in 1967 radicalized a generation that led the widespread protests of 1968.

blocks.caption: The fatal shooting of student, Benno Ohnesorg, by police during protests against the Shah of Iran's visit in 1967 radicalized a generationImage: dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: In the early 1970s, a housing shortage led parts of the student movement but also apprentices and young migrant families to squat in West Berlin's empty buildings. "You have migrant laborers and young laborers participating, so this was part of working-class rebellion against capitalist housing," says Ralf Hoffrogge, a labor movement historian at Berlin's Free University.

Today, as gentrification sweeps the city, Berlin is home to the strongest and most radical tenants' movements in Germany. In a 2021 referendum, 59% of voters in the city approved the expropriation of property from private real-estate companies. Hoffrogge was part of the campaign, and his 2025 book "Loud Berlin" ("Das laute Berlin") explores how the housing crisis has become a catalyst for a "socialist renaissance" in the city. "It's not Berlin tenants against Berlin landlords, it's tenants against global capital. I think people have started to realize these contradictions and this is why class-based policy concepts are becoming popular again."

blocks.caption: 'Housing is not a commodity': Berlin's housing crisis and rapid gentrification have triggered new political initiatives in the cityImage: IPON/IMAGO

articles.title: Were mosquitos bugging you more than usual this summer? Blame the rain
articles.summary: If it felt like mosquitoes were been particularly bad this summer — and hanging around for longer — it might not be in your head.

image.caption: Wet weather brought swarms of mosquitoes to parts of Canada this summer, while a major storm that hit southern Ontario earlier this month has led to the pests sticking around for longer. (Corlaffra/Shutterstock)

blocks.text: Canada·New
If it felt like mosquitoes were been particularly bad this summer — and hanging around for longer — it might not be in your head.
Parts of Canada had particularly bad mosquito season, with critters sticking around longer in southern Ontario
Some prairie cities saw a mosquito population boom earlier this summer, with some stores in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta running out of bug spray entirely due to high demand.
Data collected by the City of Edmonton showed the number of mosquitoes in the city was 15 times higher in July compared to the same time last year.

"While these do not represent record high mosquito numbers for our region, they are a stark contrast to the previous two summer seasons, which can magnify public perception," said Peter Daly, a biological sciences technologist at the City of Edmonton.
Saskatoon and Winnipeg also saw higher numbers of mosquitoes in July compared to last year, according to data from those cities.
In southern Ontario, experts say the record rainfall parts of the region saw this summer is likely to blame for the mosquito boom, and why they're still causing itchy red welts well into September.

Fiona Hunter, a medical and veterinary entomology professor at Brock University, said this summer, southern Ontario has seen greater numbers of the Ochlerotatus trivittatus species compared to other years.

Ochlerotatus trivittatus is known as a floodwater mosquito that lays its eggs in low-lying areas filled with water, so the amount of rain southern Ontario has seen this year has created ideal conditions for them, she said.
"Think about all the rain we've had in southern Ontario this year. Soggy fields, low spots in lawns, roadside depressions and other poorly drained areas have repeatedly filled with water," she said.
"That creates lots of potential habitat for this particular mosquito, and probably helps explain why we're seeing so many of them this year."

items: Seeing more mosquitoes than normal this time of year? You're not alone
'Skeeter syndrome' showing up in Alberta as mosquito populations boom

blocks.text: The species is known to be a very persistent biter, she said.
"So I suspect people are simply coming into contact with this species more often this year, which may be part of the reason mosquitoes seem especially bad right now."

The torrential downpour that pummelled the Greater Toronto Area and many other communities across southern and southwestern Ontario also may have triggered the hatching of a whole bunch of dormant mosquito eggs, said Rosalind Murray, an assistant professor of biology at the University of Toronto.
"And so we might see a little bit of a blip where we have a bit of a boom, especially in places that have major flood flooding like Toronto," she told CBC Radio's Metro Morning.
Mosquito season stretches into September after wet summer in Ottawa
Colder temps will drive populations down
But as soon as the region starts to see colder overnight temperatures, the mosquitoes won't be an issue anymore.
"They don't do very well when it's extremely hot, they can dry out. They also are going to die immediately once it gets cold," Murray said.
"Once we start seeing those really cool nighttime temperatures, like below 10 C, we should start to see them peter out. And as soon as we have a frost, they'll be gone."
That's what Alberta has seen happen after a recent cold snap, said Ken Fry, an entomology instructor at Olds College in Olds, Alta.
Edmonton and Calgary experienced a particularly bad mosquito season earlier this summer, driven by a large amount of rainfall early on in the year.
But then, he said, mosquito populations "pretty much crashed" due to colder temperatures in recent weeks.

items: Edmonton has 15 times more mosquitoes now than at same time last year, city scientist says

blocks.text: Daly said Edmonton has already seen numbers drop for the most dominant local mosquito species, Aedes vexans, but added that since the city has had a warm fall so far, "we’ve yet to see quite as precipitous drop in their numbers as some other years. "
Fry said the critters might make a reappearance as temperatures are expected to climb back to 20 C or higher over the next week in the region.
"But we won't have the populations, I don't think, anywhere near close to what central Canada is experiencing."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Sarah Petz is a Toronto-based senior writer with the CBC News live pages team. Born and raised in Manitoba, her career has taken her across three provinces, multiple cities and to northern Uganda.

articles.title: India news: PM Modi says developing nations unfairly blamed for emissions
articles.summary: At the inauguration of a climate conference in New Delhi, PM Modi said developing countries are unfairly blamed for carbon emissions. An IIT Bombay professor has been accused of caste abuse. DW has…

image.caption: Prime Minister Narendra Modi and several other prominent leaders were present at the inauguration of the climate conferenceImage: ANI/IMAGO

blocks.text: September 20, 2026
Developing nations unfairly blamed for emissions, Modi tells climate conference
Prime Minister Narendra Modi has said developing countries are unfairly held responsible for carbon emissions despite their comparatively low per-capita output.
Modi made the remarks on Saturday as he inaugurated a two-day international conference on environmental and climate governance in New Delhi, organized by India's National Green Tribunal.

Speaking at the opening of the "Future of Environment and Climate Dynamics" conference at Vigyan Bhawan, Modi said, "We know that often the responsibility for carbon emissions is wrongly placed upon developing countries... the historical truth is that India's contribution per capita carbon emission is less than half of the global average."
"In developed countries, per capita carbon emissions are six times higher than in India."

He said India has consistently raised this point at global forums, including at the 2015 Paris climate summit, adding that India is the only G20 nation to have met its Paris commitments ahead of schedule.

The remarks come weeks after devastating floods hit India's northern neighbor, Nepal, killing over 1400 people. Nepal contributes roughly 0.1% of global greenhouse gas emissions, making it what the World Bank calls a "negligible contributor to climate change."

The conference, which ends Sunday, brings together judges and environmental officials from 17 countries as well as Indian Supreme Court and High Court judges, senior bureaucrats, and representatives of state environmental authorities, according to the Prime Minister's Office.

articles.title: Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania: SPD seeks to fend off AfD
articles.summary: For nearly three decades, the Social Democrats have governed Germany's northeastern state. If they can fend off the AfD, the result may boost the fortunes of the German government's junior coalition…

image.caption: Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania's state legislature is housed in Schwerin CastleImage: Jens Büttner/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Stretching along Germany's Baltic coast, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania is known for the tourist draws of Rügen and Usedom, the quiet island of Hiddensee with the grave of playwright Gerhart Hauptmann, and the historic universities of Greifswald and Rostock, among the oldest in the country. The state is also shaped by its industrial heritage, including its shipyards and the vast nuclear power plant at Lubmin, built in former East Germany and closed in 1995.

Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania is Germany's most sparsely populated federal state, with a population of just 1.57 million at the end of 2025. The unemployment rate in the structurally weak state stands at 8%, above the national average. At roughly 6%, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania also has by far the lowest share of foreign nationals of any of Germany's 16 federal states.

For many former East Germans, the state is associated with long summers spent at campsites and holiday resorts along the Baltic coast. It is also home to 16 national parks, more than any other federal state in Germany, and to the Mecklenburg Lake District, centered on Lake Müritz.

Yet this federal state was also the scene of some of the earliest violent attacks on asylum-seeker accommodations following German reunification. Images of burning housing blocks in Rostock-Lichtenhagen in August 1992 were broadcast around the world. That year, the number of asylum seekers in Germany reached a provisional peak of 440,000, fueling heated debates across the country.

In August of that year, hundreds of far-right rioters attacked a residential building in Rostock that housed around 100 people from Vietnam. The building was set on fire as some 3,000 local residents applauded the attackers. Miraculously, no one was killed, though many people were injured. It was the worst outbreak of racist violence in Germany since the Second World War.
Incumbency advantage may help Manuela Schwesig

Former Chancellor Angela Merkel had her electoral district in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. For around 28 years, the state has been governed by the Social Democratic Party (SPD) in coalition with various partners.

Most recently, it has been led by the popular state premier and former federal minister Manuela Schwesig. The 52-year-old heads a coalition with the socialist Left Party. Schwesig stands a good chance of ensuring that this remains the case after the election on September 20.

Schwesig, who for a long time trailed the far-right populist Alternative for Germany party (AfD) by a wide margin in the polls, has been campaigning on the slogan "The woman against blue" — a reference to the AfD's party color.

In a televised debate with AfD lead candidate Leif-Erik Holm just over ten days before the election, the state premier described the AfD as "the most dangerous party for our country, for the economy, for social welfare, and also for us women." Addressing Holm directly, she added: "You are talking the country down."
Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania is not an AfD stronghold
Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania is the only eastern German state where the domestic intelligence agency has not classified the AfD as "confirmed right-wing extremist."

The center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU), the party of Chancellor Friedrich Merz, is polling at a historic low, the lowest in any German state. A poor showing in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania could further fuel debate over the increasingly unpopular chancellor. The environmentalist Greens are also fighting to remain in the state parliament, with support hovering around the 5% threshold for representation.

With a vote distribution like this, it is highly unlikely that a majority could be assembled to elect AfD lead candidate Leif-Erik Holm as state premier. After all, every party with a realistic chance of entering the state parliament has ruled out any cooperation with the AfD.

The party's lead candidate, Leif-Erik Holm, deliberately cultivates a down-to-earth image. At campaign events, he draws on his experience as a radio host, including with the public broadcaster NDR. A member of the Bundestag for the Alternative for Germany (AfD) since 2017, he repeatedly taps into widespread dissatisfaction with the government, the economic slowdown, and the comparatively difficult social conditions in the structurally weak and sparsely populated northeast.

Holm cannot match the popular SPD state premier, Schwesig, in head-to-head comparisons of the leading candidates. But the AfD's support in the polls, neck and neck with the SPD, underscores just how deeply divided Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania remains.
Governing the coastal state is unlikely to become any easier in the years to come.
This article has been translated from German.
